title: OpenTac: An Open Ecosystem for Customizable, Scalable, and Transferable 3D Tactile Sensing
authors: Ariel Slepyan,Geeta Chandra Raju Bethala,Jiafeng Gu,Anagha Rajendra Dangle,Yinzhe Zhou,Hongyuan Fu,Jade Sim,Tuhin Basu,Xinyi Yin,Md Faizal Karim,Gregory Hager,Homanga Bharadhwaj,Anand Bhattad,Krishna Murthy Jatavallabhula,Nitish V. Thakor
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Signal Processing (eess.SP); Systems and Control (eess.SY)

introduction:
As robots expand to perform tasks in more general, varied, and dynamic environments, their ability to manipulate quickly, reliably, and safely will increasingly depend on directly sensing and reacting to contact—that is, on tactile sensing.

However, sensors must first be customized to fit the end-effector or surface of interest. As a result, research on the use of tactile sensing is fundamentally limited by customizability: researchers must either adapt their work to sensors manufactured in fixed geometries, or they must possess sufficient design and fabrication expertise to develop custom sensors in-house. These constraints are particularly limiting when instrumenting custom-designed robot geometries or larger, irregular surfaces.

In this paper, we focus on conformal tactile skins, as they integrate distributed sensing elements into thin, flexible surfaces that can be wrapped around robot geometries, enabling fully sensorized robot bodies. However, existing tactile skins, such as FlexiTac [1], provide only normal-force (1D) estimates and require manual redesign for each new geometry. We present a sensor design that can be easily customized to fit many robot geometries, scaled in sensing area or resolution, and used to estimate normal and shear forces (3D) over local groups of sensing elements.

Several efforts have partially addressed sensor customizability and made tactile skins more capable and accessible for the robot control and learning communities  [1, 2, 3].
AnySkin provides replaceable sensing surfaces but relies on a predefined electronic layout [2], while eFlesh automates the design of a deformable sensor body but relies on separately supplied magnetometer electronics [3]. In addition to the challenges of customizing the entire sensor, existing sensors are sampled at rates ranging between 30 and 100 Hz.
Such raster scanning-based acquisition can limit the ability to resolve and respond to contacts lasting only a few milliseconds. Beyond hardware, changes in sensor geometry must also be accommodated by the software used to acquire, simulate, and process tactile observations.

To address these limitations, we introduce OpenTac, an open sensor design environment and software ecosystem for customizable, scalable tactile sensing (Fig. ). OpenTac supports the design of low-cost piezoresistive tactile skins that estimate both local normal and shear forces with millimeter-scale spatial resolution over planar and developable surfaces. Our sensor combines a flexible printed circuit board and a piezoresistive film with a structured elastomeric overlay that redistributes lateral pressure across neighboring sensing elements, allowing local shear to be decoded while retaining normal-force information. The sensing layout, electrode geometry, and mechanical overlay can be customized to the surface geometry and force range of interest.

To support this degree of customizability, OpenTac includes a full-stack ecosystem of design, simulation, and interoperability tools. OpenTac-CAD is a design tool that automatically generates sensor fabrication files from a desired geometry. Users can provide a 2D outline, select a developable surface on a 3D robot model, or specify an abstract verbal description, such as “design a star-shaped sensor that fits inside a circle with a diameter 5 cm.”
In addition, OpenTac-CAD produces a machine-readable manifest file describing the sensor’s geometry, electrical addressing, and mechanical configuration.
OpenTac-Sim provides tools to simulate the sensors and sensor-object interactions for robot manipulation tasks across any sensor design described by the manifest file.
OpenTac-Transfer enables cross-sensor transfer by mapping calibrated tactile observations across sensor layouts using their physical coordinates and local surface frames. These components allow sensors with different shapes, resolutions, and electrical layouts to share acquisition and processing tools and provide a common interface for downstream control and learning.

Scaling tactile coverage also increases the number of measurements required to read the sensor. To address this, we also provide OpenTac-Xampling, an adaptive acquisition method
which operates across different sensor outlines using adaptive partial scans. For example, on a 32×3232\times 32 skin, adaptive acquisition of sparse contact events reaches 1286 Hz, more than a 19×\times increase over full-array scans (67 Hz) achieved by conventional acquisition [4].

We evaluate all components of the OpenTac ecosystem. We use OpenTac-CAD to generate fabrication files for more than 30 sensor layouts (including robot fingers, grippers, palms, and feet), fabricate the corresponding sensors, and deploy them on four real robot embodiments.
We further evaluate the 3D force estimates against a commercial force/torque sensor.
Finally, we demonstrate that our sensor’s normal and shear force estimates enable contact-rich feedback control and manipulation policy learning.

To summarize, our main contributions are:

OpenTac: a full-stack ecosystem for automated sensor design, fabrication, simulation, cross-sensor observation mapping, and kilohertz-rate adaptive acquisition.

A customizable tactile skin that estimates normal and shear forces using a simple, scalable construction.

Evaluations spanning over 30 fabricated layouts, sensor characterization, high-speed sensing, and real-world robot control and learning, demonstrating the utility of the resulting tactile observations for contact-rich manipulation.

All OpenTac hardware, software, and firmware is available under permissive licenses, enabling replication, modification, and redistribution for research and commercial use.

1. OpenTac: a full-stack ecosystem for automated sensor design, fabrication, simulation, cross-sensor observation mapping, and kilohertz-rate adaptive acquisition.

2. A customizable tactile skin that estimates normal and shear forces using a simple, scalable construction.

3. Evaluations spanning over 30 fabricated layouts, sensor characterization, high-speed sensing, and real-world robot control and learning, demonstrating the utility of the resulting tactile observations for contact-rich manipulation.

title: Extending Harmonic Function Methods via Root Locus for Coordinated Path Generation
authors: Matteo Frascarelli,Lucia Pallottino,Alberto Landi
comment: . Extended version of a paper submitted to Automatica. Corresponding code:this https URL
abstract: We consider the offline generation of coordinated paths for NN interchangeable robots and NN goals in planar environments with polygonal obstacles. After a conformal map to a circular domain, starts and goals become the poles and zeros of a rational function RR, and the paths are the branches of its Generalized Root Locus (GRL), i.e. the streamlines of the logarithmic potential −log⁡R-\log R. We show that, for every phase outside a finite set of critical phases and a set of boundary phases, the induced gradient motion drives each robot to a distinct goal along pairwise disjoint paths that never reach the obstacles; the robot–goal assignment is produced by the construction, and with the gain used as a clock all robots move as the closed-loop roots of the GRL and arrive together at a prescribed time. Obstacles become streamlines through successive Milne–Thomson reflections, and for a finite number of reflections a finite test certifies safety for the potential that is actually computed. Reciprocal root-locus planning is recovered as a special case. The method is illustrated on two polygonal workspaces, 100 random instances compared with independent harmonic planning and artificial potentials, and a scene with ten robots and ten obstacles.
introduction:
Coordinated motion of several robots in a cluttered environment is usually organized in two layers: an offline layer that builds feasible global paths, and an online layer that tracks them and handles finite size, actuation limits and close interactions. This paper is about the first layer. We consider NN interchangeable robots and NN goals in a planar workspace with polygonal obstacles, and look for smooth paths that are collision-free by construction; assigning robots to goals is part of the problem.

Potential-based methods encode the whole problem in a scalar field. The artificial potential field (APF) of Khatib [1] may have local minima; harmonic function methods (HFM) [2] remove them, since solutions of the Laplace equation have no interior extrema. Navigation functions [3] also exclude spurious minima, but need a map onto a sphere world, hard to build for polygonal scenes. For several robots, electrostatic analogies have been used without obstacles [4], and root-locus (RL) constructions have produced collision-free formations [5] and single-robot paths among diffusive hazards [6]. The reciprocal root locus (RRL) [7, 8] handles polygonal workspaces through a conformal map, but enforces obstacle avoidance by heuristic corrections, without a proof of non-penetration.

The Generalized Root Locus (GRL) bridges these lines of work. If starts and goals are the poles and zeros of a rational function RR, the GRL branches are the streamlines of the logarithmic potential −log⁡R-\log R [9]: integral curves of a harmonic field, as in HFM, with the branch structure of the root locus. The invariance of the stream function along the gradient motion keeps each robot on its branch, but does not say where the robots go, whether two paths can meet, or whether the obstacles are respected. This paper answers these questions:

Certified coordinated motion (Theorem 1). For every phase outside a finite set of critical phases and a set of boundary phases, the GRL in the workspace consists of exactly NN disjoint arcs, each joining a start to a different goal. The gradient motion converges along them, the robot–goal assignment is induced by the construction, and with the gain used as a clock the robots leave the starts together, move as the closed-loop roots of the GRL and arrive together at a prescribed time. The result holds on any bounded domain with obstacles.

Certificate for computed obstacle potentials (Proposition 3). Obstacles are made streamlines by successive Milne–Thomson reflections. For a finite reflection depth, the boundary residual bounds the set of excluded phases, and a finite test certifies obstacle safety for the potential that is actually computed.

RRL as a special case (Section 5.5). The RRL planner [7, 8] is recovered with the same guarantees, which supplies the boundary-invariance argument that was missing.

Algorithm and experiments (Sections 6 and 7): the complete procedure, with the critical set verified by the argument principle, evaluated on reference examples, in a Monte Carlo comparison with independent harmonic planning and artificial potentials, and on a scene with ten robots and ten obstacles.

Code and an interactive companion notebook are available online (see Code availability).

The gradient motion converges along them, the robot–goal assignment is induced by the construction, and with the gain used as a clock the robots leave the starts together, move as the closed-loop roots of the GRL and arrive together at a prescribed time. The result holds on any bounded domain with obstacles.

title: DiffDreamer: Coupling World Models with Differentiable Simulation for Agile Quadrotor Control
authors: Fanxing Li,Yuxiang Huang,Shengyang Wang,Fangyu Sun,Shuyu Wu,Tianbao Zhang,Dexin Zuo,Yan Yufei,Danping Zou,Wenxian Yu
abstract: Tasks such as quadrotor dynamic-gate racing require agents to anticipate external motion while maintaining precise high-frequency control. World-model-based reinforcement learning (RL) provides a natural solution by learning latent dynamics for future imagination, yet it often entangles environmental evolution and the robot’s own dynamics in a single learned rollout, where model bias can affect policy optimization efficiency. We propose DiffDreamer, a differentiable reinforcement learning framework that tightly couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for actor optimization. In one optimization step, the learned world model propagates latent states that capture external dynamics and history-dependent features, while the differentiable simulator propagates the robot’s explicit physical state. We further decompose the actor objective into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. Experiments on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing show that DiffDreamer improves training convergence over the model-free, model-based, and differentiable-RL baselines, and final performance over these baselines and classical planning and control methods. Additional experiments assess reward decomposition and the odometry-conditioned relative-state representation through ablations. We also provide proof-of-concept real-world flight experiments for validation.
introduction:
Many robotic tasks require agents to anticipate external environmental evolution to achieve precise control. This structure is particularly prominent in agile aerial robotics. A representative example is dynamic-gate racing with quadrotors [1, 2, 3], where the robot must predict the future motion of moving gates and generate accurate control commands to pass through narrow openings at high speed. Existing solutions [2] often address this challenge through modular pipelines that decouple prediction, planning, and control. Although such designs are interpretable and effective, they usually rely on task-specific engineering and optimize each module separately.

World-model-based reinforcement learning [4, 5] provides an integrated alternative. By learning compact latent dynamics from interaction, methods such as Dreamer [4] can imagine future trajectories and optimize policies in latent space. However, in agile robotic control, a learned world model often has to capture both the evolution of the external environment and the robot’s high-frequency rigid-body dynamics within the same learned rollout. This entangles two sources of dynamics with different structures: the external dynamics are partially observable and history-dependent, whereas the robot’s internal dynamics are often smooth and available through physical modeling. As a result, policy optimization through purely learned rollouts may suffer from model bias and less accurate gradients for precise physical control. This motivates using differentiable simulation for the robot’s physical motion, so that the learned world model can focus on latent external dynamics.

Differentiable reinforcement learning (DiffRL) [6, 7] offers a complementary direction. By backpropagating through a differentiable physical model, it can provide low-variance first-order gradients for policy optimization and be particularly effective for smooth robotic systems. However, differentiable RL alone typically assumes that the transition and reward structures are differentiable and explicitly available. This makes it difficult to handle partially observable external dynamics, moving targets with unknown future motion, and non-differentiable task events such as gate-crossing rewards.

To address this problem, we propose DiffDreamer, which structurally separates robot dynamics from external environment dynamics and couples their rollouts for policy optimization. DiffDreamer synchronizes latent world-model imagination with differentiable physical rollouts: under the same action, the world model updates an implicit state representing external time-varying features, while the simulator propagates the explicit robot state. The actor receives both states as input, and its objective is decomposed into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. We compare DiffDreamer with RL, trajectory planning, and model predictive control (MPC) baselines on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing, and demonstrate its effectiveness through transfer to real quadrotor flight.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose a dual-pathway policy optimization framework that synchronizes latent imagination with differentiable physical rollouts to improve optimization accuracy and reduce the burden of learning high-frequency robot dynamics within the world model.

We conduct comprehensive experiments on two quadrotor tasks with dynamic external environments to validate the advantages of the proposed method in terms of control accuracy and predictive capabilities.

We conduct ablation studies on reward decomposition and odometry-conditioned relative-state representation to assess their contributions.

We provide proof-of-concept validation of aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing in real-world scenarios.

1. We propose a dual-pathway policy optimization framework that synchronizes latent imagination with differentiable physical rollouts to improve optimization accuracy and reduce the burden of learning high-frequency robot dynamics within the world model.

2. We conduct comprehensive experiments on two quadrotor tasks with dynamic external environments to validate the advantages of the proposed method in terms of control accuracy and predictive capabilities.

3. We conduct ablation studies on reward decomposition and odometry-conditioned relative-state representation to assess their contributions.

4. We provide proof-of-concept validation of aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing in real-world scenarios.

title: Progress Probes $P^2$: Lightweight Runtime Monitoring for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Atiksh Bhardwaj,Edward W. Duan,Junwon Seo,Prithwish Dan,Wei-Chiu Ma,Andrea Bajscy,Preston Culbertson
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform diverse manipulation tasks directly from visual observations and natural language instructions, but they remain prone to mistakes and unpredictable failures. Deploying these policies without continuous human supervision will require robust runtime monitors that detect when the policy has gone off-course. Existing monitors use external foundation models, such as vision-language models (VLMs) to supervise the policy, introducing significant complexity and computational cost for monitoring at runtime. In this work, we investigate an alternate approach: can a VLA’s own internal activations provide the information needed to monitor its execution? Our method trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate progress, then flags executions that deviate from expected progress. In experiments with the open-source VLA π0.5\pi_{0.5} and across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, this approach is competitive with or outperforms VLM-based monitors in task failure detection, as well as methods which require failure data for training. These findings suggest that simple probes of VLA internals can be used to develop reliable runtime monitors, opening a path toward building policies that can act reliably and monitor their execution without external foundation models.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have made strong progress toward the goal of generalist, language-conditioned robot policies. Models such as π0.5\pi_{0.5} [1] and GR00T [2] can execute diverse, multi-stage manipulation tasks across a variety of tasks and embodiment and, especially after task-specific fine-tuning, can achieve relatively high mutli-task success rates. However, even well-trained policies still experience a wide variety of failure modes, (e.g., poor language grounding [3], deadlocks, and mistakes [4]) which are often sudden and difficult to predict.

A natural framework for addressing such failure modes during deployment is runtime monitoring: using an external verifier or monitor to detect when the policy’s execution is straying from typical/successful deployment.
Existing approaches obtain this monitoring signal from several sources. Sentinel [5] uses an external VLM, along with an action consistency heuristic, to judge when the policy is failing to make progress on a particular task. Generalist reward models, such as Robometer [6], learn to judge task progress from datasets of robot videos. Other methods instead use policy internals directly for failure detection. For example, SAFE [4] trains a failure classifier to predict rollout success directly from policy activations, while FIPER [7] combines an internal-based anomaly score and an uncertainty metric over actions to flag anomalous rollouts.

In this work, we investigate a different use of policy internals for runtime monitoring.

Specifically, we build on recent successes in mechanistic interpretability for VLAs [8, 9], which demonstrated that the activations of the VLM backbone contain easily-decodable representations of task-relevant features such as end-effector pose, object states, and task phase.
We hypothesize that a VLA’s internal activations may also encode task progress: how far the policy has progressed through a task. In successful executions, progress advances predictably over time (monotonically decreasing), while in suboptimal or failed executions, the progress probe falls behind the elapsed time. Furthermore, task progress can be learned entirely from successful executions and can be labeled without human supervision.

We study progress probes by training them on the π0.5\pi_{0.5} [1] VLA
using a dataset of success-only task executions. At deployment, runtime monitoring consists of taking the VLA’s internal activations (that are already computed as part of the forward pass of inference), passing them through the linear progress probe, and measuring the deviation between the current estimated task progress and the expected task progress computed from successful demonstrations. Not only does our probe-based monitor require only successful data for training, but it also runs between 5×5\times and 20,000×20,000\times faster than an external foundation-model monitor.

Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, we find that linear probes can indeed accurately predict task progress for demonstrations, and that they provide an effective signal for detecting unsuccessful policy rollouts. Our monitor achieves competitive or superior failure detection performance with both Robometer and SAFE baselines, while providing fast inference and requiring only successful demonstrations for training. This result indicates that even when VLAs fail to generate successful actions, their activations still retain information useful for detecting task progress and failure, which can be obtained using a simple linear readout. Specifically, our contributions are as follows:

We demonstrate empirically that linear probes trained over demonstration data can accurately decode task progress from π0.5′​s\pi_{0.5}^{\prime}s vision-language representations, across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.

We demonstrate empirically that linear probes trained over demonstration data can accurately decode task progress from π0.5′​s\pi_{0.5}^{\prime}s vision-language representations, across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.

We develop a minimalist progress-based runtime monitor which uses these probes to detect deviations from expected progress at runtime, without failure data or an external VLM.

We evaluate our monitor on 6 VLABench tasks and 6 real-world manipulation tasks, achieving AUROC scores of 0.788 and 0.78 respectively, matching or exceeding competitive baselines including SAFE and Robometer.

title: Humanoid Mobility via Attention-based Contacts
authors: Junzhe He,Kehan Wen,Chong Zhang,Clemens Schwarke,Zewei Zhang,Kaixian Qu,Siyuan Hu,Matthias Müller,Vladlen Koltun,Marco Hutter

abstract: Humanoid mobility over complex terrain requires accurate foot placement and coordinated whole-body motion capable of robust adaptation. Reinforcement learning (RL) policies trained without motion references generalize well across terrains, yet eliciting effective whole-body coordination through reward design and exploration alone remains challenging. In contrast, reference-based methods yield natural motions but struggle to adapt beyond the predefined trajectories in their training data. We introduce a learning framework that bridges these two approaches by using motion data strictly as a training prior. An explicit, self-supervised, attention-based contact planner predicts future body–environment contacts, while a contact-conditioned tracker translates these plans into coordinated whole-body motion. Together, they establish contact as an interface between sensory observations and control actions. This abstraction allows the policy to internalize the contact-aware structure of locomotion rather than directly replicating kinematics. Consequently, a single policy can exploit data-driven motion priors for natural whole-body coordination while retaining the flexibility to discover environment-dependent behaviors through reinforcement learning. Building on the learned contact planner and tracker, a subsequent fine-tuning stage bootstraps their acquired capabilities to explore environment variations beyond those covered by the original motion data. Operating entirely from onboard observations without any reference inputs at deployment, this framework enables versatile humanoid mobility in challenging environments.

title: Echo: Coupled Action and Task Status Signal Denoising for Vision Language Action Models
authors: Yufeng Liu,Bohao Fan,Juntu Zhao,Xinyi Wang,Hang Yu,Wenzhuan Luo,Yingzhi Wang,Qinghai Li,Yingdong Hu,Junliang Guo,Richard Wang,Dequan Wang,Yang Gao,Cheng Ma

abstract: Recognizing task completion and failure enables robots to stop upon success and initiate recovery or replanning after failure. Existing methods augment Vision Language Action (VLA) policies with task status signal prediction to support these execution decisions. However, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs. Moreover, the potential of task status signals to directly guide action generation remains underexplored. We present Echo, a framework that combines task status signal learning without frame-level progress annotations with a compact design for status prediction and action generation within a single VLA. Specifically, Echo represents task status with stop and failure signals, added as two dimensions of each action chunk and denoised together with robot actions. Their combination distinguishes ongoing execution, successful completion, and failure. To learn these signals without fine-grained progress annotations, Echo constructs successful, failed, and recovery trajectories with complementary supervision properties. To enable status signal-guided action generation, Echo controls interactions between the signals and actions and denoises the signals faster than the actions. These allow later action denoising steps to condition on cleaner status estimates while preserving accurate signal prediction. Extensive real-world manipulation experiments show that Echo accurately predicts task status and consistently improves policy performance.
introduction:
Vision Language Action (VLA) models have shown strong capabilities in robotic manipulation by mapping visual observations and language instructions to robot actions (Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026). Reliable execution also requires recognizing whether a task is ongoing, has succeeded, or has failed to determine when to continue, stop, or intervene. Existing methods predict progress, completion, or failure signals either within VLA policies or through external monitoring models (Apanasevich et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026).

However, existing approaches face two limitations. First, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained frame-level supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs (Pacaud et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026). Second, the predicted signals are typically used only for monitoring, leaving their potential to improve action generation underexplored (Pacaud et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026).

We present Echo, a compact framework that jointly denoises robot actions and task status signals within a single VLA, learning the signals without frame-level progress annotations and using them to improve action generation. Echo represents task status through a stop signal (SS), indicating whether execution should terminate, and a failure signal (FS), indicating whether execution is in a failure state. Low SS indicates ongoing execution, while high SS with low FS indicates successful completion, and high SS with high FS indicates terminal failure. Within ongoing execution, elevated FS indicates a recoverable failure, as shown in Figure 1. Echo appends SS and FS as two additional dimensions of each action chunk and denoises them together with robot actions. This formulation reuses the VLA’s visual, language, and robot-state features with little additional parameter overhead.

To learn these signals without frame-level progress annotations, Echo combines successful demonstrations, failed policy rollouts, pre-intervention failure segments, and recovery demonstrations using subtask-level prompts together with success or failure labels. Failed rollouts and pre-intervention failure segments supervise terminal and recoverable failures, respectively, while their actions are excluded from imitation. Recovery demonstrations pair similar status supervision with corrective actions at corresponding recoverable failure states, linking failure recognition to recovery behavior.

To use the learned status information during action generation, Echo controls interactions among SS, FS, and robot actions while preserving accurate and complementary signal predictions. It also introduces asynchronous denoising, denoising signal tokens faster than action tokens so that later action denoising steps condition on cleaner status estimates. When the policy recognizes a recoverable failure with low SS and elevated FS, these estimates, together with the current observations, can guide action generation toward corrective behavior learned from recovery demonstrations.

Experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate accurate task-status prediction and improved performance over action-only baselines, with larger out-of-distribution gains. Component ablations, signal interventions, and failure-data scaling analyses examine how status signals influence action generation and how different data sources contribute to prediction and execution.

Our contributions are threefold: 1) We introduce a compact task status representation that incorporates stop and failure signals into VLA action chunks with little additional parameter overhead. 2) We develop a supervision scheme that learns these signals from successful, failed, and recovery data without frame-level progress annotations. 3) We design controlled interactions and asynchronous denoising to couple status prediction with action generation.

title: Geometry-Dependent Properties of Physically Crosslinked PPy-PVA Hydrogels Enable Tunable Iontophoretic Drug Delivery
authors: Heather Jin Hee Kim,Mohsen Alishahi,Kyuin Park,Mikaila K. Roncevich,Larissa M. Shepherd,Cara M. Nunez
abstract:
Objective: Iontophoresis enables noninvasive transdermal drug delivery. The control of drug release, however, has largely relied on current modulation. Here, we explore geometry-driven factors, gel microstructure, and local electric fields, as alternative levers for regulating drug transport.
Methods:  To investigate iontophoretic drug delivery, we encapsulate bovine serum albumin (BSA) in polypyrrole-polyvinyl alcohol (PPy-PVA) hydrogels. Five distinct hydrogel geometries were fabricated to impose variation in pore architecture and electric field distribution, including Hilbert curve-based designs that use increased corner density to enhance local electric field strength. Using formulation studies, we determined the ideal PPy content, drug loading efficiency, and current density. Maximum field strength of individual hydrogel geometries was simulated via finite element analysis, and microstructures were characterized by scanning electron microscopy.  Lastly, we assessed differences in the transport metrics of the hydrogel geometries through an in vitro study using a Franz diffusion cell  and an artificial membrane. Results: The engineered geometries produced clearly differentiated microstructures and electric field strengths. Drug delivery studies demonstrated that iontophoresis substantially enhanced permeability compared with passive diffusion, with each geometry yielding  different profiles in cumulative release, flux, and permeability. Notably, the average iontophoretic permeability was  (3.80± 1.93)×10−5(3.80\,\pm\,1.93)\times 10^{-5}, exceeding values reported  in previous studies using artificial membranes. Conclusion: This study showed that the geometry-driven fabrication of drug-loaded hydrogel can achieve  different delivery characteristics in both iontophoretic and passive transport  using artificial membranes. Significance: Geometry-mediated control complements existing approaches for iontophoretic drug delivery without requiring individual current-density control.
introduction:
Transdermal drug delivery, the delivery of ionized drug molecules through the layers of the skin, has gained increased attention due to its minimally invasive administration, potential for reduced skin side effects, and improved patient adherence to treatment [1]. The primary challenge of transdermal drug delivery is penetrating the stratum corneum, the outermost layer of the epidermis. This layer is composed of keratinized corneocytes embedded in a dense lipid matrix and serves as a formidable barrier to most therapeutic molecules [2, 3]. For large drug molecules or other peptide-based therapeutics, the stratum corneum significantly hinders passive delivery.

Our work focuses on iontophoresis, which applies a mild constant or pulsed current to drive ionized drug molecules across the skin via an imposed electric field [4] (Fig. 1). The required current density varies depending on the delivery medium and the study context (e.g., in vitro or in vivo), and has been reported in the literature to range from as low as 5 μ​A​cm−2\mu\mathrm{A\,cm^{-2}} to as high as 3 mA cm-2 [5]. A typical iontophoretic drug delivery system consists of a power source, a pair of electrodes serving as the anode and cathode, and a drug reservoir, which is typically a gel or solution containing the active drug placed against the skin.
Upon generation of an electric field from the applied current, charged drug molecules are repelled from the electrode of like charge and driven through the stratum corneum. The kinetics of iontophoretic delivery follow the Nernst-Planck equation [6], where the flux is governed by both electrochemical gradients and electric field strength.  Particularly, chemically or physically crosslinked hydrogel-based iontophoresis has been successfully employed to deliver a wide range of therapeutics [7], including bovine serum albumin (BSA) [8, 9], lidocaine [10], insulin [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 5], and vaccines [16].
Iontophoretic delivery using gels enables fine control over release kinetics by tuning parameters such as current density, waveform, and pulsing schemes [17].
While this approach offers substantial flexibility, most strategies for controlled release have focused on modulating electrical input, whereas alternative routes, such as tailoring the gel’s permeability or structural properties, remain comparatively underexplored.  To further expand the controllability of drug release, this work is motivated by the freeze-thaw process of physically crosslinked hydrogels, where gel properties are highly sensitive to geometry due to mold-induced mechanical stress. We hypothesize that mold-induced hydrogel geometry can act as an indirect mediator that modulates key transport-relevant properties of drug-loaded hydrogels, namely their porous microstructure and local electric field strength, both of which appear in the governing equations for iontophoretic transport.

In this work, we conduct an in vitro study to investigate how hydrogel geometry serves as an indirect modulator of drug release behavior by influencing both microstructure and electric field strength during freeze-thaw-induced physical crosslinking. Using bovine serum albumin (BSA) as a model drug, we investigate how geometry-driven variations in the gel affect (1) microstructure and (2) electric field distribution, and how these factors collectively govern drug release. To this end, we design five distinct hydrogel geometries using mold-defined templates with varied shapes (but consistent area) to generate a range of electric field intensities. Because freeze-thaw processing inherently couples geometry with microstructural evolution, each geometry produces a unique microstructure arising from mechanical stresses experienced during crosslinking within the mold (Section I-B4). The gel was formulated using a one-factor-at-a-time process across all geometries (Section III-B3). We then conducted a drug delivery study to assess whether transport parameters differ across gel geometries (Section II-F). In Section III-D, we present results, which show that geometry-mediated variations in pore structure and electric-field localization influence iontophoretic transport outcomes.

The governing equations for iontophoresis are the Poisson-Nernst-Planck (PNP) equations, which couple ionic transport and electrostatics.
The Nernst-Planck equation describes the flux, JiJ_{i}, of species ii as the combined result of (1) diffusion due to a concentration gradient (−Di∇ci-D_{i}\nabla c_{i}), (2) electromigration under an electric potential gradient (zi​Di​FR​Tci∇ϕ\frac{z_{i}D_{i}F}{RT}\,c_{i}\nabla\phi), and (3) convection driven by the fluid velocity (ci​𝐯c_{i}\mathbf{v}) (Eq.1). In this expression, DiD_{i} is the diffusion coefficient of species ii, ∇ci\nabla c_{i} the gradient of the concentration of species ii, ziz_{i} is the valence of species ii, FF is Faraday’s constant, RR is the universal gas constant, TT is the absolute temperature, ∇ϕ\nabla\phi is the electric potential gradient, and 𝐯\mathbf{v} is bulk fluid velocity vector.

Complementing this, the Poisson equation (Eq. 2) expresses Gauss’s law in differential form (Eq. 3) by relating the divergence of the electric displacement field to the local charge density, where ϕ\phi is the electric potential, ε\varepsilon is the permittivity of the medium, and ρ\rho is the charge density. Together, the equations couple ionic motion with the resulting electric field. Poisson’s law determines the electric field from charge distribution, while the Nernst-Planck equation describes how ions respond to that field.

For a planar surface, Gauss’s law (Eq. 4) gives the relation between the electric field, EE, and surface charge density, σ\sigma, as:

where εn\varepsilon_{n} is the normal component of the permittivity at the surface.

Optimization of an electrode’s electric field strength is critical across a range of applications, including electroadhesion [18] and field-responsive gas sensor systems [19]. In these prior works, electrodes were deliberately engineered with regions of high charge density, such as sharp corners, edges, or areas of pronounced curvature, to generate locally intensified electric fields, thereby enhancing electroadhesive forces and improving sensor sensitivity. Following Gauss’s law (Eq. 4), electric-field lines converge and emerge perpendicularly from these geometrical features, resulting in pronounced field amplification near tips and edges. Such localized field enhancement is expected to play a similarly important role in influencing iontophoretic drug transport.

To exploit this electrostatic phenomenon, we employ parametrically generated Hilbert-Piano curves in our electrode geometries. Hilbert-Piano curves are a class of space-filling fractal curves characterized by recursive geometric complexity (Supplementary Fig. S1).
Hilbert-Piano curves generate a large number of corners and sharp angles, which can be harnessed to concentrate electric fields and amplify local field intensity in electrode designs [19, 18].

Hydrogels play a central role in iontophoretic drug delivery systems, however, the hydrogel itself must be ionically conductive. Therefore, among the available materials that enable this, we use conductive polypyrrole (PPy) as it stands out not only for its intrinsic electronic conductivity, but also its chemical stability, environmental robustness, and biocompatibility [20, 21, 22]. When doped, PPy supports mobile charge carriers along its conjugated backbone, making it especially attractive for electroactive drug-delivery platforms. Blending PPy with polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) yields a composite hydrogel that is both mechanically resilient and ionically conductive, an ideal environment for loading macromolecules such as bovine serum albumin (BSA).

BSA is a globular protein consisting of 583 amino acids with a molecular weight of approximately 66.5 kDa [23]. BSA is frequently employed as a model macromolecular drug in transdermal and nanoparticle-based delivery studies, where it often serves as a surrogate for other large therapeutic proteins, such as insulin [24, 25]. Because BSA shares structural and functional similarities with human serum albumin, it enables its use in pharmacokinetic modeling and drug-protein interaction research without the cost or ethical concerns associated with human-derived materials [26]. Furthermore, BSA-based nanocarriers are among the most widely investigated drug delivery platforms due to their stability, solubility, and efficient uptake into tissues [27].

The freeze-thaw (F/T) technique is one of the most widely used physical crosslinking methods and is particularly attractive because it generates porous networks without chemical crosslinkers [28]. In this process, a precursor polymer solution is subjected to repeated cycles of F/T. These physically crosslinked regions persist upon thawing, producing a stable, semi-crystalline network [29].  During freezing, ice formation induces volumetric expansion, so gels confined in rigid molds develop significant internal stresses as the phase change progresses. In F/T hydrogels, ice crystallization and melting act as a porogen, with fluid-matrix interactions and volume changes reshaping pore size, connectivity, and network morphology. Under rigid confinement and consistent F/T conditions, these stresses and local expansions strongly govern pore nucleation, alignment, and evolution within the gel network [30]. The role of mold-induced geometric confinement in shaping microstructure, permeability, and drug delivery performance remains underexplored relative to other F/T parameters [31].

title: Dispersive Tree Agreements for Multi-Robot Coordination
authors: Shashank A. Deshpande,Blake T. Edwards,Jonathan P. How
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics
abstract:
Multi-robot coordination of nonlinear systems is naturally
formulated as joint-space optimal control subject to constraints
over groups of robots. Existing methods that approach joint
optimality remain largely centralized, offline, and confined to
collision-free motion planning, while decentralized, real-time
counterparts target safe navigation without pursuing the joint
optimum. This paper develops a decentralized, real-time planner
that approaches the joint optimum as an anytime process. We extend
a recent single-robot framework that searches dispersive trees of
forward-propagated commands for differentially flat systems to
coordinate a multi-robot team near-optimally. We first show that the inter-robot coupling can be effectively
replaced by some local constraints, under which locally grown
dispersive trees contain a near-optimal agreement. It is this
structure that the robots pursue by decentralized column
generation, negotiating rents on the shared space that guide the
search of each robot’s tree. The negotiation settles on an agreement
whose near-optimality is certified at quiescence. Our
protocol, WarpWeaver, implements this negotiation as an
asynchronous real-time loop over a receding horizon, and
demonstrates effective closure to quiesced agreements even when
real-time deadlines cut the negotiation short. In
simulation, WarpWeaver reduces total travel time by up to 22%22\%
against centralized offline planners on the Dynobench suite and by up to 37%37\% against a
decentralized real-time baseline, and nearly doubles the success
rate of a task-specific planner on graph connectivity. Hardware
experiments on six robots planning onboard demonstrate real-world
implementability.
introduction:
This paper addresses the coordination of a team of robots with
differentially flat nonlinear dynamics, formulated as optimal control in the joint
space of the team subject to constraints over groups of robots.
We seek control inputs
whose cost lies near the joint optimum, via
distributed computation across the robots in real time, to
maintain robustness to changes in the individual objectives of
the robots as well as in the dynamics of the environment. Existing approaches to this problem
divide broadly into centralized, offline planners with
guarantees of asymptotic optimality, and real-time decentralized
planners that work with simplified dynamics, without pursuing
the joint optimum.

A range of centralized planners derive from multi-agent path
finding [1] and handle pairwise conflicts in a
high-level search on top of low-level single-robot planners
running model predictive control [2],
sampling-based planning [3], or search over
graphs of discontinuity-bounded motion primitives
[4, 5, 6].
Sampling-based planners search the composite configuration
space of the team [7, 8]. These planners provide
asymptotic guarantees of completeness or optimality, and focus
on motion planning with pairwise separation.

Decentralized planning, on the other hand, comes with real-time
advantages such as robustness to changes in the individual
objectives or in the environment. Decentralized trajectory
optimization involves
high-frequency replanning of safe splines around the incumbents
communicated by peer robots, while often simplifying the
robots’ dynamics [9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]. Consensus-based
distributed optimization instead lets the robots negotiate, with
gradient-based local optimization driven by penalties on
mutual disagreement [15, 16].
Coordination across these methods, however, often settles in
local optima,
without pursuing the joint optimum.

In summary, real-time multi-robot coordination deals with multiple
sources of complexity. First, planning and control at the level
of a single robot must respect the nonlinear dynamics of its
control system. In addition, these
control trajectories must coordinate to satisfy various
constraints over groups of robots while evading the many local
minima of the joint problem.
Finally, the algorithm that addresses these challenges must
decentralize across the robots under limited communication and
maintain robustness to communication delays within the team.
While existing approaches handle this complexity in part, this
paper develops a decentralized framework that tackles each of its
sources in unison.

We employ dispersive forward tree search [17],
which finds near-optimal control inputs for differentially flat
systems, for single-robot planning and control. To solve coordination, we first show that the coupling among the
robots can be absorbed into suitable constraints on each robot
alone, so that tractably sized dispersive trees grown locally by the
robots jointly contain a near-optimal agreement. It is this structure that the
remainder of our development pursues. We formulate the selection of this
joint agreement as an integer linear program and approach its
solution by column generation
[18, 19], in which the
dual of its linear relaxation sets rents on the shared space.
Under these rents, the search for a new column becomes a
single-robot problem that each robot solves near-optimally with
its own dispersive forward tree.
Notably, this column generation procedure is effectively
decentralized, to distribute the computational load of the
process across the robots while limiting communication within
the team to a manageable amount. We show that the resulting process implements an
anytime negotiation whose agreement is certified near-optimal
once it reaches quiescence, up to the resolution of the search and a gap that the agents compute online. This development culminates in
WarpWeaver, the real-time multi-robot planner that we propose,
which runs the negotiation asynchronously across the team over a
receding horizon and remains robust to bounded communication
delays. Our experiments thereby demonstrate that this negotiation,
driven by decentralized column generation, is a pattern well
suited to real-time multi-robot coordination, as the
agreements that it commits within real-time deadlines come close in
cost to those that it reaches when given time to quiesce.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions.

∙\bullet Joint optimal control as distributed
dispersive forward search. We cast a broad class of multi-robot
coordination problems as joint-space optimal control of
differentially flat nonlinear systems, and prove that suitably constrained, locally grown
dispersive forward trees contain a near-optimal agreement
(Proposition 1).

∙\bullet Decentralized column generation. We
pursue this structure by decentralized column generation under
limited communication, in which rents on the shared space guide the
tree search of each robot, and prove that the negotiated agreement
is certified near-optimal at quiescence, relative to the joint
solutions robust at the search resolution
(Propositions 4 and 2).

∙\bullet Real-time protocol. We develop
WarpWeaver, an asynchronous protocol that runs decentralized
column generation over a receding horizon onboard each robot, to
coordinate the team in real time under bounded communication
delays, whose agreements within real-time deadlines come
close in cost to quiesced ones.

∙\bullet Evaluation and hardware
experiments. We benchmark WarpWeaver in simulation against
centralized offline, decentralized real-time, and task-specific
planners. It reduces total travel time by up to 22%22\% against
centralized offline planners on Dynobench and by up to 37%37\% against
a decentralized real-time baseline. Further, on a graph connectivity
task, it nearly doubles the success rate of a task-specific planner. We further deploy it on a team of six robots, each planning
onboard in real time.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section II reviews related work. Section III
formulates the joint optimal control problem and its flat
reformulation, and Section IV reviews dispersive forward
tree search. Section V develops the decentralized
column generation scheme, its near-optimality certificate, and the
WarpWeaver protocol. Section VI presents the simulation
experiments and benchmarks, and Section VII the real-robot
experiments. We conclude in Section VIII. The proofs are
deferred to Appendix A.

title: SCOPE: Scene-graph Construction Optimized by Plan Error-correction for Robot Long-term Planning Datasets
authors: Chaoyue Li,Zeyu Gao,Yanfeng Lu,Fan Luo
comment: . Accepted at IROS 2026. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) stands as a fundamental challenge in robotics, essential for enabling autonomous agents to execute complex, long-horizon tasks in diverse environments. While Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce a new paradigm for TAMP by leveraging extensive common sense, their inherent reasoning limitations hinder direct application, and fine-tuning strategies to enhance these capabilities are currently bottlenecked by the scarcity of high-quality datasets. Existing automated generation methods often suffer from homogeneity, limiting model generalization, and unsolvability, where hallucinated scene graphs create physical mismatches with task goals. To address these issues, we propose Scene-graph Construction Optimized by Plan Error-correction (SCOPE), an automated framework designed to generate diverse and executable TAMP datasets. SCOPE incorporates multi-level diversity metrics to maximize the information entropy of scenarios. Crucially, it introduces a Plan Feedback Error-correction pipeline that utilizes planner execution failures as feedback signals to retroactively rectify logical inconsistencies in scene graphs, ensuring physical feasibility. Experimental results demonstrate that SCOPE exhibits greater robustness to erroneous scene graphs and generates higher-quality data. When utilized for LLM fine-tuning, SCOPE-generated data yield a downstream TAMP model that achieves an absolute 12.33% gain in success rate over its counterpart fine-tuned with data generated by DELTA, a state-of-the-art PDDL-based planner.
More demos and information are available on https://scope-page.github.io/.
introduction:
Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) stands as a fundamental challenge in the field of robotics. Traditional approaches [1, 2, 3] rely primarily on rule-based designs and heuristic searches. However, these methods often lack sufficient generalization capabilities. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) [4, 5] has introduced a new paradigm [6, 7] for addressing TAMP challenges. By leveraging their extensive common sense knowledge, LLMs demonstrate significant potential in handling complex TAMP tasks in different scenarios, enhancing the universality of planning systems.

Current methods utilizing LLMs for TAMP can be broadly categorized into Symbolic Planning and Direct Planning. Symbolic Planning [8, 9, 10] employs the LLM as a translator that decomposes tasks based on hand-crafted rules to generate problem definitions for traditional planners. While this approach achieves a relatively high success rate, it relies heavily on manually defined domains and rules. Consequently, this paradigm exhibits limited error tolerance, making full automation difficult. Conversely, the Direct Planning methods [6, 11, 12] utilize the LLM directly as a planner. These methods exploit the common sense reasoning capabilities of the model and require minimal manual prior constraints, allowing users to accomplish a wide range of tasks through natural language. Nevertheless, the success rate of this approach is often limited by the inherent shortcomings of LLMs in temporal reasoning and their tendency towards hallucination. Ultimately, the performance of both paradigms is intrinsically constrained by the underlying planning capabilities of the LLMs.

Therefore, fine-tuning LLMs with extensive data serves as an effective strategy [13, 14] to internalize planning logic and enhance temporal reasoning capabilities. A standard TAMP fine-tuning sample consists of three core elements: the scene graph describing the environmental state, the instruction defining the task goal, and the plan serving as the solution path. However, constructing TAMP datasets currently requires balancing data quality and annotation cost. Manually annotated datasets [15] offer high quality yet incur prohibitive costs, making them difficult to scale for fine-tuning needs. While data constructed using LLMs [16] offers a low-cost automated alternative, it often suffers from low quality.

This deficiency primarily manifests in two aspects. First, the generated content suffers from a lack of diversity. Due to the preference of LLMs, the scene graphs often exhibit high repetitiveness, resulting in insufficient information entropy within the dataset and limiting the generalization ability of the model. Second, the generated tasks frequently suffer from unsolvability because of the wrong scene graphs. Influenced by hallucinations, automatically generated scene graphs often contain logical flaws, such as missing key interactive objects or incorrect attributes. This mismatch between the environment and the task renders the generated problems physically unsolvable, thereby introducing a significant amount of noise into the training data.

To address these challenges, we propose Scene-graph Construction Optimized by Plan Error-correction (SCOPE), an automated generation framework designed specifically for constructing high-quality TAMP datasets. To mitigate the homogeneity inherent in LLM-generated content, SCOPE incorporates multi-level Diversity Metrics during the Scene Graph Construction phases. Specifically, we monitor Global Diversity to ensure a broad coverage of task types while leveraging Local Diversity to enrich fine-grained variations in object attributes and spatial relationships, thereby maximizing the information entropy of the dataset. Second, to tackle the prevalent issue of unsolvability in automatically generated data, SCOPE introduces a Plan Feedback Error-correction pipeline. This pipeline establishes a closed-loop system for generation and verification, where execution results from the planner serve as feedback signals. This process allows the system to retroactively identify and correct logical inconsistencies within the scene graph while iteratively generating feasible planning sequences, effectively solving mismatches between the environment and the task.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose SCOPE, an automated data generation framework that integrates diversity-aware generation and Plan Feedback Error-correction. By maximizing data diversity and iteratively rectifying logical inconsistencies through execution feedback, SCOPE effectively constructs highly diverse and physically executable TAMP datasets with high quality.

We investigate the impact of data quality on the end-to-end planning performance of fine-tuned LLMs through extensive experiments, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Validated in the AI2-THOR environment, our results demonstrate that the high-quality data generated by SCOPE significantly improves the planning success rate, achieving an absolute 12.33% gain over data generated by DELTA.

1. We propose SCOPE, an automated data generation framework that integrates diversity-aware generation and Plan Feedback Error-correction. By maximizing data diversity and iteratively rectifying logical inconsistencies through execution feedback, SCOPE effectively constructs highly diverse and physically executable TAMP datasets with high quality.

2. We investigate the impact of data quality on the end-to-end planning performance of fine-tuned LLMs through extensive experiments, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Validated in the AI2-THOR environment, our results demonstrate that the high-quality data generated by SCOPE significantly improves the planning success rate, achieving an absolute 12.33% gain over data generated by DELTA.

title: Point-Level Refinable Semantic Mapping for Spatial Understanding
authors: Taimeng Fu,Yi Du,Zitong Zhan,Qiwei Du,Shaoshu Su,Zhipeng Zhao,Chen Wang
abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for long-horizon robot autonomy, enabling robots to reason about objects, their spatial relationships, and past observations across time. However, existing object-centric semantic maps are primarily designed for static environments and rely on an append-only point integration strategy, where newly observed points are accumulated but previously integrated points are rarely reevaluated. Consequently, perception errors accumulate over time, and outdated points persist after objects move or disappear. Although recent dynamic mapping methods update object-level representations in changing scenes, they do not explicitly revise noisy or obsolete points within each object. We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object representations through probabilistic point-level confidence updating. Each object point maintains a confidence score that is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: consistent observations reinforce reliable points, while inconsistent segmentation masks, depth measurements, and visibility cues suppress spurious and outdated points. Combined with object tracking and re-identification to preserve instance identities under motion and relocation, our framework enables object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated. Experiments demonstrate improved mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet, show robustness in dynamic environments and under perception noise, and provide an effective spatial memory for object navigation and embodied question-answering with success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.
introduction:
Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for robot autonomy [1] by grounding open-ended semantic concepts in 3D space [2]. They enable robots to localize task-relevant objects, reason about object relationships, and maintain persistent spatial context for embodied tasks, e.g., vision-language navigation [3] and mobile manipulation [4].

Recent open-vocabulary mapping systems [5, 6, 7] construct object-centric 3D semantic maps by integrating RGB-D observations with open-vocabulary perception models. However, real-world robotic deployment requires long-term operation in dynamic environments, where objects are frequently moved, removed, or rearranged. Existing methods are largely designed for static scenes and rely on an append-only point integration strategy: newly observed points are continuously added to object instances, while previously integrated points are rarely revisited or revised.

Several recent methods have extended semantic mapping to dynamic environments by detecting object changes and updating object-level map representations [8, 9, 10]. For example, Khronos [8] identifies changed objects through depth consistency, while OpenIN [9] and DualMap [10] associate movable objects with supporting anchors to maintain object identities. However, these approaches primarily reason about scene changes at the object or relation level, without explicitly revising noisy or outdated points within each object instance. As a result, local artifacts introduced by perception errors or stale observations can remain embedded in the object representation, degrading long-term mapping quality.

To address both dynamic environments and noisy perception, we propose an online refinable open-vocabulary semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object-centric maps over time. The key idea is to maintain a probabilistic confidence estimate for every object point, rather than treating integrated points as permanent entries. Each confidence score is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: points consistently supported by new observations are reinforced, while those inconsistent with segmentation masks, depth measurements, or visibility cues are progressively down-weighted and eventually removed. This enables semantic maps to preserve reliable geometry while eliminating perception artifacts and outdated points caused by object motion. To maintain consistent object identities, the framework further combines 2D tracking for in-view motion with feature-based re-identification after objects leave and re-enter the field of view, as shown in Fig. 1.

To evaluate its effectiveness as an online spatial memory for autonomous robots, we integrate the proposed semantic mapping framework into a vision-language navigation (VLN) framework [11] and evaluate it on object navigation and embodied question answering tasks in real-world environments.
The main contributions of this work are:

We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework with point-level confidence updating, enabling object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated.

We introduce a multi-view temporal update mechanism that reinforces reliable object points while suppressing spurious and outdated points caused by perception errors and object motion, improving mapping accuracy and robustness in dynamic environments.

We integrate object tracking and feature-based re-identification to preserve consistent object identities under motion and demonstrate the proposed map as an effective online spatial memory for vision-language navigation and embodied question answering.

1. We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework with point-level confidence updating, enabling object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated.

2. We introduce a multi-view temporal update mechanism that reinforces reliable object points while suppressing spurious and outdated points caused by perception errors and object motion, improving mapping accuracy and robustness in dynamic environments.

3. We integrate object tracking and feature-based re-identification to preserve consistent object identities under motion and demonstrate the proposed map as an effective online spatial memory for vision-language navigation and embodied question answering.

title: Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models
authors: Qi Lv,Jiayi Lin,Yuxin Jiang,Jianzong Wang,Xiang Deng,Mike Shou Zheng
comment: Project Page:this https URL
abstract:
Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions.
Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions.
However, reconstruction-driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls.
We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling.
SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics.
Cross-modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction.
The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future-derived residual information.
A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions.
At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions.
On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo.
Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts.
Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.
introduction:
Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions, supporting policy evaluation and model-based planning (Yang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024).
Accurate simulation requires modeling robot motion and resulting scene changes.
Latent action models encode visual transitions as proxy actions (Bruce et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025), allowing world models to learn dynamics from large-scale videos without explicit action annotations (Gao et al., 2026).
These latent actions are learned through future-observation reconstruction, with the current observation providing visual context (Gao et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2026).
For action-conditioned simulation, inferred latent actions serve as supervision for mapping robot controls into the learned latent action space.

Learning this mapping is challenging since reconstruction objectives encourage latent actions to encode robot motion together with object responses and other scene changes (Nikulin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025).
For example, similar end-effector motions may produce different object responses under different contact states (Gu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026), introducing scene-dependent variation beyond robot motion into the adaptation target.
These interaction outcomes are useful for world modeling, since accurate simulation requires predicting how robot motion affects the surrounding scene.
This motivates a dedicated kinematic component for action adaptation, together with a residual component retaining complementary transition information for dynamics learning.

To this end, we propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling.
Robot skeletons describe robot configuration and motion while abstracting scene appearance.
Related robot world models use skeleton sequences or kinematic renderings as direct conditioning signals for generation (Wang et al., 2025b; Wu and Gao, 2026; Xu et al., 2026).
SkeLAM uses paired RGB and skeleton transitions to learn kinematic and residual components from RGB observations.
Skeleton supervision grounds the kinematic latent in robot motion, while the residual latent supplies complementary information for RGB reconstruction.
Together, the two components jointly support reconstruction, providing a dedicated target for action adaptation while retaining information for dynamics learning.
During representation learning, skeletons supervise the RGB latents, while the deployed interface uses RGB observations and robot actions.

We further introduce cross-modal swap reconstruction, which replaces the RGB kinematic latent with its paired skeleton counterpart while retaining the RGB residual.
Reconstructing the same transition under this substitution encourages compatible motion conditioning in the RGB decoder, extending cross-modal correspondence beyond alignment in latent space.
The world model learns from both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout prepares it for the zero-residual condition used at deployment.
A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions.
At inference, generation uses the current observation and robot actions.

To assess motion accuracy and visual fidelity, we evaluate SkeLAM on DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024).
Compared with DreamDojo, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1%.
Motion probing shows that the kinematic component approaches the performance of the concatenated representation with half the latent dimensions, while latent interventions and component ablations support its role in generation.
Qualitative results further demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts.
Open-loop policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model that separates the conditioning roles of robot motion and complementary visual dynamics, providing a dedicated kinematic target for robot action adaptation.

We introduce cross-modal swap reconstruction to encourage compatible RGB and skeleton motion conditioning during generation.
Combined with branch dropout, this design supports robot action conditioning through the
kinematic pathway learned from visual transitions.

Experiments on DROID demonstrate gains in motion accuracy and visual fidelity, supported by representation analyses and component ablations.
We further show zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer and agreement between predicted and measured policy success rates.

1. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model that separates the conditioning roles of robot motion and complementary visual dynamics, providing a dedicated kinematic target for robot action adaptation.

2. We introduce cross-modal swap reconstruction to encourage compatible RGB and skeleton motion conditioning during generation.
Combined with branch dropout, this design supports robot action conditioning through the
kinematic pathway learned from visual transitions.

3. Experiments on DROID demonstrate gains in motion accuracy and visual fidelity, supported by representation analyses and component ablations.
We further show zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer and agreement between predicted and measured policy success rates.

title: VecTile: A Low-Cost Flexible Tactile Array for 3-DoF Force Sensing
authors: Jian Hou,Xin Zhou,Adam J. Spiers
comment: . Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027
abstract:
Tactile sensing provides robots with contact information difficult to obtain from vision alone.
Shear force is particularly important for understanding tangential contact, guiding corrective motions, and maintaining grasp stability, yet flexible and low-cost tactile arrays often measure only normal force.
We introduce VecTile, a low-cost, 6 mm thin, flexible tactile array capable of three-axis force sensing.
VecTile combines a piezoresistive layer with passive silicone nubs that convert normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns.
The sensor can be fabricated in-house without specialized equipment. The complete system costs less than 35 USD for a 4×\times4 array.
We validate the sensing mechanism through finite element analysis and hardware experiments.
In controlled single-taxel tests over 1–5 N normal force and up to 1.5 N shear force, VecTile achieves root-mean-square errors of 0.39 N and 0.16 N for normal and shear forces.
A VecTile calibrated while flat retains accuracy when curved, while a five-minute manual calibration is sufficient for practical use.
Two applications demonstrate its utility. First, shear readings are sensitive enough to stop a sharp scalpel from puncturing a balloon after contact. Second, the sensor substantially improves Diffusion Policy-guided power-plug insertion. All designs and code will be released upon paper acceptance. Project website: https://jiannnh.github.io/VecTile/.
introduction:
Tactile sensing gives robots a sense of touch during manipulation. It reveals force, friction, stiffness, and other properties that are difficult to infer from vision alone [1, 2]. This information is particularly important for grasp-stability estimation [3, 4], object recognition [5, 6], and in-hand manipulation [7, 8, 9].

During manipulation, the normal-force component captures only part of the contact state. While the shear components reveal the direction and magnitude of tangential loading, supporting grasp-stability assessment, friction and slip reasoning, and contact regulation [10, 11]. Flexibility is also important because conformable tactile skins can cover non-planar and adaptive surfaces, including rounded fingers and soft grippers [12, 13]. Because direct contact exposes tactile sensors to wear and damage, low cost and repairability are important for practical deployment [14, 15].

These considerations motivate tactile skins that combine 3-degree-of-freedom (DoF) force sensing, flexibility, and low cost. Existing tactile architectures, however, trade among these properties due to fabrication and integration complexities [2]: Vision-based [11, 16, 17] and magnetic-based [10, 15] sensors can recover rich multi-axis contact information but are rigid, while thin capacitive [12] and piezoresistive [13] arrays more readily conform to curved surfaces yet do not provide shear force information. An easily accessible flexible tactile array providing local 3-DoF force measurements therefore remains underexplored.

We introduce VecTile (Fig. 1), named as such due to its capability of reading a 3-DoF force vector at each tactile pixel (taxel). VecTile is a low-cost, flexible, 6​mm6~\mathrm{mm}-thin, 4×44\times 4 tactile array (16 local 3-DoF taxels at a 10​mm10~\mathrm{mm} pitch) that combines a piezoresistive array with passive silicone nubs.

The complete sensor and readout board cost less than 35 USD (of which 25 USD is spent on an Arduino Nano that can be replaced with a lower-cost microcontroller and ADC circuit if needed). Raw frames stream at 343 Hz, and the measured end-to-end latency relative to a commercial force/torque (F/T) reference is approximately 25​ms25~\mathrm{ms}. Most conveniently, this sensor can be easily produced in-house without the need for expensive equipment or tools. At its core is a combination of a standard flexible PCB (FPC), whose fabrication can be out-sourced at low cost (we used JLCPCB’s services) and silicone parts that can be easily produced via 3D printed molds (we used PLA molds from a Bambu Lab P1S) and hobby-grade vacuum chamber (less than 150 USD).

After Section II outlining related work, Section III details the electronic design, the nub-based transduction mechanism validated via finite element analysis, as well as the fabrication process.
Section IV experimentally evaluates various nub heights and quantifies their force-reconstruction accuracy on physical sensors, resulting in a design with 0.39​N0.39~\mathrm{N} normal RMSE and 0.16​N0.16~\mathrm{N} shear RMSE with a range of 11–5​N5~\mathrm{N} normal force and up to 1.5​N1.5~\mathrm{N} shear per taxel.
We further assess performance differences between flat, convex, and concave configurations and demonstrate a practical calibration process through short manual interactions against an F/T reference.

Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of VecTile on compliant gripper fingers in two downstream tasks (Section V). In the scalpel–balloon interaction, we show that the sensor’s shear force sensitivity allows a sharp scalpel to push against a fully blown balloon without rupturing it. A visuotactile plug-insertion task (Fig. 1) shows the sensor’s practicality via a learned manipulation policy under partially visual occlusion.
