title: A Sparse Topometric Graph for Scalable Cross-Session Indoor Navigation
authors: Eun Sun Lee,Minkyun Seo,Gwangtak Bae,Junho Kim,Seunggu Kang,Jaesik Park,Young Min Kim
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
A conventional embodied agent in an indoor environment builds a map by accumulating noisy real-world measurements and results from heavy inference to guide navigation.
While the detailed measurements may differ due to scene changes or sensor settings, the unique topological structure of navigable passages or the connectivity between rooms may provide training-free guidance that complements local observations.
We propose a sparse topometric graph as an efficient structural representation for robust indoor navigation, alleviating the need for fine-grained matching, which is computationally expensive, memory-intensive, and prone to real-world variations.
The map consists of nodes that encode local 3D geometry and distance-weighted edges that capture traversable connectivity.
A learned graph-matching network finds consistent subgraph structures across sessions by considering both node-level geometric descriptors and neighborhood connectivity.
The holistic contextual matching is robust to local ambiguities caused by weak distinctiveness or repetitive structure, and establishes stable correspondences despite local scene changes, different sensor modalities, or limited spatial overlap.
We analyze the practicality of the graph through cross-session point-goal navigation, where a goal specified in a prior reference map must be reached from an unknown initial pose in a later session.
Experiments show that our method achieves the highest success rates (77.1% on Gibson [34] and 40.0% under 3D-FRONT [9] scene changes), while reducing memory by more than two orders of magnitude compared to point-level representations.
The proposed approach further supports cross-session alignment and goal-directed navigation with strong scalability and robust real-world transfer.
introduction:
Embodied agents in daily life need to understand spatial context to interact in unstructured environments.
Capturing the spatial map of the deployed environment often requires composing multiple measurements with minimal overlap, as indoor scenes often contain complex concavities, frequent occlusions, and confined navigable spaces due to furniture, rooms, and narrow passages with corners.
Reusing the acquired map in a separate session poses additional difficulties.
Transferring the high-quality geometry of the entire deployed space may require extensive spatial memory, and reusing the map with a different embodiment may encounter scene changes and different sensor configurations with unknown relative poses.

Prior navigation studies [6, 21, 25, 7] have used different spatial representations for mapping, localization, and planning in 2D top-down maps of large-scale indoor environments.
Dense metric maps [6, 21, 12, 7] preserve detailed geometry and support path planning, but their storage and matching costs rapidly increase with environment scale.
Keyframe- [5, 23, 4] and appearance-based [2, 14, 15, 25] maps are compact and visually informative, but their reliability can degrade under viewpoint and scene changes.
Semantic and hierarchical scene graphs [11, 13, 32, 36] provide higher-level structure through layouts, objects, or language descriptions, but often depend on reliable detections, explicit labels, or predefined semantic categories.

In this paper, we propose a sparse topometric graph that can reliably capture geometric context despite prevalent ambiguities in indoor environments with repetitive structures, moved furniture, and heterogeneous sensor modalities.
In the presence of such variations, local features are insufficient to extract reliable geometric context, and a broader spatial arrangement must be considered.
Our proposed graph representation summarizes the spatial organization of traversable space. Each node is centered on traversable structure rather than on a sampled point in the cloud, aggregates the observed 3D points within a fixed-radius neighborhood, and stores a compact geometry-only descriptor, while each edge represents free-space connectivity with a distance-based weight.
This fixed-radius aggregation makes local geometry reusable at the graph level instead of tying descriptors to raw point samples [20, 28].
Compressing each local point set into a fixed-size node descriptor keeps the map size proportional to the number of graph nodes rather than the raw scene geometry, while preserving enough local and structural information for cross-session map reuse.

We demonstrate the usability of the representation in cross-session point-goal navigation.
The agent starts from an unknown initial pose and must reach the goal pose, defined on the reference map built in a previous session.
The agent first aligns its current observations relative to the reference map and selects waypoints toward the goal while taking the navigable path topology into account.
We train a graph-matching network to predict cross-session correspondences between graph nodes by jointly considering local geometry and connectivity between neighboring nodes.
The predicted correspondences are used to estimate the relative transformation between the reference and current sessions, after which the graph-based navigation policy guides the agent toward the transferred goal.
This setting lets us study whether a single sparse representation can support both cross-session alignment and downstream navigation.

Fig. 1 illustrates our pipeline with a real-world cross-session example.
The example highlights a key challenge.
Local geometric descriptors or appearance-based cues can be ambiguous when similar structures repeat across partially overlapping sessions.
The proposed representation and graph matching reduce these ambiguities by considering both node-level geometry and neighboring graph connectivity.

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose a sparse topometric graph for cross-session indoor map reuse. It represents traversable space with compact geometry-only node descriptors and distance-weighted graph connectivity, providing a scalable map representation.

We introduce a graph-node descriptor that aggregates fixed-radius 3D observations around reusable node centers. This makes local geometry available at the graph level instead of tying descriptors to individual point-cloud samples.

We introduce a learned graph-matching approach that predicts cross-session node correspondences using both local geometric similarity and graph connectivity, and we use the same graph for cross-session alignment and waypoint selection.

We evaluate the method on simulated cross-session navigation, large-scale indoor scenes, scene-change settings, and a real-world indoor study, demonstrating efficient and reliable cross-session map use.

1. We propose a sparse topometric graph for cross-session indoor map reuse. It represents traversable space with compact geometry-only node descriptors and distance-weighted graph connectivity, providing a scalable map representation.

2. We introduce a graph-node descriptor that aggregates fixed-radius 3D observations around reusable node centers. This makes local geometry available at the graph level instead of tying descriptors to individual point-cloud samples.

3. We introduce a learned graph-matching approach that predicts cross-session node correspondences using both local geometric similarity and graph connectivity, and we use the same graph for cross-session alignment and waypoint selection.

4. We evaluate the method on simulated cross-session navigation, large-scale indoor scenes, scene-change settings, and a real-world indoor study, demonstrating efficient and reliable cross-session map use.

title: FastHarness: Experience-Driven Review Scheduling for Vision-Language-Action Policies
authors: Tao Lin,Yuxin Du,Haoxiao Wang,Zile Zhong,Bo Zhao
comment: Github:this https URL
abstract: Agentic robot systems combine language-model reasoning with robot policies to monitor execution and recover from failures. However, reviewing every action chunk incurs substantial overhead, even in familiar situations. We introduce FastHarness, an experience-driven execution harness that adaptively schedules GPT-6 Astra supervision of a π0.5\pi_{0.5} policy. A fast path uses stage memory and reviewed outcomes to reduce review frequency as experience accumulates, while a complementary recovery path focuses supervision on correcting errors. Once recovery is verified, routine execution resumes, with failure experience retained to guide future interventions. The policy remains frozen and generates fresh actions from current observations. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, reviewer token use decreases by an average of 57.2% per task from the first evaluated episode to the mean of the final five episodes. Mean episode time decreases from 85.5 to 52.0 minutes over the same interval. On the same tasks, mean success increases from 80% for GPT-as-Policy (π0.5\pi_{0.5} + GPT-6 Astra) to 97.19% with FastHarness. These results highlight adaptive supervision as a practical route to more efficient agentic robotics without additional model training.
introduction:
Agentic robot systems (Zhang et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2025) combine learned policies with language-model reasoning to monitor execution and recover from errors. A vision-language-action (VLA) policy (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026c; Lin et al., 2026a; Brohan et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2026b) maps observations and instructions to actions, while a language model uses execution feedback to assess progress and guide corrections (Huang et al., 2022). GPT-as-Policy follows this approach by pairing π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) with GPT-6 Astra (Su et al., 2026). An execution harness coordinates the two models, determining when to request a review and how the resulting feedback affects subsequent actions.

Frequent model calls, however, can make execution slow and costly. Reviewing every action chunk repeats this overhead even in task stages that the policy has already completed reliably. Errors require a different response: a missed grasp or dropped object may need several rounds of correction before execution can continue. Repeated task execution provides evidence for distinguishing these situations. The challenge is to use that evidence to reduce redundant review while retaining the supervision needed for recovery.

We introduce FastHarness, an experience-driven harness that uses reviewed outcomes to decide when model supervision is needed (Figure 1). Repeatedly successful stages can proceed with less frequent review, while remembered failures prompt closer inspection when similar situations recur. The harness updates its memory and review schedule as experience accumulates. The π0.5\pi_{0.5} policy remains fixed and generates each action chunk from the current observation.

FastHarness implements this adaptation through two complementary paths (Figure 2). During routine execution, the fast path uses the current task stage and its reviewed history to set the review frequency. When an error is detected, the recovery path guides local repair under continued review. After the reviewer verifies recovery, the harness resumes ordinary scheduling. It retains the failure record to guide future interventions.

We evaluate FastHarness on four simulated manipulation tasks, examining both execution efficiency and task success. Across repeated runs, reviewer token use decreases by an average of 57.2% per task, and mean episode time falls from 85.5 to 52.0 minutes. These comparisons use the first evaluated episode and the mean of the final five episodes. On these same tasks, mean success increases from 80% for the baseline to 97.19% with FastHarness. Execution traces illustrate how the harness adjusts review frequency and resumes routine execution after recovery.

title: FocusVLA: Future-Intent Guided Dynamic View Routing for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Huixin Xu,Ziya Yu,Peng Li
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become an important paradigm for robotic manipulation by unifying visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Since reliable manipulation requires sufficient observation of objects, end-effectors, and their spatial relationships, multi-view inputs are widely used to provide complementary spatial information. However, our experiments show that existing VLA models do not fully exploit such multi-view complementarity. The policy tends to persistently rely on the wrist view, lacking the ability to dynamically adjust global-local view dependency across manipulation stages, which limits stage adaptability and robustness. To address this issue, we propose FocusVLA, a stage-aware multi-view routing framework. FocusVLA predicts future interaction intent from historical actions and uses it to guide dynamic view routing during action generation. By adaptively coordinating global and local observations across different task stages, FocusVLA improves multi-view utilization. On RoboTwin 2.0, FocusVLA improves the average success rate over the strongest baseline π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 10.10 pp. In real-world evaluation, FocusVLA improves the success rate from 71.7% to 85.0%, achieving a 13.3% gain over π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Moreover, the intent prediction and dynamic routing modules of FocusVLA can be integrated into existing VLA frameworks without modifying their core architectures.
introduction:
Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [23, 18, 6, 28, 5, 43, 24, 44, 14, 33, 47] have shown strong potential for generalist robotic manipulation by unifying visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. In real-world manipulation, robust action generation often requires visual observations that can handle occlusions, viewpoint variations, and fine-grained interactions. Therefore, multi-view inputs are widely used to provide complementary visual information [35, 25, 20]: third-person cameras provide global scene context for target localization and motion planning, while wrist cameras provide local cues for alignment, grasping, and contact-rich execution. However, existing VLA models typically fuse visual observations with language instructions and robot states into a fixed context for action generation. Although this paradigm effectively integrates multimodal information, it rarely considers that the policy’s visual dependency may change across manipulation stages.

Our empirical analysis further shows that, under the static fusion paradigm, the model is prone to view-dependency inertia during action generation: the policy may develop a strong reliance on a particular view at an early task stage according to the current manipulation demand. Although such reliance may be reasonable at the early stage, the lack of explicit awareness of task progress causes the early-formed observation preference to persist into later stages, making it difficult for the policy to dynamically adjust the contributions of different views to action generation according to changing manipulation requirements. This phenomenon suggests that improving multi-view utilization requires not only fusing multi-view information, but also enabling the policy to dynamically select and coordinate different view observations during action execution. Motivated by these observations, we aim to mitigate the stage-view misalignment caused by static fusion. Achieving this goal requires answering two key questions: (1) how can a VLA policy acquire a representation that reflects task progress and use it to infer the visual requirements of upcoming manipulation stages? (2) how can such a representation be transformed into effective multi-view routing signals without disrupting the pretrained VLA backbone?

To answer these questions, we propose FocusVLA, a stage-aware dynamic view routing framework for multi-view VLA policies, as shown in Fig. 1. FocusVLA predicts future action intent from multimodal observations and short-term action history, and uses it to generate action-step-wise routing weights that dynamically coordinate visual features from different views during action generation. The framework is non-invasive, requiring no modification to the visual encoder, language model, or action-generation backbone. We evaluate FocusVLA in both simulation and real-world settings. The simulation experiments cover all 50 RoboTwin [11] tasks, and the real-world experiments include 6 representative manipulation tasks with diverse object configurations, viewpoint variations, and interaction requirements. Results show that FocusVLA consistently outperforms static multi-view fusion baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness in mitigating stage-view misalignment and improving policy adaptability.

In summary, our contributions are: (1) We identify and quantify a temporal failure in static multi-view VLA policies: view dependence formed at earlier stages persists after visual requirements change, causing stage–view misalignment. (2) We propose FocusVLA, a task-progress-aware visual modulation framework that converts future action intent into action-step-wise view-routing weights for non-invasive dynamic multi-view modulation. (3) We evaluate FocusVLA on all 50 RoboTwin simulation tasks and 6 real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating improved adaptability and robustness over static multi-view baselines.

title: CoHelix: Event-Based Multi-Propeller Rotation-Rate Tracking with Shared Projective Geometry
authors: Radim Spetlik,Tobiáš Vinklárek,Jan Klivan,Tomáš Kestřánek,Matouš Vrba,Jiří Matas
abstract:
Estimating propeller rates from a moving event camera requires separating blade rotation from the changing image geometry.
Background activity mixes with blade events, while repeated blade appearances admit half- and double-rate ambiguities.
We propose CoHelix, a recursive filter that estimates one shared homography and separate rotation states for four rigidly mounted, coplanar propellers.
Each admitted event updates its assigned rotation state, and its accepted geometry measurements correct the shared homography used to interpret later events from every propeller.
We report lock, the fraction of evaluated time for which an estimate remains within 22 % of synchronized ground truth, because mean error alone does not show how long a tracker follows the true rate.
With fixed-rate initialization, leave-one-recording-out evaluation on moving-camera data gives CoHelix 62.962.9 % lock, compared with 39.839.8 % for HelixTrack [26] and 22.222.2 % for EventPro [4].
With other settings fixed, allowing four geometry contributors instead of one raises lock from 3.43.4 % to 62.962.9 %.
On a private target–follower dataset with a different target quadcopter, CoHelix retains the measurement settings selected on moving-camera data and uses a fixed initial rate. It reaches 95.995.9 % lock, compared with 56.256.2 % for HelixTrack and 61.161.1 % for EventPro.
introduction:
We study rotation-rate tracking for four two-blade propellers observed by a moving event camera. Relative motion between the camera and airframe changes each propeller’s image projection while its blades rotate. Recovering the rates requires estimating this changing geometry and the individual rotations from the same events.

Propeller rates set the thrust of a multicopter, so a commanded change of its motion starts as a change of these rates. Cameras already detect and localize drones, also by their propellers [23, 28, 30, 27], and radar measures propeller rates [5]. Event cameras [12] resolve the brightness changes produced by individual blade passages without forming frames.

Event cameras also respond to brightness changes caused by camera motion. Background structure swept through a propeller’s annulus adds events that mix with the blade events, and four nearly identical propellers make event assignment ambiguous. A rate estimator must therefore separate blade events from background motion before interpreting their timing.

Interpreting blade events requires knowing where each projected propeller lies. The blades sweep a circular disc in their own rotor plane. Perspective maps this disc to a moving, generally non-circular image region. We represent blade orientation by a periodic phase. Mapping an event to the rotor plane determines its propeller assignment and blade angle. Map errors affect phase and rate estimates.

Existing event-based rate estimators estimate propeller geometry from accumulated events rather than updating it after each event. HelixTrack [26] updates phase per event but refines one propeller’s homography from accumulated events. EventPro [4] estimates each propeller centre from clustered events and its in-plane rate from an adaptive event batch. Neither method jointly uses the propellers to constrain their common geometry.

For rigidly mounted, coplanar propellers, one homography maps their fixed rotor-plane layout into the image. Each propeller still has its own phase, rate and acceleration. The resulting estimation problem couples one changing projection to four independent rotations.

We propose CoHelix, a recursive filter that estimates this homography and the four rotation states through individual-event updates (Fig. 1). Each admitted event corrects its assigned rotation state, and its accepted geometry measurements also correct the shared geometry. That geometry correction changes how later events from every propeller are assigned and interpreted. In contrast to HelixTrack [26], the coupling acts through a shared map updated from individual events, while the rotation dynamics remain separate.

Evaluating the resulting rates requires accounting for the two-blade ambiguity. A two-blade propeller looks unchanged after a half turn, so an estimate at twice the reference rate fits the observed events as well as the reference rate does. In addition to mean absolute and relative rate errors, we report the lock percentage: the fraction of evaluated time for which a reported rate remains within 22 % of synchronized ground truth. Missing output counts as not locked; half- and double-rate estimates fail this test.

In summary, our contributions are:

We introduce CoHelix, a recursive estimator of a shared projective map and independent propeller rotations. The accepted geometry measurements of each event correct the geometry used to interpret later events across all four propellers. Comparisons quantify the effect of geometry contributors and of the tested Kalman and windowed Gauss–Newton formulations (Secs. 4.4–4.5).

CoHelix reaches the highest lock percentage among the evaluated methods on two datasets with different quadcopters. On the benchmark from [26], leave-one-recording-out evaluation with a fixed initial rate gives 62.962.9 % lock, compared with 39.839.8 % for HelixTrack [26] and 22.222.2 % for EventPro [4]. With the selected measurement settings unchanged, CoHelix reaches 95.995.9 % lock on a private target–follower dataset (Sec. 4.3).

title: Probabilistic Energy Modeling Unifies Versatile Swarm Control
authors: Xiang Zhou,Xiangyu Zhu,Xintong Wang,Qingyuan Yang,Rui Huang,Feng Xue,Lin Li,Qingrui Zhang
abstract: Robotic swarms must coordinate across diverse missions, yet existing controllers often require redesign, retuning, or retraining when objectives change. Here we show that probabilistic energy modeling provides a unifying representation for versatile swarm control, in which diverse missions emerge from compositions of shared interaction principles rather than task-specific control formulations. By exploiting the correspondence between Gibbs random field energy minimization and structured reward maximization, we encode fundamental swarm behaviors as reusable energy terms within a unified probabilistic objective. Decentralized policies trained within this representation are composed into a single controller through lightweight policy gating, without retraining. An interpretable action-attention mechanism captures non-uniform local interactions, while dimensionless normalization supports transfer across swarm scales and platforms. Demonstrated on aerial swarms, the unified policy generalizes zero-shot across six mission classes, 10–100 agents, two hardware platforms, and indoor cluttered and GPS-denied woodland environments. Large-scale simulations achieve 0.96–1.00 task success rates with 1–10 ms per-agent inference latency, while physical deployments confirm zero-shot transfer to real platforms and unstructured environments. These results establish probabilistic energy modeling as a scalable and transferable framework for decentralized swarm control.

title: GelSlim 5.0: Unifying Vision and Touch with a Single Fingertip Camera
authors: Xiangdong Wang,I-Hsuan Huang,Xiaohao Xu,Xili Yi,Nima Fazeli,Xiaonan Huang
abstract: Vision and touch provide complementary cues for object pose and local contact geometry, but external cameras are often occluded at the contact site. We present GelSlim 5.0, a fingertip sensor that acquires visual and tactile observations with one fixed camera and a continuous UV-responsive contact layer. By switching illumination, the camera sequentially acquires through-membrane visual images and contact-sensitive tactile images from a shared viewpoint, avoiding inter-camera extrinsic calibration. To combine these observations, we introduce VisTacFusion, a multimodal transformer with separate prediction paths for planar object pose and contact geometry. Asymmetric bottleneck fusion incorporates visual context while preserving tactile spatial features for depth and surface-normal estimation. Modality dropout enables inference with paired inputs or either modality alone. On real validation data from 12 known objects, paired inputs reduce depth MSE, angular error, and translation L1L_{1} by 61.2%, 72.3%, and 61.3%, respectively, relative to tactile-only inference with the same model. Relative to visual-only inference, the corresponding reductions are 93.7%, 6.1%, and 8.6%. Project website
introduction:
Contact-rich manipulation requires estimating both object pose and the local geometry of contact. Vision supplies object context, while optical tactile sensors such as GelSight and GelSlim capture detailed contact structure [1, 2]. The modalities can resolve different ambiguities: visual context can distinguish object poses that produce similar contact patches, while tactile measurements reveal local surface geometry that visual appearance alone may not resolve.

With external cameras, however, the hand and object can occlude the contact site, and viewpoint differences complicate spatial association with tactile measurements. A shared fingertip camera places visual sensing at the contact interface and provides a common frame for relating object appearance to contact geometry. Prior visuotactile sensors obtain scene access through semitransparent skins [3], controllable films [4], UV-visible markers [5], or spatial multiplexing [6].
Building on these designs, we couple a continuous contact interface with an estimator for object pose and spatially resolved contact geometry.

We introduce GelSlim 5.0, a fingertip sensor that co-locates vision and touch within the GelSlim 4.0 body design [7]. A continuous UV-responsive contact layer allows one fixed camera to record through-membrane visual images with UV off and contact-sensitive tactile images with UV on (Fig. 1).
The observations are acquired sequentially under approximately stationary contact and share a viewpoint and image coordinates, supporting spatial association without inter-camera extrinsic calibration.
Table I positions the sensor among prior interfaces.

To exploit these complementary observations, VisTacFusion uses separate prediction paths for planar object pose and contact geometry. Tactile-initialized queries provide a pose estimate, while intermediate tactile features preserve spatial detail for contact-depth and surface-normal estimation. A shared visual bottleneck conditions both paths, allowing object context to inform pose and geometry predictions. Modality dropout trains the model to operate with either input alone or the pair.

Our contributions are (1) a fingertip sensor that co-locates vision and touch using a continuous UV-responsive contact interface; (2) an estimator that combines visual context with separate pose queries and spatial geometry features; and (3) an evaluation on 12 known objects covering modality complementarity, encoder and fusion choices, and training configuration. Within-session validation shows lower contact-depth and pose errors for paired observations than for either input alone in the same estimator.

title: Whole-Body Motion Guided Reference Generation for Uncertainty-Aware Compliant Assistance
authors: Muyuan Ma,Long Cheng,Lijun Han,Haotian Zhai,Xinpan Meng,Xiuze Xia,Houcheng Li,Zeyu Liu
abstract: Exoskeletons have shown great potential for augmenting human physical capabilities, yet generating reliable assistance remains challenging because human motion patterns and interaction requirements vary substantially in practice. To address this problem, a dual-loop assistance strategy is proposed to couple multimodal exoskeleton trajectory generation with variable admittance control, where trajectory variance links the outer-loop generator and the inner-loop controller. The generator synthesizes future exoskeleton trajectories through denoising, primarily using whole-body human motion and exoskeleton proprioception, with task descriptions as auxiliary semantic cues. To reduce cross-modal representation mismatch, a three-stage training pipeline is introduced to progressively optimize the human motion encoder, the exoskeleton proprioception encoder, and the trajectory generator. In the inner loop, multiple future trajectories are sampled from the generator to estimate the trajectory mean and variance. The mean is used as the control reference, while the variance provides an uncertainty measure for prediction reliability. This measure is further incorporated into a stiffness regulation law, enabling compliant assistance with input-to-state stability under bounded lumped interaction input. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces muscle activation levels compared with standard baselines, while also decreasing users’ metabolic energy expenditure relative to the unassisted condition.
introduction:
Exoskeletons can augment human strength, reduce physical effort, and assist individuals with motor impairments [1]. These capabilities make such systems broadly applicable to rehabilitation [2], military operations [3], and physically demanding industrial tasks [4]. However, designing exoskeleton assistance strategies that provide effective support while maintaining safe and comfortable physical interaction remains challenging, because the human and the exoskeleton form a tightly coupled dynamical system whose behavior varies across users and tasks [5]. Therefore, effective exoskeleton assistance requires reliable assistive input generation and compliant physical interaction under varying motion and interaction conditions [6].

Existing studies on exoskeleton assistance commonly generate assistive inputs in the form of either joint torque trajectories [7, 8] or reference motion trajectories [9, 10]. Torque trajectories directly prescribe joint-level assistance, whereas motion trajectories provide desired joint references that are converted into assistive torques through low-level control. For torque-based assistance, [11] estimated human joint torque from electromyographic (EMG) signals and generated exoskeleton assistive torque, validating the effectiveness of assistance in flexion and extension tasks. Moreover, [12] constructed an EMG-torque estimator based on radial basis function neural networks and integrated it with a Slotine–Li controller for exoskeleton assistance. To improve the efficiency of torque estimation, [13] introduced a physics-informed neural network for multiple joint angle and torque estimation. Furthermore, [14] designed a task-agnostic controller that instantaneously estimates lower-limb biological joint moments using a temporal convolutional network, assisting users across 28 lower-limb tasks. Despite these advances, torque-based methods often rely on human joint torque data collected under controlled laboratory conditions. Such data are difficult to obtain in practical settings, which limits the scalability and real-world applicability of these methods. For reference-based assistance, [15] generated ankle joint reference trajectories through cubic spline interpolation to assist human locomotion. In addition, [16] leveraged dynamic movement primitives (DMPs) to generate reference trajectories online. Furthermore, [17] employed a graph spiking neural network to generate globally optimal desired trajectories for lower limb exoskeletons, enabling safe and stable walking in complex indoor environments. For upper limb exoskeletons, [18] used a diffusion model to generate future motion trajectories and validated its effectiveness on four motion tasks. Although reference-based methods can provide effective assistance within specific task categories [19, 20], most of them generate trajectories mainly from limited inertial measurement unit (IMU) or EMG signals. The absence of richer multimodal information, such as visual cues, human motion states, and task-related context, limits reliable reference generation under varying assistance conditions [21].

The generated reference trajectories may not always match individual motion habits and preferred movement patterns across users [22]. To mitigate the resulting interaction issues, compliant control has become a commonly used low-level control strategy for exoskeletons [23], enabling dynamic regulation of the relationship between human-exoskeleton interaction forces and reference trajectories [24, 25]. This mechanism allows the exoskeleton to balance accurate reference tracking with compliance to the user’s voluntary motion [26]. Based on this principle, admittance control has been employed to reshape reference trajectories online according to interaction forces, showing favorable performance in level-ground walking experiments with two subjects [27]. An event-triggered hybrid position-force control method was further introduced to adapt the control strategy to varying interaction forces [28]. To improve tracking safety, a tangent-type barrier Lyapunov function (BLF) controller was designed to constrain position tracking errors within predefined closed-loop boundaries, thereby reducing human muscular effort in experiments with eight subjects [29]. In addition, an adaptive modular neural control framework improved position tracking performance using only the robot’s embedded position encoders, and its effectiveness was validated on five subjects [30]. Beyond these compliant control schemes, interaction forces have also been incorporated into the weighting matrix of the cost function in model predictive control, which further reduces human-exoskeleton interaction forces during assistance [31]. However, most existing control strategies regulate compliance mainly in response to interaction forces or tracking errors [32, 33, 34]. These feedback signals mainly indicate human-exoskeleton disagreement after it occurs, but provide limited information about whether the reference trajectory is reliable. As a result, the controller may still enforce tracking of an unsuitable reference, leading to unnecessary interaction forces and reduced comfort.

In this article, a dual-loop exoskeleton assistance framework is proposed that couples multimodal trajectory generation with compliant interaction control, using trajectory uncertainty as the coupling variable between the outer-loop generator and the inner-loop variable admittance controller. To achieve reliable trajectory generation, the generator produces future exoskeleton trajectories primarily conditioned on whole-body human motion and exoskeleton proprioceptive states, with task descriptions providing auxiliary semantic cues. A flow-matching objective is used to learn a conditional motion field that progressively maps Gaussian noise to future trajectory samples [35]. In addition, to alleviate representation misalignment among different modalities, a three-stage training pipeline is applied to sequentially learn human motion representations, align exoskeleton proprioceptive representations, and optimize the trajectory generator. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to explicitly leverage whole-body human motion as guidance for exoskeleton trajectory generation, enabling the generated reference trajectories to incorporate global motion context beyond local exoskeleton proprioception.

For the inner-loop admittance controller, the reference trajectory of the exoskeleton is derived from the mean of multiple sampled future trajectories. The corresponding trajectory variance is regarded as a measure of trajectory uncertainty and serves as an input to the stiffness regulation law subject to stability constraints. When the estimated trajectory uncertainty increases, the regulation law decreases the interaction stiffness to improve compliance with the user’s voluntary motion. When the estimated trajectory uncertainty decreases, the stiffness is increased to enhance tracking of the generated reference trajectory. The proposed framework is illustrated in Fig. 1, including the dual-loop assistance structure composed of the trajectory generator and the variable admittance controller. The contributions of this article are as follows.

A dual-loop exoskeleton assistance framework is proposed to bridge generative motion assistance and compliant physical interaction control through trajectory uncertainty. By using uncertainty as an explicit coupling variable, the framework coordinates trajectory generation with compliant admittance regulation within a unified assistance architecture.

A dual-loop exoskeleton assistance framework is proposed to bridge generative motion assistance and compliant physical interaction control through trajectory uncertainty. By using uncertainty as an explicit coupling variable, the framework coordinates trajectory generation with compliant admittance regulation within a unified assistance architecture.

A multimodal exoskeleton trajectory generation method is developed to synthesize reliable reference trajectories under multimodal conditions. The method primarily leverages whole-body human motion and exoskeleton proprioceptive states as dynamic physical conditions, while incorporating task descriptions as auxiliary semantic cues. A three-stage training pipeline is further introduced to reduce cross-modal representation mismatch.

An uncertainty-aware variable admittance control strategy is designed for compliant physical interaction. The mean of sampled future trajectories defines the controller reference, and the temporal variation of the filtered trajectory uncertainty guides stiffness regulation. This strategy adjusts interaction compliance under stability constraints to balance active assistance and the user’s voluntary motion.

The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section II presents the multimodal exoskeleton trajectory generator, including its network architecture, three-stage training pipeline, and optimization objectives. Section III introduces the uncertainty-aware variable admittance controller and the associated stiffness regulation law. Section IV reports the experimental results and comparative analyses. Section V concludes this article.

title: Learning Robot Behavior Priors from Non-Robotic Synthetic Data
authors: Mateusz Odrowaz-Sypniewski,Michael Amir,Jasmine Bayrooti,Ajay Shankar,Amanda Prorok
abstract:
Real robot data, rich across tasks and morphologies, is often treated as the bottleneck for training robot learning models, including embodied foundation models that aim for zero-shot physical transfer.
In this paper, we investigate
the degree to which such models can acquire necessary structure
using data from systems without embodiment.
To this end, we test if inexpensive, procedurally generated synthetic data can yield useful priors before a model observes any real-world behavior.
We study this through robot action prediction, a natural pretraining objective and a direct test of whether structure learned from arbitrary synthetic tasks transfers to embodied settings.
We introduce three data generation pipelines that model mathematical abstractions of robotic control, and use them as pretraining priors for a Transformer.
We demonstrate that a model trained purely on this non-robotic data attains non-trivial zero-shot prediction performance on unseen physical robot tasks via an in-context learning mechanism, and that our specialized control priors notably improve upon generic causal priors.
We also compare against a compute-matched baseline trained on real robot data, and find that it outperforms our model but only on the datasets it was trained on.
These findings suggest that procedurally generated, mathematical abstractions can yield useful robotic priors, offering a potential complement to expensive embodied data collection.
introduction:
Can robots learn from non-robotic data? Data-driven learning underpins recent advances in robot control [1, 2, 3], with vision-language-action (VLA) models and generalist policies relying heavily on internet-scale video, simulation, and physical demonstrations [4, 5].
While diversifying training data across embodiments is a compelling research direction [6, 7], collecting physical demonstrations is expensive, and simulators merely shift the burden to domain-specific engineering.
Instead, we explore whether it is possible to learn from generic, entirely unembodied sources.

Consider action prediction, the task of predicting held-out actions from a context of state-action tuples.
Intuitively, the prediction task across different robot embodiments may share basic regularities tied to general notions of control.
Prior exposure to these generic, abstract dynamics could serve as a useful starting point for downstream generalization.
Indeed, by operating downstream of any visual encoders, such a method can be complementary to the grounding that, say, VLAs acquire from internet-scale data.

In this work, we demonstrate that generic, mathematical abstractions of control—generated through policy-induced synthetic rollouts—can induce transferable priors for robot action prediction without requiring any embodied data.
We implement this approach using Prior-Data Fitted Networks [8], which train Transformers on synthetic datasets sampled from task priors to enable zero-shot in-context predictions11
1
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          We use ‘zero-shot’ to denote pretraining without robot data; deployment is always an in-context (few-shot) process..
We hypothesize that sequential decision-making tasks require specialized structural priors, as opposed to, e.g., the domain-agnostic causal models used by methods such as TabPFN [9].
Our approach to this is to develop synthetic data generators based on procedurally generated Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), Contextual Bandits, and Linear Dynamical Systems (LDS).

By utilizing only mathematical abstractions rather than physical simulations [10, 11] or real-world data, our approach departs significantly from a typical embodied learning paradigm.
We evaluate across a diverse suite of held-out robotic datasets (Figure 1), and find that while a generic tabular prior struggles to transfer to real robot domains, a model pretrained purely on our synthetic control generators achieves zero-shot action prediction well above chance, despite having never observed a robot during training.
We also evaluate our approach against a compute-matched baseline trained on real, embodied robot data.
The two behave differently across the split: embodied training is far stronger on the tasks it was trained on (a gap that measures what our abstractions do not supply), while our model, for which every task is equally unseen, performs consistently across both groups and overtakes the baseline on the unseen task set.

title: Consistent Distributed Invariant EKF SLAM with Point and Object Features
authors: Mengya Xu,Xianjia Yu,Ha Sier,Shoudong Huang,Tomi Westerlund
comment: Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
abstract:
Multi-robot SLAM allows robots to improve their estimates by exchanging map information, but repeated exchanges create unknown correlations between local estimators.
Covariance intersection (CI) can fuse estimates without tracking these correlations.
In right-invariant extended Kalman filter (RI-EKF) SLAM, however, point features obtain their invariant errors through the robot rotation, so a neighbor’s map estimate is expressed in its own error coordinates and is correlated with its pose, and cannot be fused by CI directly.
This paper presents Joint-CI, a unified fusion method for distributed RI-EKF SLAM with point, object, and mixed point–object maps.
Using a neighboring robot’s local posterior and an inter-robot observation, a joint estimate of the receiving robot’s pose and the common features is constructed in the receiving robot’s error coordinates, retaining the robot–feature and feature–feature correlations.
Partial-state CI then fuses this estimate with the receiving robot’s local posterior.
We show that the unified formulation and the fusion preserve the six unobservable directions associated with global rotation and translation, and that communication and fusion preserve first-order covariance consistency given consistent local posteriors.
Monte Carlo simulations and a real-world dataset-derived experiment show that Joint-CI improves estimation accuracy while maintaining consistent, mildly conservative uncertainty.
The code is available at
https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Joint-CI-for-Distributed-RI-EKF-SLAM-E14B/.
introduction:
Multi-robot SLAM improves coverage and estimation accuracy by allowing robots to exchange locally acquired map information.
Representative systems such as DDF-SAM [1], Kimera-Multi [2], and Swarm-SLAM [3] employ distributed or decentralized nonlinear optimization over factor-graph or pose-graph representations.
These approaches provide powerful batch or incremental optimization capabilities, but repeatedly solving a growing optimization problem can impose computational and latency costs on lightweight robotic platforms.
Filtering-based methods provide a complementary solution by recursively updating the current posterior as new measurements and communicated estimates arrive.

Point features are generic and efficient to detect and match, and have therefore been widely used in both single-robot and multi-robot SLAM.
Advances in machine learning have also increased interest in high-level features such as objects, which provide persistent semantic identities and strong geometric constraints [4, 5, 6, 7].
Practical systems have further demonstrated the value of mixed map representations, in which low-level point features and high-level object features are maintained together [8, 9, 10].
For filtering-based SLAM, estimation consistency is essential because underestimated uncertainty can degrade both state estimation and uncertainty-aware downstream decisions [11].
Conventional EKF SLAM can become inconsistent because linearization at the estimated states may introduce spurious information along unobservable directions [12, 13, 14].
Right-invariant EKF (RI-EKF) formulations address this issue by defining the estimation error through the symmetry of the state space, which preserves the appropriate unobservable directions.
They have been developed for both point-feature SLAM [15, 16] and object-feature SLAM [17].

Distributed filtering introduces an additional difficulty because previous information exchange creates generally unknown cross-correlations between local estimators.
Covariance intersection (CI) [18] provides a conservative fusion rule without explicitly tracking these correlations and has been applied to SLAM [19] and decentralized cooperative localization [20, 21].
Partial-state CI extends this idea to estimates containing different or overlapping subsets of a common state [22, 23, 24].
Distributed invariant filters have also applied CI to pose estimation on Lie groups [25, 26], without estimating a shared map.
For object-level multi-robot SLAM, Li et al. [27] use per-object invariant errors, representing each object as an independent 𝕊​𝔼​(3)\mathbb{SE}(3) component, so that neighboring robot poses and common object estimates can be combined separately.

Despite these advances, fusing map information between RI-EKF SLAM estimators remains nontrivial.
Exchanging only pose estimates discards the information contained in the shared map, and the per-object invariant errors in [27] rely on object orientations and therefore do not directly cover point features.
In RI-EKF SLAM, point features, which carry no orientation of their own, obtain their invariant errors through the robot rotation [15, 16], and the object formulation in [17] adopts the same coupling, allowing point, object, and mixed maps to share one error representation.
In this coupled formulation, exchanging map features raises two issues.
First, each robot’s feature errors are defined relative to its own rotation error, so a neighbor’s feature covariance cannot be combined directly with the receiving robot’s posterior.
Second, a neighbor’s pose and feature errors are correlated through its own SLAM estimation, and in the coupled formulation they additionally share the same rotation error.
A communicated covariance that ignores these correlations is not guaranteed to be consistent.

This paper presents Joint-CI, a single construction that addresses both issues for distributed RI-EKF SLAM with point, object, and mixed point–object maps.
Joint-CI re-expresses the communicated robot pose and common features in the receiving filter’s error coordinates as one correlated partial state, derives its complete first-order covariance from the neighboring posterior and the inter-robot observation, and then applies standard partial-state CI.
The main contributions are:
1) We derive a unified construction of the communicated robot–feature partial state and its complete first-order covariance in error coordinates compatible with the receiving filter, for point, object, and mixed maps.
2) We show that the unified local RI-EKF formulation and the subsequent fusion preserve the global gauge directions. Given consistent local posteriors, we further establish first-order covariance consistency of the communicated estimate and subsequent CI fusion.
3) We evaluate estimation accuracy, statistical consistency, communication and computational costs, and operation in multi-neighbor networks through Monte Carlo simulations and a real-world dataset-derived experiment.

title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Chenyuan Chen,Ran Ding,Lechen Zhang,Zewen He,Yoshihiko Nakamura

abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy’s success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%). introduction:
Whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) models [1, 2, 3], paired with learned whole-body controllers [4, 5], have advanced humanoid loco-manipulation considerably. Yet most of them act on the current observation alone, ignoring temporal dependencies, and thus fail in dynamic scenes where objects change state or are hidden [6, 7], moved or removed. Everyday cues are brief and seldom repeated: a guest waves from one of several identical tables while a waiter carries a tray, and when the waiter turns back, the hand is already down. Fig. 1 shows this situation on a real G1: a cola stops on two seats and a sprite on one, the robot turns away to fetch the cola, and when it comes back the seats look the same again, so a policy that sees only the current view cannot tell where the cola stopped first. Loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is thus non-Markovian: earlier events determine later decisions, which calls for memory. We refer to it as pre-history memory: the record of the object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. Such memory is especially hard for a humanoid, whose head camera moves as it turns and walks, so cues leave the view, and whose memory must be updated causally while whole-body control runs. Even dual-system designs [2], in which a VLM planner acts as System 2, can reason over the history only if they locate the key frames. Existing memory strategies, mostly developed for tabletop arms, retain long frame histories [8, 9], which are costly and dilute brief cues; compress them [10, 11], losing detail; sample frames at fixed intervals [12], missing brief cues; or select event frames tied to the robot’s own operations or learned from demonstrations [13, 14].

As humans remember the moments when the things they care about change rather than every moment [15], we propose WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory for whole-body VLAs. First, a frozen SAM3 [16], a promptable video segmentation model, tracks the task objects in the head-camera stream, and we detect when they appear, disappear, move or change shape, compensating for the camera’s own motion. Second, these object events causally select the key frames that fill an adaptive memory budget, stored as native backbone tokens along with mask-pooled object tokens. Finally, the action expert reads this memory via cross-attention and FiLM, so that whole-body actions depend on what happened, not only on what is visible.

Existing humanoid benchmarks [17, 18, 19, 20] keep the goal in view and do not test this problem, whereas memory benchmarks [12, 21] are tabletop manipulation. We therefore introduce a memory-dependent humanoid loco-manipulation benchmark. Our contributions are as follows:

We propose WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory for whole-body VLAs, in which object events, rather than even sampling, select the key frames of an adaptive budget, read together with object tokens.

We introduce HuMeGo, a memory-dependent humanoid loco-manipulation benchmark: six simulated tasks covering object, spatial and temporal memory, where the scene ends the cue and decisions are scored apart from manipulation, and six real-world G1 tasks, where the robot also turns away from the cue.

WholeBodyMem keeps the right frames rather than more frames, outperforms memoryless and uniform-memory baselines in decisions and success, helps even on SIMPLE, and carries over to a real G1.

title: Calibration-free IMU-based Relative Orientation Estimation under Dynamic Human Motion
authors: Ruiyuan Li,Hassan Osman,Ajay Seth,Manon Kok
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Sensors Journal
abstract:
Recent magnetometer-free inertial measurement unit (IMU) methods can reduce drift in joint motion estimation using rigid-body constraints, but they typically require pre-calibrated sensor locations, assumptions of specific joint models (e.g., hinge joints) or limited motion types, or an external reference for global orientation.
Furthermore, challenges related to high-frequency impacts (e.g. at foot strikes during gait) and numerical differentiation of noisy measurements have not been explicitly addressed.
We propose an extended Kalman filter that estimates relative IMU orientation and sensor location simultaneously, requiring neither offline sensor location calibration nor a global orientation anchor.
A systematic simulation study shows that the quality of the relative orientation and the sensor location estimates depends on different motion-intensity sources: the joint center acceleration and the relative angular velocity, respectively.
A low-pass filter (LPF) is used to mitigate real-signal outliers before applying the rigid-body constraint.
When applied to the OpenSense dataset with real IMU measurements across four subjects with three lower-body joint types during walking and complex tasks including various motion types, the proposed method achieves an overall relative orientation error of 2.61∘, compared with 10.40∘ for a baseline using offline-estimated sensor locations and 7.43∘ for a baseline using marker-derived sensor locations. These results show that the proposed calibration-free estimation framework handles real IMU data effectively and achieves accurate relative orientation without offline sensor location calibration.
introduction:
Accurate joint kinematics estimation is fundamental to human motion tracking and reconstruction, with applications in rehabilitation, sports, and entertainment [1, 2, 3]. Inertial measurement units (IMUs) are a practical option for human motion estimation, as they are inexpensive, portable and lightweight, which allows their use outside the laboratory [4, 5, 6]. Joint kinematics can be estimated from single IMU (global) orientation estimates, which are commonly obtained by fusing gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer measurements [7, 8]. However, sensor errors, e.g. due to indoor magnetic disturbances corrupting the magnetometer measurements, lead to erroneous orientation estimates.
Since joint kinematics such as joint angles are described by the relative orientation between adjacent body segments, typically the relative orientation is of most interest. Relative orientation between adjacent sensors can be estimated without the use of magnetometers [6], which is the focus of this work. Note that our focus is on relative sensor orientation, and sensor-to-segment calibration to obtain relative segment orientation is therefore outside the scope.

Existing methods for relative orientation estimation typically rely on assumptions regarding joint type [9, 10], offline calibration [11], or have primarily been validated on simulated IMU measurements [12] or real walking motions [11, 13], limiting their practical applicability.
In this work, we enable magnetometer-free and calibration-free 3D joint kinematic estimation using real IMU measurements during diverse human motions.

To this end, we extend the method of [11] to jointly estimate the relative sensor orientation and sensor locations online using only acceleration and angular velocity measurements, eliminating the need for offline sensor location calibration.
A systematic simulation study shows that, under sufficient joint center acceleration intensity, online sensor location estimation does not degrade orientation estimation accuracy. It further shows that orientation and sensor location estimation are primarily governed by joint center acceleration and relative angular velocity, respectively.
To improve reliability on real IMU measurements, we mitigate high-frequency measurement outliers caused by foot-strike impacts in the acceleration and numerical differentiation of angular velocity using a low-pass filter (LPF).
Finally, the proposed framework is extensively validated on the OpenSense dataset [14], containing walking and diverse lower-body motions.

title: RGraph-Eval: Task-Grounded Scene Graphs for Evaluating Robot Video Generation
authors: Aleksandr Lazarev,Sofia Zimina,Roman Kuznetsov,Tatiana Zemskova,Iaroslav Koshelev,Dmitry Yudin
abstract: Generated robot videos can look convincing while depicting the wrong interaction: a different object is moved, a grasp disappears, or a placement ends outside its destination. We introduce RGraph-Eval, a reference-based framework that makes these discrepancies explicit through task-grounded temporal scene graphs. Unlike approaches that construct separate evidence representations for different evaluation dimensions, we organize task entities, interactions, and motion within a unified, interpretable scene graph representation. A foundation-model pipeline identifies manipulation roles, grounds persistent object masks, infers and verifies state transitions and action intervals, and reconstructs manipulated-object motion in three dimensions. Applying this representation to a generated video and a reference demonstration supports an interpretable RGraph-Eval score with visible-object, relation-change, and 3D path-shape components. We also introduce ShareRobot-SG, a collection of 1,000 manipulation scenes from ten ShareRobot sources annotated with the multimodal representation. Our evaluation separates graph-generation quality from agreement with human video judgments, and includes comparisons with adapted SVG2 and SG-Ego, a benchmark of three video generators. The framework connects robot-video assessment to the observable entities and interactions underlying a task, while making the graph annotations reusable beyond evaluation. Code will be publicly available at https://github.com/SashaDance/rgraph-eval.
introduction:
Video generation depicts possible robot behavior from an initial observation and a language goal, supporting behavior inspection, visual demonstrations, and data generation for robot learning (Mei et al., 2026). Generated videos can serve as an additional source of training data, complementing demonstrations collected through physical interaction. Recent work explores scalable robot data synthesis with compositional world models (Ye et al., 2026) and learning robotic manipulation by imitating generated videos without physical demonstrations (Patel et al., 2026). However, using generated videos as a data source requires assessing their quality: visually realistic sequences may still depict incorrect object motion, inconsistent interactions, or failed task outcomes. Evaluation should therefore assess not only visual appearance but also whether the generated behavior preserves task-relevant entities, interactions, and final states.

Consider the instruction “stack the white plate onto the red plate.” A plausible video can move the wrong plate, omit the grasp, or leave the white plate beside the red one. Such errors may occupy a small region while the background remains stable. Conversely, different speeds or intermediate motions can preserve the intended interaction. Evaluation must distinguish appearance, object identity, temporal interaction, and the achieved state.

Existing evaluators address complementary parts of this problem. General video benchmarks assess visual and temporal quality (Huang et al., 2024). Robotics and world-model benchmarks emphasize instruction following and physical consistency (Deng et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025). Reference-based methods compare a prediction with an observed execution (Wei et al., 2026). Learned reward models additionally approximate human preferences or task progress (Liu et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026; He et al., 2025). These approaches provide useful assessments, but their scores need not identify which visible object or interaction accounts for a disagreement. A structural representation can supply that missing connection between an assessment and the evidence in the video.

Task-grounded temporal scene graphs connect assessment to this evidence. We call these graphs task-grounded because their entities and relations are selected with respect to the manipulation goal: they represent the robot, manipulated object, relevant supports and target, and their task-relevant interactions rather than exhaustively describing the entire scene. Nodes identify task entities, masks ground them in image regions, relations describe changing interactions, and trajectories capture motion.

Graph-based assessment depends on extraction quality: incorrect object assignments propagate through tracking, relations, and geometry, while language models may infer goal-consistent rather than observed outcomes. We address these risks through visual grounding, persistent tracking, and independent verification, and evaluate graph quality separately from human alignment.

Figure 1 summarizes the framework. We make three contributions. First, we introduce a foundation-model pipeline for annotating manipulation videos with grounded temporal graphs, including masks, states, actions, and estimated 3D motion. Second, we present ShareRobot-SG, a 1,000-scene collection spanning ten manipulation sources for studying the quality and breadth of this representation. Third, we introduce reference-based RGraph-Eval assessment with an explicit component decomposition, evaluated through human alignment, generator comparison, and component analysis.

title: To Route or to Adapt? Multi-Expert Diffusion Planners in Unseen Regions
authors: Yun Li,Ehsan Javanmardi,Simon Thompson,Jiachen Gong,Qunli Zhang,Zifan Zeng,Shiming Liu,Peng Wang,Yidu Zhang,Manabu Tsukada
comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026). . Code and weights:this https URL
abstract:
Diffusion trajectory planners with domain-specific experts
face a practical question in unseen regions: can they
rely on selecting among existing experts, or must the
planner itself adapt? We study this question using a
planner with a shared adapter and per-domain expert
adapters. Across three real-world held-out maps, none
of eight test-time routing schemes improves the
fleet-mean lateral offset over the static default,
which uses the same expert for every scene. Even an
oracle that selects the best expert for each scene
reduces the mean offset by only 0.90.9 m. In contrast,
reward-based fine-tuning on just 2020 target-region
scenes yields substantially larger gains. On matched
evaluation slices, joint replay achieves a fleet-mean
offset of 6.96.9 m, compared with 12.412.4 m for the
static default. Comparisons under the same target-region
training budget show that target-region training drives
the improvement, while replaying training scenes limits
forgetting on the original ODDs. On nuPlan, fine-tuning
across training cities also improves open-loop offsets,
although closed-loop performance deteriorates.
Further diagnostics reveal that two test-time adaptation
baselines achieve low offsets by producing degenerate
trajectories. These results show the limited headroom
for selecting among existing experts and the greater
open-loop gains available from adapting the planner.
introduction:
Deploying a trajectory planner in an unseen region
presents a challenge for models trained with
domain-specific experts. One approach is to select
the most suitable expert for each new scene,
reusing what the planner has already learned.
Another is to update the model using data from
the new region. The former avoids additional
training but is limited by the available experts;
the latter can change the planner’s predictions
but risks degrading performance on the original
training domains. How much can expert selection
actually achieve before adaptation becomes necessary?

We investigate this question using a reward-fine-tuned
diffusion trajectory planner [1, 2] with a shared adapter and four
per-ODD expert adapters. The four training ODDs
are ODD-Hongo (the University of Tokyo’s Hongo
campus), ODD-Kashiwa (suburban Kashiwa),
ODD-Shalun (a controlled test site),
and ODD-Nagoya (Nagoya University campus).
The three held-out maps are Knowledge Hub
(a research campus), Ishiodai (a suburban
district), and Morikoro (an open park), all in
Aichi Prefecture, Japan.
Within the Generator–Selector framework of the
Autoware end-to-end reference
architecture [3], we compare
methods that select among existing expert
trajectories with methods that modify the
planner’s adapter weights,
as shown in Figure 1.

We first examine whether routing can make better
use of the existing experts. Across the three
held-out maps, none of eight routing schemes
improves the fleet-mean lateral offset over the
static default, which uses the geographically
nearest training expert (ODD-Nagoya on all three
maps). More importantly, an oracle that selects
the lowest-offset expert trajectory for each
scene improves the mean offset by only 0.90.9 m.
Even perfect selection among the four existing
trajectories therefore offers little additional
benefit. We next examine whether updating the
planner can overcome this limitation.
Fine-tuning the shared adapter on geometrically
perturbed training scenes improves performance
on the open-park map, while reward-based
fine-tuning with 2020 target-region scenes
provides substantially larger gains.
On matched evaluation slices, joint replay,
which mixes target-region and training scenes
during fine-tuning, achieves a fleet-mean
offset of 6.96.9 m, compared with 12.412.4 m
for the static default. Comparisons with
other fine-tuning methods show that
target-region training drives the improvement,
while replay primarily preserves performance
on the original training ODDs.

We also examine the limits of these improvements.
On nuPlan, fine-tuning across three training
cities reduces open-loop lateral offset in each
held-out city but degrades closed-loop performance.
In addition, two test-time adaptation baselines
produce low lateral offsets by collapsing toward
nearly stationary or scene-independent trajectories.
These observations distinguish improvements
in open-loop trajectory metrics from improvements
in driving behaviour, which remain to be established
for the proposed adaptation methods.

title: AstroBench: Benchmarking Free-Floating Capture and Space Robotic Manipulation
authors: Zizhe Wang(1),Jia Deng(1),Xin Lu(1),Zehao Jia(1),Yi Huang(2),Yao Zhu(2) ((1) Astroup Lab, Beijing, China, (2) Harbin Institute of Technology, Beijing Research Institute)
comment: . Code and assets:this https URL; project website:this https URL
abstract: Capturing a loose object inside a spacecraft requires a robot to approach a target that can translate and rotate, and whose motion changes when contact is made. These conditions motivate evaluation beyond manipulation of supported objects. We introduce AstroBench, an open benchmark for free-floating capture and space robotic manipulation with a fixed-base arm. The task suite combines four initial-motion tracks with sample-storage operations based on MELFI hardware and cap and captive-screw servicing based on the Robotic Refueling Mission. The two workcells provide nine task definitions and 29 task–target combinations. A metadata-filtered Objaverse inventory supplies 8,414 object instances for asset expansion, alongside five cabin visual contexts and versioned task instructions. We report two acquisition-focused experiments using existing checkpoints. A frozen π0.5\pi_{0.5} DROID joint-position policy captures 2 of 200 static targets and 4 of 200 moving targets across twenty object identities. A cube-specific ACT policy captures 8 of 10 static targets and 6 of 10 moving targets in a separate experiment. Each experiment retains its recorded observation, action and capture configuration. The results document difficult direct transfer for the tested generalist checkpoint and successful task-specific capture behavior, while identifying concrete settings for studying motion-aware perception and contact-sensitive control. Code, task definitions and editable workcell assets are available at https://github.com/AstroUpLab/AstroBench.
introduction:
Loose-object recovery, sample handling and equipment servicing are useful capabilities for robots operating inside spacecraft. A robot may need to intercept a drifting tool, transfer a sample card into a storage box, or engage a service interface with a specialized tool. Although these tasks share components with terrestrial manipulation, their physical setup changes the role of support, approach direction and contact. A free object has no table to resist an incidental push. A storage or service interface instead provides an explicit fixture, whose geometry determines where the robot can move and how the operation should be completed.

Free-floating capture offers a particularly direct way to study this difference. Even a target initialized at rest can move after the fingers touch it. A translating or rotating target adds an interception problem: the robot must align the gripper with a useful grasp configuration before that configuration moves away. The visual observation, the action prediction and the resulting contact therefore correspond to different moments of a changing scene. Capture performance depends jointly on recognizing the object, approaching it, and coordinating contact with gripper closure.

Existing robot benchmarks have established effective ways to organize language-conditioned tasks, test transfer and vary environments [1, 2, 3]. Space Robotics Bench further develops robot-learning infrastructure for mission-relevant space environments [4]. We build on this approach by focusing on free-floating object acquisition and a small set of hardware-grounded space operations. The benchmark separates the target object, initial motion, visual context and operation goal, so that each can be recorded and varied explicitly.

AstroBench contains three task groups (Fig. 1). Free-floating capture uses static, drifting, tumbling and faster-tumbling initial conditions. A MELFI-inspired storage workcell supports card transfer, insertion and extraction, together with lid opening and closing. An RRM-inspired service workcell supports removal and stowage of FDV1 and SMA caps and loosening or tightening of captive screws. The hardware workcells are authored from NASA and ESA references, with identifiable moving parts, target frames and tool interfaces. The arm has a fixed base throughout; the free-floating body in the capture tasks is the target object.

This paper evaluates capture as an acquisition event: an episode succeeds when the target first satisfies the recorded capture detector. We examine two existing policy configurations. The first is a frozen π0.5\pi_{0.5} DROID joint-position checkpoint evaluated on twenty objects, each under static and dynamic conditions. The second is ACT trained on a local cube task, evaluated at ten positions under both conditions. The experiments document what each tested system can capture and provide concrete traces for further analysis.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we organize a space manipulation suite that combines controlled initial object motion with storage and servicing tasks derived from real hardware references. Second, we release an extensible resource comprising an 8,414-instance object inventory, five cabin visual contexts, editable workcell assets and explicit language-conditioned task specifications. Third, we report acquisition results and reproducible execution settings for a generalist-policy transfer experiment and a task-specific imitation-learning experiment. Together, these resources support study of object motion, contact formation and precise operation goals in a common task framework.

title: Tilt-Rotor Quadcopter with Learned Residual Control and Mode-Dependent State Estimation
authors: Ninad Joshi,Prabhat Kumar
