title: ProTrav: Probabilistic Traversability with Elevation Uncertainty Propagation for Risk-aware Off-road Navigation
authors: Chuanlin Zuo,Miloš Prágr,Arun Kumar Singh,Mohammad Loni,Reza Ghabcheloo
abstract:
Reliable traversability estimation is essential for autonomous navigation on unstructured terrain.
State-of-the-art approaches typically evaluate traversability from deterministic terrain elevation, thereby overlooking spatial correlations in the terrain and failing to account for how elevation uncertainty propagates through nonlinear traversability mappings.
We propose ProTrav, a probabilistic terrain representation that uses function-space sampling to generate spatially correlated terrain realizations and propagate elevation uncertainty to traversability cost.
First, a Sparse Variational Gaussian Process (SVGP) reconstructs a probabilistic elevation field from observations.
Then, posterior function-space sampling generates spatially correlated terrain realizations, preserving spatial dependencies between neighboring locations while propagating elevation uncertainty through geometric features into traversability cost.
Consequently, a distribution of traversability cost at arbitrary location is established, where the mean and standard deviation quantify the expected traversability cost and associated uncertainty, respectively.
A risk term is defined by moment-based Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) and incorporated into a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller for risk-aware navigation.
Simulation experiments demonstrate navigation success rates exceeding 90% on different terrains, compared with below 40% for a baseline, while reducing attitude variations.
Furthermore, the proposed approach is validated on a robot traversing real-world off-road terrain.
introduction:
Autonomous navigation in off-road environments depends on an accurate representation of terrain traversability [1, 2].
Unlike structured roads, off-road terrain exhibits substantial geometric variation, where slope, roughness, and step height directly affect robot stability and mobility.
We focus on LiDAR, which is widely used for terrain perception due to its ability to provide accurate distance measurements.
However, in practical environments, LiDAR observations are inherently sparse, irregularly distributed, and affected by measurement noise and occlusion.
Therefore, uncertainty is an intrinsic property of terrain perception.

Recent work has begun incorporating probabilistic terrain models into traversability analysis and path planning to account for this perceptual uncertainty [3].
In most such approaches, however, geometric features are computed from a single deterministic elevation estimate, typically the posterior mean of a probabilistic terrain elevation model [4].
Approaches that explicitly enumerate elevation uncertainty commonly use it only as a mask or inject it into the cost through heuristic inflation, rather than propagating it through subsequent feature extraction [5].
Such mean-first strategy introduces a fundamental limitation for traversability estimation because geometric features are usually nonlinear mappings of elevation.
By Jensen’s inequality, the expected feature generally cannot be recovered by evaluating a nonlinear mapping at the expected elevation.
This issue can arise, for example, near a partially observed negative obstacle as shown in Fig. 1.
There, mean elevation field may smooth the underlying discontinuity and underestimate its risk.
More generally, extracting features directly from the expected elevation can suppress terrain variations that are critical for identifying steep slopes, steps, and partially observed regions.
Furthermore, treating elevation uncertainty independently at individual cells neglects the spatial correlations of continuous terrain.
Since geometric features are inherently neighborhood operators instead of one location, their uncertainty depends on the joint uncertainty of the underlying elevation patch.
Ignoring these spatial dependencies can therefore further prevent faithful characterization of traversability [6].

We address these limitations by formulating terrain traversability estimation as a probabilistic terrain representation problem.
The terrain surface is modeled as a continuous stochastic function using a Sparse Variational Gaussian Process (SVGP).
We draw function-space realizations from the SVGP posterior, obtaining spatially correlated elevation fields.
For each realization, slope, roughness, and step height are computed and combined into a traversability cost, from which an empirical distribution of traversability costs is obtained across the realizations.
The mean and standard deviation of this distribution characterize the expected traversability cost and its associated uncertainty, respectively.
Based on these moments, a risk term is constructed using an Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) and incorporated into the cost function of a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller, forming a risk-aware navigation framework.
The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows.

Terrain traversability estimation is formulated as a probabilistic terrain representation problem, explicitly propagating perception and elevation uncertainty to traversability cost.

A function-space sampling strategy based on the posterior used to generate spatially correlated terrain realizations and characterize uncertainty in nonlinear geometric and traversability mapping.

A risk-aware MPPI navigation framework integrating ProTrav with UCB-based risk, validated across diverse terrains in both simulation and real-world experiments.

1. Terrain traversability estimation is formulated as a probabilistic terrain representation problem, explicitly propagating perception and elevation uncertainty to traversability cost.

2. A function-space sampling strategy based on the posterior used to generate spatially correlated terrain realizations and characterize uncertainty in nonlinear geometric and traversability mapping.

3. A risk-aware MPPI navigation framework integrating ProTrav with UCB-based risk, validated across diverse terrains in both simulation and real-world experiments.

title: TEAR: Task-Evidence Authority Routing for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Shicheng Zhang,Hui Liu,Haoliang Li
abstract:
Reliable robotic manipulation in field-deployed settings requires more than
executing a capable controller. As the execution conditions change, the system
must decide, online and on the robot side, which control source should hold
authority. Human teleoperation adapts readily to contact-rich and
semantically ambiguous situations but depends on a stable communication
link. Local autonomy is executed without continuous human intervention, but may
fail under semantic ambiguity, long-horizon drift, and unforeseen
contingencies. These two control sources exhibit complementary reliability
profiles.
We formulate this complementarity as a control-authority routing problem and
present Task-Evidence Authority Routing for Robotic Manipulation
(TEAR), an edge-deployable framework that allocates authority between human
teleoperation and local autonomy. TEAR arbitrates on the robot side using
network-state evidence, which governs the usability of teleoperation, and
task-semantic evidence, which reflects whether autonomous execution remains
consistent with the current task. A lightweight temporal arbitrator observes
both forms of evidence together with robot state and current authority to
time authority transfers.
Across simulated and real-world trials under dynamic network conditions,
TEAR achieves task success rates close to pure teleoperation while limiting teleoperation to 19.8–27.4% of control steps and improves success by 30–40% over
autonomy-only execution in our settings. These results demonstrate the
potential of complementary authority routing to sustain successful
manipulation with substantially reduced dependence on continuous human
control.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation [35, 14, 29] is increasingly deployed beyond structured laboratory settings, in production-oriented and field-deployed environments where both communication quality and task conditions can vary over time. In such settings, reliability depends not only on the capability of the robot controller, but also on which source of control is in charge as execution conditions change.
Human teleoperation remains one of the most dependable mechanisms for contact-rich and semantically ambiguous manipulation, because human experts can immediately adapt to unexpected contacts, partial observability, object displacement, and other contingencies. This reliability, however, is conditional on a stable communication loop. Classical teleoperation research has shown that latency and packet loss fundamentally affect transparency, stability, and user performance.
More recent networked robotics studies further emphasise that latency, jitter, and packet loss remain practical bottlenecks for remote operation systems [20, 22]. When the link deteriorates, the human may still know what should be done, but the robot no longer receives commands.

A direct response to this communication bottleneck is to reduce dependence on the remote operator through autonomous robot policies. Modern imitation learning and foundation model policies can map visual observations and task instructions to robot actions, and recent vision language action (VLA) models further transfer semantic knowledge from large scale vision language pretraining to robotic control [6, 42, 21, 3, 30]. Because such policies execute locally on the robot, they no longer depend on continuous human commands or on a stable command link, which directly addresses the failure mode described above. Autonomy alone, however, does not remove the need for human judgment. Learned policies may still stall, drift, or fail under semantic ambiguity, distribution shift, and unforeseen task contingencies. The two control sources therefore fail in different ways. Teleoperation remains adaptive but network dependent, and autonomous execution is locally available but semantically brittle.

Since neither control source alone can sustain reliable execution under
changing communication and task conditions, prior work has studied how
human and autonomous control can be coordinated. Classical shared autonomy
blends human and robot commands or infers the operator’s goal to assist
task execution [9, 17, 13, 16].
Mode-switching frameworks further automate transitions between autonomous
and teleoperated modes while accounting for communication
cost [22]. Recent delay-aware shared autonomy adjusts the
contributions of human and autonomous control using teleoperation
transparency and autonomy confidence under network
delay [11]. Policy uncertainty has also been used
to determine when human intervention is required during autonomous
execution [15].

Our target setting further considers changes in both communication
quality and autonomous task execution during manipulation. The remote
command stream can be affected by latency, jitter, and packet loss, while
the local autonomous policy may encounter stalled progress, weak
engagement with the target, or undesired task states. Authority allocation
therefore requires evidence about the usability of remote control and the
current state of autonomous execution. The decision must also remain
available on the robot side as communication conditions change.
Motivated by this setting, we formulate control allocation as an
authority-routing problem between remote human teleoperation and an
independently executable local policy. The router observes both network
and task evidence over time and determines when authority should be
transferred between control courses.

We therefore present Task-Evidence Authority Routing (TEAR), an
edge-deployable framework for robot-side authority routing between human
teleoperation and local VLA control. First, TEAR combines network-state
evidence with task-semantic evidence. Network evidence characterizes the
usability of remote teleoperation, while task-semantic evidence captures
the execution state of local autonomy using a frozen vision-language
model and task-specific text probes prepared offline from the task
specification and demonstrations. Second, a causal temporal convolutional
network predicts upcoming handoffs from the recent history of network
conditions, task-semantic cues, robot proprioception, and current
authority. Third, a stateful gate with hysteresis and cooldown converts
predicted events into discrete authority transfers. Evidence estimation
and routing run locally without online queries from external models.

Across simulation and real-world experiments under time-varying network
conditions, we demonstrate that TEAR achieves task success rates close to
continuous teleoperation while using teleoperation for only
19.8–27.4% of control steps, improving success by 30–40%
points over autonomy-only execution in our evaluated settings. In summary, our contributions are:

We introduce TEAR, an edge-deployable framework that jointly uses
network-state and task-semantic evidence to predict handoff events over
time, and converts these predictions into stable authority transfers
through a stateful gate with hysteresis and cooldown.

We evaluate TEAR in simulated and real-world manipulation under
time-varying network impairment, demonstrating its task success close to
continuous teleoperation with substantially less human control, and
analyze the visual and network evidence associated with expert handoffs.

1. We introduce TEAR, an edge-deployable framework that jointly uses
network-state and task-semantic evidence to predict handoff events over
time, and converts these predictions into stable authority transfers
through a stateful gate with hysteresis and cooldown.

2. We evaluate TEAR in simulated and real-world manipulation under
time-varying network impairment, demonstrating its task success close to
continuous teleoperation with substantially less human control, and
analyze the visual and network evidence associated with expert handoffs.

title: Robot Motion Transition with Human Motion Prior
authors: Taehyun Byun,Taemoon Jeong,Yoonbyung Chai,Woojin Wie,Insu Park,Kyungjae Lee,Sungjoon Choi
abstract:
Humanoid motion-tracking policies can reproduce diverse behaviors, yet connecting independently acquired motions into a continuous sequence remains challenging. Interpolation connects boundary poses without considering whether their relative position, heading, and timing provide suitable conditions for a transition. A generative motion prior can produce richer motion, but poorly arranged boundaries may cause it to generate excessive locomotion, turning, or another unintended action. We present Spatio-Temporal Alignment with a Motion Prior (STAMP), a framework for connecting independently acquired humanoid motions through a Robot-to-Human-to-Robot process. STAMP uses human motion space to draw on rich motion priors and reuse transition knowledge across robot embodiments. Its key component is a learned alignment model that determines the boundary conditions for motion inbetweening. Given the two motions retargeted to a human rig, the alignment model ranks candidate positions, headings, and transition durations for the following motion. A human motion prior generates the transition under the selected alignment.
The completed sequence is retargeted to the robot and used as a reference to train a motion-tracking policy. We evaluate the tracking success of the generated transitions on Unitree G1 and ROBOTIS K1. Physical robot demonstrations further show that STAMP connects independently acquired motions into long-horizon sequences. Project page: https://childtoy.github.io/STAMP-project
introduction:
Recent advances in physics-based motion tracking enable humanoid robots to reproduce diverse and dynamic motions [1, 2, 3]. However, tracking individual motions and connecting independently acquired motions into a continuous sequence are different problems.

Robot motions are commonly generated and validated as separate clips. When two clips are connected, the position and heading of the following motion and the time available for the transition are not given. Two motions can each be plausible on their own but difficult to connect under an arbitrary relative placement. These spatial and temporal choices determine the body movement required between their boundaries.

A simple approach is to return the robot to a predefined pose between motions, but this stop-and-restart behavior interrupts the motion flow. Another approach is to interpolate directly between the two boundary poses. However, directly interpolating boundary poses alone does
not account for the incoming and outgoing motion or foot-contact changes. For a humanoid, a change in the support foot may require a step or a transfer of body weight that pose interpolation does not explicitly model.

Recent approaches handle humanoid motion transitions through graph-based motion switching, motion matching, or policy blending [4, 5, 6]. These methods transition at intermediate states selected for compatibility, or blend policies around the switching point. As a result, the constituent motions may be truncated or altered, and the content of each motion is not necessarily preserved. STAMP instead connects the end of the preceding motion to the start of the following motion while preserving both input clips.

Motion inbetweening generates missing motion between given boundary
conditions [7, 8, 9].
Human motion data provide rich examples of body movements and contact
changes for learning such transitions [10, 11].
MotionBricks further demonstrates the use of motion inbetweening for
real-world humanoid control [12].

However, inbetweening boundaries extracted from a continuous motion
already have a defined spatial and temporal relationship. Independently
acquired motions do not provide this relationship. Applying a motion
prior to an arbitrary arrangement may require excessive locomotion,
turning, or another unintended action to connect the motions. Connecting such motions therefore requires selecting suitable boundary conditions before generating the transition.

To address this problem, we propose Spatio-Temporal Alignment with a Motion Prior (STAMP), a Robot-to-Human-to-Robot framework that connects robot motions through a shared human motion space. STAMP learns from continuous human motion to rank candidate positions, headings, and transition durations, then uses a human motion prior to generate a transition under the selected conditions. The completed sequence is retargeted to the target robot and used to train a robot-specific motion-tracking policy. Experiments on Unitree G1 and ROBOTIS K1 evaluate the trackability of the resulting transitions, and physical robot demonstrations show their use in longer motion compositions.

Our contributions are summarized as follows.

We introduce STAMP, a Robot-to-Human-to-Robot framework
that uses human motion knowledge to connect independently
acquired humanoid motions across different robot embodiments.

We introduce STAMP, a Robot-to-Human-to-Robot framework
that uses human motion knowledge to connect independently
acquired humanoid motions across different robot embodiments.

We learn a spatial and temporal alignment model from
continuous human motions and counterfactual boundary arrangements.
The model ranks candidate positions, headings, and transition
durations to select boundary conditions for motion inbetweening.

We evaluate robot tracking success on Unitree G1 and ROBOTIS K1 against
interpolation and generative motion baselines, analyze alignment
selection through a ranking ablation, and demonstrate long-horizon
motion compositions on the ROBOTIS K1.

that uses human motion knowledge to connect independently
acquired humanoid motions across different robot embodiments.

The model ranks candidate positions, headings, and transition

title: Adaptive Aerial Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning via LLM-Assisted Proactive Task Generation
authors: Jingyu Ru,Xiangyuan Xie,Lixuan Jin,Jian An,Xingming Zhang,Binghao Li,Siyu Wang,Xiang Zhou,Lei Yuan,Hongli Xu,Yang Yu
abstract: Loco-manipulation extends the workspace of conventional manipulation by combining mobility with physical interaction, while aerial loco-manipulation further expands this capability into three-dimensional space, enabling robots to reach environments inaccessible to ground-based systems. Moving to an aerial platform, however, gives rise to a demanding control problem, since the vehicle must track trajectories accurately in three dimensions while the motion of the arm and its interaction with the environment continuously shift the center of mass, alter the inertia, and impose force and moment disturbances on the body. Conventional controllers address these effects through explicit models and estimation, whereas learning-based controllers infer dynamics from experience, yet control rewards provide no direct target for the response information retained from history, and fixed task sampling can leave persistent tracking difficulties insufficiently explored. We present ALMA, an aerial loco-manipulation framework for adaptive flight control under external arm commands. ALMA employs a contextual flight policy that adapts from recent measurements and actions, using action-conditioned prediction of future measurement representations to train its context to retain response information relevant to flight control. To expand the experience available for this adaptation, an evolutionary process uses a large language model (LLM) to analyze observed control difficulties and propose new structures of arm motion for subsequent training. In simulation, ALMA reduces position root-mean-square error (RMSE) by up to 24.7% relative to the strongest baseline, while the same policy transfers zero-shot to the aerial manipulator and reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion relative to the real-world baseline.
introduction:
Loco-manipulation extends the workspace of conventional manipulation by combining mobility with physical interaction, while aerial loco-manipulation further expands this capability into three-dimensional space, enabling robots to reach and operate in elevated, cluttered, and hazardous environments inaccessible to ground-based systems Ollero et al. (2021). However, changes in arm configuration continuously alter the mass distribution and inertia of the complete system, while joint accelerations and physical contact generate reaction forces and moments on the aerial base Yadav et al. (2024). The flight controller must therefore maintain accurate trajectory tracking while adapting to changes in system response that are only partially revealed by available measurements.

Conventional aerial manipulation controllers compensate for uncertain manipulation effects through analytically designed feedback and adaptive laws Yadav et al. (2024); Sharma et al. (2025), whereas learning-based methods infer dynamics information from experience. Aco2 Jin et al. (2026) learns a history-dependent context using contrastive supervision to distinguish payload conditions, while the controller in Ujjawal et al. (2026) learns multi-step dynamics residuals and adapts their predictions online for disturbance compensation. Their auxiliary objectives respectively organize context by task identity and train a residual predictor for a prescribed compensation law, while predictive-state methods use future observations to supervise the internal representation used for decision making Venkatraman et al. (2017); Hefny et al. (2018). For aerial manipulation, similar instantaneous measurements can correspond to different hidden actuator and disturbance states that require different corrective actions. Predicting future measurement representations conditioned on recorded actions provides a direct training target for retaining these response distinctions in the history representation used by the flight policy. Since the available response information depends on the motion conditions encountered during training, repeatedly sampling fixed motion patterns can leave persistent tracking difficulties insufficiently explored, motivating adaptive sampling Jiang et al. (2021); Mehta et al. (2020) and task generation Parker-Holder et al. (2022) that direct subsequent experience according to the policy’s evolving performance.

We present ALMA, an aerial loco-manipulation framework for adaptive flight control under external arm commands. Inspired by the JEPA Assran et al. (2023), ALMA trains its contextual flight policy by predicting learned representations of future measurements from recent history and subsequent actions, thereby supervising the information retained for control. Since learning this adaptation also depends on the responses encountered during training, ALMA uses a large language model (LLM) to analyze episode records, identify motion patterns associated with poor tracking, and propose new structures of arm motion that direct subsequent experience toward difficulties insufficiently addressed by the initial task distribution. Predictive supervision thus trains the context using measured action–response relationships, while task generation broadens the motion conditions that supply subsequent experience, connecting response learning with the policy’s remaining tracking difficulties. Both components operate during training, while deployment retains the contextual flight policy to adapt to the changing effects of manipulation.

In simulation, ALMA achieves the lowest mean position RMSE among evaluated controllers, reducing error relative to the strongest baseline by 24.5% under static arm commands and 24.7% under periodic commands, while ablations support the tracking benefit of predictive supervision and the generalization benefit of task generation, with base performance retained. The same policy transfers zero-shot to the aerial manipulator and reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion relative to the real-world baseline.

title: EBV-CAN: Vision--Language Grounding for Contact-Aided Endoscope Navigation
authors: Chi Kit Ng,Shuchang Liu,Jinsong Lin,Yidong Zhang,Xizi Wang,Ho Yin Chim,Hongliang Ren
abstract: Flexible endoscopes exploit structural compliance to traverse narrow lumens, pipes, and cavities, where navigation involves distributed environmental contact. This compliance makes tip motion depend on the evolving support configuration. We present external bird’s-eye-view contact-aided navigation (EBV-CAN), a vision-language policy that combines one initial global static bird’s-eye image with evolving endoscopic observations and motor state. Three supervised semantic queries locate the tip, next waypoint, and instructed target on the cached global image; their residual representations predict bending and insertion commands. We introduce the Vision-Language Contact-Aided (VLCA) dataset, linking 517 demonstrations and 75k action samples to 958k spatial entries and 93k remaining-route records. On 50 held-out episodes, tip-coordinate and waypoint localization reach 97.5% and 94.8%. Swapping the target instruction under identical observations changes target attention and motor output across 17 dual-target episodes. Across 1,920 physical trials of eight policies trained under a shared protocol, EBV-CAN achieves 183/240 successes (76.25%) under automatic blue-area scoring. Gated recurrent unit behavior cloning (GRU-BC) achieves the lowest matched-task offline mean absolute error (MAE), 0.056, and 1/240 physical successes, establishing distinct rankings for action imitation and task completion. Successful multi-guide executions and representative failures connect spatial progress, steering transitions, and visibility to physical navigation.
introduction:
Flexible endoscopes and continuum robots combine a slender body with distributed compliance, enabling access through confined and curved spaces [1, 2, 3]. Navigation couples perception, robot mechanics, and sequential decisions: the controller selects a route, advances the shaft, and adjusts the distal view as the robot interacts with its surroundings. Reviews of medical robotics and autonomous intraluminal navigation identify this coordination as a central component of increasing robotic autonomy [4, 5]. For a flexible endoscope with a short actively bending tip and a long passive shaft, the control problem extends along the body. Insertion changes the loaded shaft configuration, while friction and external support change the relation between motor commands and tip displacement [6, 7].

Environmental support provides a mechanism for contact-aided navigation (CAN). A guide constrains part of the passive shaft, creating a support location around which further insertion and distal bending redirect the tip (Fig. 1). Rao et al. exploit environmental contact to produce multiple curvatures in a single-segment tendon-driven robot through motion planning [8]. Ng et al. demonstrate contact-aided endoscope navigation with force-informed reinforcement learning in a deformable stomach simulation [9]. These results motivate learning the timing of guide approach, supported bending, and subsequent advancement from physical demonstrations. In this setting, a successful motor command depends on both the destination and the robot’s progress through a sequence of interactions.

Visual feedback offers complementary evidence at two spatial scales. Endoscopic images resolve nearby surfaces and apparent motion; a global view identifies the arrangement of guides and candidate targets. Learned endoscopic controllers already use monocular depth, virtual eye-in-hand observations, and bronchoscopic images for navigation [10, 11, 12]. Here, the central question is how evolving local evidence updates route progress in a global scene observed once. Near a guide, the endoscopic view (EV) is dominated by nearby geometry, while the instructed destination remains a global property. The controller therefore needs a persistent spatial reference together with a changing estimate of its tip and next waypoint.

Language supplies the target identity within this spatial problem. Language-conditioned imitation and vision-language-action (VLA) models provide mechanisms for mapping task descriptions to behavior [13, 14, 15]. For contact-aided navigation, the practical question is specific: under identical visual observations, does changing the selected target change the spatial prediction and the motor command? Answering this question benefits from annotations that connect an instruction to an object, a route, and a sequence of physical actions. Dense spatial labels also make route progress directly evaluable alongside action imitation.

Evaluation also has a sequential dimension. Offline action mean absolute error (MAE) measures agreement with expert actions at recorded states, whereas physical execution generates subsequent observations through the policy’s own actions. This distinction is central to sequential imitation learning [16]. Contact-aided navigation makes it concrete: a small steering change alters the shaft’s approach to a guide, the support configuration, and the next visible scene. We therefore evaluate action fidelity, spatial progress, and physical endpoints as complementary properties of a navigation policy.

We study this problem on a planar physical platform with two degrees of freedom (DoFs): bending and insertion. The policy receives one initial external bird’s-eye-view (EBV) image, followed by EV images and causal motor state. Continuous feedback comes from the EV and motor channels; the initial EBV provides fixed global context. This observation contract isolates local-to-global estimation under stable scene registration. Contact-related supervision describes visible shaft support and image-space route progress, with visual and motor observations carrying the interaction evidence.

Our external bird’s-eye-view contact-aided navigation (EBV-CAN) policy reads frozen initial-EBV features produced by self-distillation with no labels, version 2 (DINOv2), [1] using tip, waypoint, and target queries conditioned on local observations and language. Spatial supervision connects those queries to route progress, while their residual representations drive bending and insertion. This couples interpretable spatial outputs to feedback control.

The accompanying Vision-Language Contact-Aided (VLCA) dataset links physical demonstrations to object boxes, tip coordinates, canonical guide identities, ordered episode plans, and frame-dependent remaining routes. This combination provides supervision at the observation, spatial-progress, and motor-action levels. Our contributions are:

A spatially grounded vision-language control formulation for contact-aided navigation: evolving endoscopic evidence updates tip and route progress on one initial global static image, and language-conditioned residual queries connect these estimates to motor commands.

VLCA, a physical navigation dataset that connects dense scene geometry to sequential control through canonical guide identities, ordered plans, and remaining-route labels. Its 517 demonstrations, 74,693 action samples, and 957,616 spatial entries support joint study of localization, route transitions, and action prediction.

Physical evidence that action imitation and contact-aided task completion yield distinct policy rankings. Under a shared training protocol and automatic endpoint criterion, EBV-CAN achieves 76.25% success over 240 trials, exceeding the strongest baseline by 60.0 percentage points; spatial and instruction interventions identify how local feedback and target language affect its predictions.

1. A spatially grounded vision-language control formulation for contact-aided navigation: evolving endoscopic evidence updates tip and route progress on one initial global static image, and language-conditioned residual queries connect these estimates to motor commands.

2. VLCA, a physical navigation dataset that connects dense scene geometry to sequential control through canonical guide identities, ordered plans, and remaining-route labels. Its 517 demonstrations, 74,693 action samples, and 957,616 spatial entries support joint study of localization, route transitions, and action prediction.

3. Physical evidence that action imitation and contact-aided task completion yield distinct policy rankings. title: Causal Analysis of Failures of Cyber-Physical Systems with Continuous Inputs
authors: Tom Yaacov,David A. Kelly,Khen Elimelech,Hana Chockler
abstract: Modern autonomous Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs), such as self-driving cars, operate in increasingly complex environments while expected to maintain high reliability. The black-box nature of many of these systems makes it impossible to fully verify their behavior prior to deployment. When a failure occurs, it is important to analyze it to guide improvements to system robustness. A recent work introduced the novel concept of leveraging the framework of actual causality for CPS failure explanation. However, that work considered only a discrete, binary causal model that cannot capture continuous changes in system inputs. In this paper, we address these limitations by extending the actual causality framework with the notion of distance to account for the continuous characteristics of the system. Specifically, we introduce the novel concepts of distance-weighted actual cause and distance-weighted degree of responsibility, enabling causal influence to account for the magnitude of changes required to avoid a failure, rather than only its cardinality. While motivated by the continuous nature of CPSs, this constitutes a general extension of the theory of actual causality and enables more fine-grained analysis of continuous inputs in any causal model. Building on these notions, we present an efficient, practical, system-agnostic explanation-derivation algorithm that uses distance-weighted responsibility to guide the explanation search. We experimentally evaluate our approach across a number of environments from two autonomous-driving simulators with black-box neural controllers. The results show that the proposed extension provides more effective guidance than the current discrete approach.
introduction:
Autonomous robots and Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) are becoming increasingly prevalent in modern life. Such systems leverage digital components to control physical machines that operate in and interact with the real world. To operate safely and reliably, these systems must be robust, i.e., resist failures and maintain performance under a wide range of circumstances [1, 2]. However, due to the complexity of modern systems and the intractability of real-world scenarios, verifying their robustness prior to deployment is unrealistic. This is especially true for systems built on “black-box” neural components, such as controllers and perception units, which typically can only be verified empirically.

When a failure occurs, it is important to analyze it to help ensure that similar scenarios do not repeat in the future, or at least to ensure the user is better prepared to mitigate them if they do.
Perhaps the most useful output of this analysis is an explanation,
identifying the elements in the potentially rich scenario that led to a failure.

Problem definition:
Our goal is, given a specific failure example (input environment and simulated system run), to derive an explanation of the cause of failure. We aim to derive a valid explanation while minimizing the computational effort required to find it.

While the usefulness of causal analysis has been demonstrated for discrete systems, there is little work to connect it to CPS, which have challenging properties such as continuous input variables and temporally extended operations. A recent work [3] was the first to leverage the framework of actual causality to explain CPS failures. We note that, unlike the more common framework of general causality [4], which derives forward-looking, probabilistic causal models, actual causality [5] is backward-looking, using causal models to explain specific past events. The work in [3] took the first step toward bridging the gap between CPSs and actual causality, providing guidelines for integrating a system-testing model with a causal model to ensure correct failure explanations. Since the standard search for such explanations quickly becomes intractable, it also introduced an efficient heuristic-guided explanation-derivation algorithm based on causal degree of responsibility [6, 5]—a quantification of the causal influence of an input variable.

While serving as a stepping stone, that work made significant assumptions. Most importantly, it did not allow for continuous variability of the testing-model inputs. This is a critical limitation, as explanation derivation requires examining modified scenarios and reasoning about their effect on system behavior. Yet, the causal-model inputs accepted only binary valuations: elements could either exist or not exist, but could not vary continuously. This assumption clashes with the continuous nature of CPSs and potentially limits the utility and accuracy of explanations that can be derived. Moreover, this limitation carries over to responsibility, the key heuristic guiding the explanation search. When evaluating modified scenarios to compute an element’s responsibility, the approach cannot distinguish between small and large modifications, as all modifications are treated equally. Consequently, the responsibility measure loses much of its nuance, providing less effective guidance for the search.

In this work, we address these limitations by extending actual causality to account for the continuous characteristics of CPSs and exploiting this extension to effectively derive causal explanations of system failures. In particular, we extend actual causality with the notion of distance, enabling a more fine-grained analysis of continuous inputs. While motivated by the continuous nature of CPSs, this extension constitutes a novel contribution to the theory of actual causality in general, allowing causal influence to account for the magnitude of interventions (i.e., changes to input variables) rather than only their presence. We then leverage this extension and propose an improved responsibility-guided search approach for failure explanations.

Specifically, we make the following contributions: (1) We extend the framework for CPS failure explanation presented in [3] to support continuous causal models. (2) We extend the framework of actual causality itself with the notions of distance-weighted actual cause and distance-weighted responsibility, allowing causal analysis to account for the magnitude of interventions. (3) Building on these notions, we present an improved and more efficient explanation-derivation algorithm for black-box CPSs that uses distance-weighted responsibility to guide the explanation search. (4) We experimentally evaluate our approach against prior work on autonomous-driving systems, demonstrating that it provides more effective and scalable guidance for explanation search.
We further evaluate distance-weighted responsibility by assessing how well it prioritizes the elements involved across multiple possible explanations for a failure, providing further evidence of its effectiveness.

The paper is organized as follows. Sec. II provides preliminaries on the CPS testing model and the actual causality framework and formulates our objectives. Sec. III describes the extension of the actual causality framework with the notion of distance. Sec. IV presents the distance-responsibility-guided failure explanation generation algorithm. The experimental evaluation is covered in Sec. V, and Sec. VI concludes the paper.

Related Work.
Actual causality [5, 7] is well-suited for explaining events that have already occurred and has been extensively applied in explainable AI (XAI), including image, audio and medical classification [7, 8, 9, 10]. The XAI tool ReX approximates causal responsibility to efficiently derive causal explanations [11]. These approaches, like ours, treat the AI model as a black box. Notably, [8] also uses causal responsibility [6] for guiding explanation generation, but is specifically designed for image classification.

In the context of CPSs, the most relevant work to this paper is [3], which uses actual causality to explain failures.
Its algorithm is based on causal responsibility, however, it treats all variables as binary, hence
cannot capture or manipulate continuous dependencies between inputs and outcomes.
Counterfactual reasoning has recently been used for CPS failure analysis [12].
Actual causality extends and generalizes counterfactual reasoning, allowing to capture more subtle dependencies
 [5].

Sensitivity analysis, described in [13], perturbs the position of obstacles in failure-causing scenes to analyze CPSs. This analysis
can identify parts of the environment associated with the failure, but does not generate explanations.
[14] uses a debugger to generate explanations of instrumented CPS failures, an approach whose feasibility depends strongly on the model.
In contrast, our method treats the system as a black box.
[15] learns a Bayesian model from simulation data and uses it to generate explanations, a fundamentally different approach from actual causality. [16] and [17] construct ontology-based representations that integrate sensor and environment information with higher-level knowledge for robotic reasoning. Unlike our approach, these methods rely on explicit knowledge representations and reasoning mechanisms tailored to the robotic system. [18] compares system input/output traces using a state-machine encoding of the CPS rather than performing causal analysis; such a state machine may be unavailable or too complex to explain.

title: When One Step Is Enough: An Empirical Study of Euler Integration in Flow-Matching Policies
authors: Shivakanth Sujit,Luca Nunziante,Rousslan Fernand Julien Dossa,Kai Arulkumaran
comment: Accepted at the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
abstract:
Flow matching is now the dominant approach for vision-language action (VLA) robot policies, thanks to its expressiveness and simple training objective.
However, inference for standard flow matching requires iteratively solving an ODE, limiting the control frequency at deployment.
While several works have proposed novel methods to allow for single-shot action generation, we ask whether such additional objectives are actually necessary.
We find that across six flow matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale: multi-step integration confers little to no consistent advantage at inference. We empirically find that this holds as long as models are sufficiently trained and have enough capacity.
Practically, the implication is that for large VLAs, the single-step policy comes essentially for free from the multi-step model, enabling low-latency deployment without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives.
introduction:
Diffusion and flow matching models have now become the common choice for training robotic control policies for manipulation [8, 35, 41, 26, 13], consistently outperforming simple regression/Gaussian baselines. To generate action samples, these models learn a vector field that drives noise samples, taken from a source distribution, to a target distribution. Of these, flow matching is now the dominant paradigm by virtue of its simpler form (solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE) instead of a stochastic differential equation (SDE)). Many of the latest robot foundation models, in the form of vision-language-action (VLA) models, combine a large, pretrained vision-language model (VLM) backbone [21, 37, 3, 1], providing existing image and text understanding, with a flow matching action head [32, 43, 29, 4, 39, 5].

In flow matching policies, a velocity field is learned and generating actions requires integrating the learned velocity field, typically with an Euler integrator that evaluates the network NN times.
Higher NN results in lower discretization error at the cost of increased latency, thus limiting control frequency, and subsequently hurting fluid motion in dynamic or contact-rich tasks.
Recent works mitigate these issues by distilling the multi-step policy into a single-step proxy [26], introducing distribution-shaping objectives that are expensive for large-scale VLAs [16], or augmenting the flow matching objective to encourage straight-line flows that need fewer integration steps [27, 38, 11, 12].
This multi-step formulation also necessitates backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) for gradient-based optimization of reinforcement learning (RL) objectives, which is costly and prone to unstable gradients.

Due to the simplicity of its formulation, in practice VLAs are trained with the rectified flow matching objective) [19], where the target velocity along each training pair is constant, producing linear interpolation paths between source and target samples. It is not the case in general that the learned trajectories are straight, as intersecting linear paths produce curved learned trajectories, which in image generation degrades single-step sample quality [19].
However, for robot control, given the current observation and state, the nature of the conditional target distribution may differ substantially from the image generation setting.
Prior work [25] finds that, for control policies, the performance advantage of generative models over regression ones mainly comes from stochasticity injection and the dense supervision signal during training, rather than from modeling multimodality, which they find largely absent in robotics datasets (including the ones understood to be multimodal like Push T), likely due to their high-dimensional observation space.
Concurrent work [7] reaches a similar conclusion for VLAs, but studies a single architecture, focusing on training hyperparameters on LIBERO [18] and its variants, with a small real-world experiment. In contrast, we study six VLAs across multiple benchmarks, run a large-scale real-world evaluation, and analyse the smoothness and diversity of the generated trajectories.

We ask whether large-scale VLAs trained with the rectified flow objective and no additional regularization can be integrated in a single step at inference without loss of performance.

title: Live Thread Reconstruction for Autonomous Manipulation
authors: Emma Huang,Omar Hernandez,Zih-Yun Chiu,Michael Yip
abstract:
Autonomous robotic surgery has drawn increased attention in recent years due to its potential to relieve surgeons of time-consuming, mentally straining, and tedious tasks, particularly during prolonged operations.
One suitable task for automation is suturing, which involves tracking the thread as it deforms during needle retrieval, de-tangling, knot tightening, and other tasks. Unlike rigid-object manipulation, deformable thread manipulation has no fixed pose to track and effectively infinite degrees of freedom, making its configuration difficult to predict and requiring the thread’s state to be re-estimated rather than assumed. At the same time, thread manipulations involve sequential motions that depend on past and current thread contact points, which must be accurately and continuously tracked. This paper presents an image-to-manipulation pipeline that concurrently generates live thread reconstruction while conducting safe and optimized sequential manipulations to achieve long-horizon tasks.
introduction:
Autonomous robotic surgery has drawn increased attention in recent years due to its potential to relieve surgeons of time-consuming, tedious tasks, particularly during prolonged operations. By improving the speed and quality of surgeries, automation can help treat more patients and mitigate the impact of the global surgeon shortage. One highly suitable task for automation is suturing, which requires complex manipulation of the highly deformable thread during retrieval, pulling, knot tightening, de-tangling, and loop formation. Deformable object manipulation is itself a longstanding open problem in robotics: unlike rigid objects, a surgical thread has effectively infinite degrees of freedom, so its state cannot be summarized by a fixed pose and must instead be continuously re-estimated as it bends, crosses itself, and slides through the gripper. Executing suturing maneuvers successfully therefore requires the thread to be continuously tracked and accurately handled despite highly unpredictable configurations and noisy sensing.

Despite recent advancements, current methods remain limited in their scope and applicability. Many approaches initialize manipulation with the thread or needle already secured in the gripper, entirely bypassing the difficult but critical step of deformable object handling. Other techniques rely on static thread reconstruction [1, 2], which restricts the system to simple manipulations and requires predictable thread configurations to succeed, since re-solving the full configuration space of a deformable thread from scratch at each step is intractable for long-horizon tasks. Furthermore, while imitation learning has been applied to needle pickup and knot tying [3, 4], these models largely operate as black boxes, offering little control over essential safety constraints required in the operating room.

To bridge this gap in surgical robot automation, we propose an integrated pipeline that advances from raw images to autonomous manipulation by live tracking the thread through long horizon tasks. Our approach consists of four primary components: (1) initial reconstruction of the thread, needle, and surgical environment; (2) autonomous, continuous reconstruction utilizing a Kalman Filter for noise reduction and temporal consistency; (3) constrained thread grasp-point optimization based on safety and task criteria; and (4) autonomous thread manipulation to complete the designated tasks.

Our main contributions toward advancing medical robotics are as follows:

Real-time thread reconstruction that remains robust to complex intersections and occlusions.

The integration of thread-gripper interaction modeling to improve both reconstruction reliability and overall manipulation efficiency.

Experimental evaluation of the proposed thread manipulation methods on needle pick-up and knot tightening, demonstrating reliable performance under continuous, live reconstruction.

title: Co^2Gen: Collaboratively Generating Task Plans for Decentralized Multi-Robot and Human Collaboration
authors: Yi Loo,Siddhant Shrivastava,Minh Long Pham,Malika Meghjani
abstract: Visual Language Action (VLA) models are designed to be generalist robot models that can be implemented across embodiments, tasks and environments. However, their ability to collaborate with other robots and humans remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a framework to automate the generation of multi-robot collaborative data for decentralized VLA training without requiring human teleoperation. Our framework first utilizes a decentralized collaborative planning approach to generate multi-robot collaborative robot plans in the form of an executable function. We then utilize the collaborative plan to produce collaborative demonstration data to finetune VLA models in a decentralized manner. We show that our approach produces demonstration data that when used to finetune VLA models on decentralized collaboration tasks matches the task performance of VLA models finetuned on human-teleoperated collaborative data.
introduction:
Visual Language Action (VLA) models [11, 3, 2, 6] unify visual perception, language understanding and low-level robot actions into a single model, enabling them to generalize across embodiments, tasks and environments. Modern VLA models pre-train on large scale human demonstration datasets [18, 10] and utilize Supervised Finetuning (SFT) on smaller task specific datasets for task adaptation [11, 21]. If these VLA models are to be deployed on robots in real world environments, they invariably have to operate in the vicinity or even directly collaborate and coordinate with other robots and humans. However, the modren VLA models’ ability to perform collaborative tasks with other robots or even humans in zero-shot remains underexplored.

In this paper, we show that VLA models, even when finetuned on task specific single robot demonstrations, fail to coordinate with each other on collaborative manipulation tasks as most of the pretrained data of VLA models come from non-collaborative single robot demonstration data. Hence, the VLA models fail to learn to coordinate their policy execution with one another. We then show that finetuning on demonstration data that is collected collaboratively in a multi-robot manner does improve VLA models performance on decentralized collaborative tasks. Furthermore, we extend these results to zero-shot human collaboration as well.

However, the data collection process for simultaneous multi-robot collaborative data can prove challenging due to either additional human cost for each additional robot or the lack of teleoperation interfaces to collect said demonstration data. To bridge this gap, we propose Co2Gen: Collaborative Plan Generation for Decentralized VLA Training for Collaborative Tasks, a framework to autonomously generate collaborative data for multi-robot systems without multi-robot collaborative demonstrations. Our key insight is that collaborative robot demonstrations require the coordination and sequencing of each individual robot’s sub-tasks to be conditioned on the successful sub-task execution and state of another robot. For example in Figure 1, the arm on the right should only perform its sub-task of placing its cube when the cabinet is in an open position. Hence, any collaborative plan would need to sequence robot sub-tasks conditioned on both environment state and sub-tasks of other robots.

Given a collaborative task prompt and environment state, our proposed approach, Co2Gen, first leverages Visual Language Models (VLM) to generate a collaborative execution plan in the form of executable Pythonic function [22, 14]. We structure the plan generation process to be decentralized, where each robot utilizes a VLM to collaboratively propose and refine the generated execution plan using a collaborative Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) process [25, 19]. The resultant execution plans composes and calls on individual skills that are available for each robot and utilizes VLMs as a semantic verifier to check for sub-task preconditions for each robot skill execution.

We then utilize the generated collaborative execution plan to generate collaborative robot demonstration data together with a human verifier to check for task success. Finally, we finetune the VLAs on resultant demonstration data. Each robot’s VLA model is finetuned separately in a decentralized manner from its local data stream. We show that it enables VLAs to match the task execution success rate of VLAs finetuned on human teleoperated collaborative demonstrations. We further show that they also retain the match the for zero-shot human-robot collaboration across manipulation tasks. To summarize, our contributions are:

We show that VLA models fail to generalize to simple collaborative tasks even when finetuned on task specific single-robot demonstrations.

We show that VLA models fail to generalize to simple collaborative tasks even when finetuned on task specific single-robot demonstrations.

We show that collaborative robot demonstrations finetuning massively improves VLA models’ performance on collaborative tasks.

We propose Co2Gen, an autonomous way to produce collaborative robot data through an executable Python function that composes single robot skills into collaborative plans. The collaborative plan is also generated in a decentralized manner by utilizing a collaborative MCTS process.

title: Continuous-Time Motion Planning and Steering with Global Convergence
authors: Mohsen Amiri,Sima Didari,Davoud Ataee Tarzanagh,Hankyu Moon,Yeongdae Kwon
abstract:
Motion planning is central to robotics, and it is increasingly used to
correct the motions proposed by learned planners and policies. In both uses, constraints must hold at every
instant of the motion, not only at sampled times. To our knowledge, no
algorithm provably converges to a globally optimal motion once a
smoothness cost is combined with such constraints. We cast planning and
steering as a single continuous-time program: robots avoid one another and
static or moving obstacles, and a learned proposal is steered by keeping the
motion close to it. The program is elementary to state, yet nonconvex. We
propose GlobMP (Global Motion Planning), a gradient projection method over
piecewise-polynomial curves, on which each constraint is one polynomial per piece that must
stay nonnegative over the whole motion; it alternates cost reduction with
feasibility restoration. Under
mild assumptions, we show that, from a fine grid start, its cost approaches the global optimum as the number of polynomial pieces grows, with every constraint met to any chosen tolerance, or exactly on stable instances. We
demonstrate its superior performance over strong baselines in real and
synthetic experiments, including teams of up to 200200 robots, multi-robot
planning on the Robotarium testbed and an extended benchmark, maze
navigation, and steering tactile-reactive policies on a bimanual humanoid.
introduction:
Motion planning is a fundamental problem in robotics: it asks for a trajectory that connects a given initial state to a goal while satisfying motion constraints, such as avoiding collisions (LaValle, 1998). It underlies navigation, manipulation
(Sundaralingam & Hermans, 2019; Gao et al., 2024; Amice et al., 2024),
multi-robot coordination (Li et al., 2021; Tang et al., 2025; Shaoul et al., 2025),
and, increasingly, the steering of learned planners and policies
(Janner et al., 2022; Carvalho et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023; Giaretta et al., 2026).

Motion planners approach this problem in several ways, each with a gap.
Sampling-based planners explore many routes (Karaman & Frazzoli, 2011), yet
smoothing their waypoints can introduce collisions; optimization-based
planners improve a motion locally
(Zucker et al., 2013; Tedrake & the Drake Development Team, 2019), with TrajOpt (Schulman et al., 2014) also supporting
continuous collision checks. Constraints enforced
at sampled times do not ensure feasibility between them
(Hargraves & Paris, 1987; Figure 1). Convex-region planners search a decomposition
of free space (Deits & Tedrake, 2015a; Marcucci et al., 2023), and semidefinite
relaxations certify a polynomial motion as globally optimal only when the
relaxation is tight (Graesdal et al., 2026). Even shortest-path complexity depends on
the geometry: polynomial-time in the real-RAM model among planar discs
(Chang et al., 2005), NP-hard among polyhedra
in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} (Canny & Reif, 1987), and still open in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} even among disjoint unit discs or axis-aligned unit cubes
(Mitchell, 2017).

Our setting is a point robot in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} that travels between prescribed
boundary states around obstacles while minimizing a smoothness cost; steering a learned planner or policy is the

avoiding collisions; to

a derivative cost such as acceleration or snap is combined with collision
constraints on the whole time interval. We introduce GlobMP and show that, from a fine grid start, its cost approaches the
global optimum as the number of pieces grows, within any constraint tolerance or exactly on stable instances.

title: CMAR-search: Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning for Object Search in Dynamic Interactive Environments
authors: Kaiyao Liao,Qingfeng Li,Xinlei Zhang,Chen Chen,Qing Sun,Jianwei Niu
comment: Published in ICRA 2026.
abstract: Dynamic interactive object search in large-scale human environments presents substantial challenges for existing methods. Current scene representations like 3D Scene Graphs (3DSG) only provide coarse-grained spatial segmentation and cannot identify functional areas such as storage or leisure areas. Without functional area understanding, existing methods are constrained to exhaustive sequential exploration at large scales, resulting in inefficient search behaviors—particularly in open-layout environments with numerous interactive objects such as drawers and cabinets. Moreover, these methods lack adaptability to environmental dynamics such as object relocations. To address these limitations, this paper proposes CMAR-search, a novel framework built upon Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning (CMAR). Our approach leverages commonsense about area functionalities and aggregates environmental memory to construct a Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG), which organizes the environment into functional areas with their associated containers. Through this structured representation, CMAR enables hierarchical action planning at both macro-area and micro-container levels, empowering the system to efficiently identify and inspect semantically relevant areas for effective object search. Notably, CMAR continuously integrates real-time perception, accumulated memory, and commonsense to dynamically relocalize objects in changing environments. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that CMAR-search significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in both success rate and search efficiency for object search in dynamic interactive environments.
introduction:
In human-centered environments, interactive object search is a fundamental embodied AI task where a robot must locate target objects through navigation and physical interaction such as opening cabinets and drawers. This problem becomes particularly challenging in large-scale, dynamic settings that demand long-horizon reasoning and semantic understanding of spatial layouts. Current approaches typically extract environmental information into 3D Scene Graphs (3DSG) that structurally represent rooms and objects [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and utilize Large Language Models (LLMs) for high-level reasoning of robotic actions [6, 7, 8, 9]. However, as environmental complexity increases, these methods encounter several critical issues: (1) In open-layout home environments, existing scene representation methods struggle to effectively segment functional areas, making it difficult to narrow down possible object search ranges; (2) their reliance on atomic actions—such as opening only one container at a time—considerably slows down search processes when handling multiple containers; and (3) they lack robust adaptation to environmental dynamics, showing limited integration of historical memory and object commonsense for efficient object relocation, which significantly restricts their real-world applicability.

First, in decision granularity, our Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG), constructed using object-functional commonsense and spatial relationships, enables LLMs to perform macro-level planning using functional areas as units. The system directs LLMs to generate comprehensive search commands for entire areas at once, significantly reducing the number of LLMs calls and mitigating error accumulation. At the micro-level, these commands are decomposed into optimized sub-steps for inspecting all containers. Our CMAR-based sequence—considering distance, semantic similarity, and risk factors—determines the optimal execution order, further enhancing search efficiency. Second, in dynamic response, the CMAR mechanism synergistically retrieves historical memory and object-functional commonsense to infer optimal search strategies. This framework allows the robot to systematically explore new environments and adapt to changes in a human-like manner, leading to significant improvements in success rate and efficiency in dynamic interactive object search tasks.

This paper proposes CMAR-search, a novel framework for dynamic interactive object search, which introduces CMAR to enable adaptation to environmental dynamics (e.g., object relocations) by synergistically leveraging real-time perception, historical memory, and commonsense, significantly improving search robustness in changing environments.

The framework constructs an F3DSG that organizes environments into functional areas with their associated containers, enabling hierarchical action planning at both macro-area and micro-container levels to efficiently identify and inspect semantically relevant areas, reducing unnecessary exploration in large-scale environments.

Extensive experiments in both simulated and real-world environments demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in success rate and efficiency for dynamic interactive object search tasks.

title: PATH: Preference-Aware Traversability Estimation for Robotic Teleoperation in Off-Road Navigation
authors: Xianghao Meng,Wenshuo Wang,Cheng Shao,Lewei Feng,Qingxiao Liu,Canyu Wang,Junqiang Xi
abstract: Traversability estimation is critical for ground vehicle teleoperation, yet existing methods often neglect the human operator’s preferences for speed and risk tolerance. To address this gap, we propose PATH-Net, a Preference-Aware Traversability estimation Hierarchical Network that adaptively generates preference-conditioned traversability cost maps and speed profiles for off-road teleoperation. Our framework integrates visual and geometric bird’s-eye-view features with short-term historical vehicle states through a multi-head shared-backbone architecture. Our PATH-Net infers traversability cost maps while optimizing speed recommendations by using maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning and sparse speed supervision. Our method incorporates operator preference via an asymmetric feature aggregation mechanism, splitting inference into a cost branch that prioritizes high-risk traversability regions and a speed branch that outputs preference-adjusted recommended speeds. Experiments with 15 operators across 225 teleoperated trajectories show alignment with user-specific navigation strategies, achieving modified Hausdorff distance of 0.17​m0.17\,\mathrm{m} (aggressive) and 0.15​m0.15\,\mathrm{m} (conservative). In the questionnaire assessment, participants reported lower NASA-TLX workload scores with PATH-Net recommendations than without recommendations, decreasing from 34.734.7 to 22.222.2. These results support preference-conditioned trajectory and speed recommendation for off-road teleoperation.
introduction:
Unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) have become indispensable tools for exploration and inspection in hazardous environments, where direct human presence is impractical or unsafe (e.g., nuclear facilities, disaster zones) [1]. While teleoperation remains the dominant control paradigm for navigating complex unstructured terrain, its effectiveness is fundamentally constrained in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) scenarios. Human operators in such settings must synthesize partial information streams, limited to delayed visual feeds and coarse vehicle-state telemetry [2], while deprived of critical physical cues like vestibular feedback and tactile vibrations that enable instinctive control in manned vehicles. This sensory mismatch induces high cognitive load, frequently manifesting as compromised depth perception and degraded situational awareness [3], which collectively elevate the risk of erroneous maneuvering decisions. To mitigate these limitations, there is growing recognition that teleoperation frameworks must evolve beyond pure remote control toward context-aware decision-support systems capable of augmenting human perception and judgment.

Off-road traversability assessment has evolved through multimodal sensor fusion [4]. Pioneering methods primarily utilized exteroceptive geometric information (e.g., digital elevation and 3D LiDAR point clouds) to extract topographic features such as local gradients, discontinuity heights, and roughness metric [5, 6]. While effective for structural hazards, these geometric approaches face inherent limitations when discriminating terrains with analogous structures [7, 8] but different mechanical properties such as soft grass and solid rock. To address this, vision-based semantic segmentation emerged as a complementary solution [9, 10]. Nevertheless, most supervised learning paradigms demand labor-intensive pixel-wise labeling, which constrains their scalability in unstructured environments [11, 12]. Recent advances adopt self-supervision by exploiting proprioceptive signals [13, 14], including inertial measurements, wheel-terrain interaction forces, and suspension dynamics, as implicit traversability indicators [15, 16, 17, 18]. Concurrently, visual foundation models like DINOv2 offer pre-trained feature embeddings that mitigate annotation dependency, demonstrating remarkable transferability across off-road domains [19, 20, 21].

The robotic traversability prediction undergoes a paradigm shift alongside the diversification of sensory data modalities [22, 23, 14]. Early approaches relies on deterministic heuristics, where hand-crafted functions mapped geometric features to traversability scores [24]. Recent methods have embraced data-driven learning frameworks, evolving along three research thrusts: (i) continuous cost representations learning, (ii)navigation behavior imitation, and (iii) policy optimization from sensory observations [25]. Representation learning methods such as HDIF (How Does It Feel?) [15] and Velociraptor [20] extract traversability features from visual-geometric inputs, with some architectures additionally predicting speed constraints. Notably, these approaches address a critical limitation of classical planners by capturing terrain properties that defy pure geometric characterization. Complementarily, inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a principled framework for cost function inference. Maximum entropy IRL and its extensions treat demonstrations as outcomes of near-optimal policies, enabling the recovery of implicit cost functions that explain observed navigation behaviors. This proves particularly valuable for encoding human operator preferences and safety considerations that remain opaque to geometry-based planners [26, 27].

Despite these advancements, directly applying traversability assessment methods tailored for autonomous systems to teleoperated off-road vehicles has two limitations. First, they are predominantly operator-agnostic and platform-centric [28, 29], optimizing for single, fixed traversability metrics (e.g., energy efficiency or vibration minimization) while neglecting operator preference. Although terrain–vehicle interaction determines the physical feasibility of traversal, operators may still choose different routes and speed profiles for the same environment [30, 31]. For instance, a route deemed optimal by algorithms may prove unacceptable to risk-averse operators due to their perceived safety differences. This misalignment between system recommendations and human judgment can erode trust [32] and trigger automation rejection [33]. Second, many approaches rely on static environmental representations, failing to incorporate dynamic vehicle-state context [26]. Vehicle motion states such as speed transients, angular kinematics, roll/pitch dynamics could influence terrain negotiation strategies for human operators. Therefore, historical motion contains complementary information beyond single-frame terrain analysis, particularly for operator’s adjustment anticipation.

In this paper, we propose PATH-Net (a Preference-Aware Traversability estimation Hierarchical Network) for robotic teleoperation, which directly learns candidates of cost functions and speed maps from operator demonstrations. Unlike traversability models that produce a single cost function, our PATH-Net leverages a questionnaire-derived preference parameter to asymmetrically aggregate these candidates, emphasizing upper-tail costs or selecting recommended speed profiles according to the operator preference. This design allows one trained model to generate aggressive, neutral, and conservative navigation advice without training separate models for various operators. This paper’s contributions are as follows:

We introduce a spatiotemporal-BEV temporal convolutional network to dynamically couple terrain perception with vehicle motion history, enabling interactive traversability prediction and yielding kinematic-specific costs and speeds.

Our multi-head network with entropy-regularized IRL unifies aggressive/conservative demonstrations through shared feature extraction and parallel prediction of cost functions and speed profiles.

We introduce a risk-aware approach that employs conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) optimization for upper-tail cost aggregation and quantile-based speed selection, enabling explicit trade-offs between risk and efficiency. A single parameter controls both the conservatism of the cost map via CVaR’s risk threshold and the recommended speed bounds via quantile selection, generating interpretable behaviors ranging from aggressive to cautious.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II formulates the teleoperation decision-support problem and provides an overview of PATH-Net. Section III presents the feature extraction, cost and speed learning, and asymmetric aggregation methods. Section IV describes the experimental platform, dataset, and evaluation protocol. Section V reports the experimental results, and Section VI concludes the paper.
