title: OASIS: Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System for Open-Vocabulary Retrieval and Navigation in Dynamic Environments
authors: Kaiyao Liao,Qingfeng Li,Chen Chen,Xiaoze Wu,Qing Sun,Jianwei Niu
comment: Accepted for oral presentation at ACM Multimedia (ACM MM) 2026. including supplementary material
abstract: Reliable robotic mapping in dynamic real-world environments is essential for embodied intelligence and long-term autonomy. However, existing methods often involve a trade-off: lightweight online mapping is efficient but captures limited semantic context, while dense mapping provides richer semantics at higher computational cost and is more vulnerable to distractors. They also struggle to relocalize objects after scene changes. To address these challenges, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS), a unified system for online mapping, complex open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments. Motivated by the observation that indoor scenes are organized around stable semantic anchors, OASIS represents the environment using a sparse set of anchor nodes, each maintaining a unified multimodal representation that integrates semantic descriptions, visual features, and geometric states for reasoning, verification, and navigation. Its compact anchor-centric memory supports on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval, reducing redundant storage while improving retrieval reliability. To handle scene dynamics, OASIS further reuses transient observations collected during navigation to relocalize moved objects. Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, including standard retrieval benchmarks and navigation tasks under both static and dynamic settings, demonstrate that our system can perform complex open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation, while also enabling relocation of displaced objects after scene changes.
introduction:
Modern embodied agents face increasingly complex tasks in unstructured environments, where instructions involve rich, open-vocabulary descriptions beyond simple object categories. A user might command a robot to “find the sealed silver can on a round table” or “locate the bed with a lit lamp.” Fulfilling such requests requires a scene representation that transcends traditional geometric mapping, demanding fine-grained attribute recognition (e.g., color, material, state) and spatial relationship reasoning. Crucially, these capabilities must remain robust in dynamic real-world settings where objects are frequently repositioned. Consequently, the challenge has shifted from static mapping to constructing a dynamic, semantic-rich scene graph capable of supporting intricate queries and adapting to environmental changes on the fly.

However, deploying semantic maps in real-world systems still involves a practical trade-off between efficiency and reasoning capability. Dense mapping approaches (Gu et al., 2024; Werby et al., 2024; Mirzaei et al., 2025) embed rich semantics into many spatial elements, providing detailed understanding but sometimes introducing clutter and distractors, while also requiring relatively high computational and memory resources. Conversely, lightweight methods (Maggio et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025) are more efficient, but may not preserve enough spatial context for complex reasoning, making it harder to distinguish visually similar objects based on their surroundings or attributes. A remaining challenge appears in dynamic environments. Although some methods address object relocalization, they often depend on repeated re-observation. During active navigation, rapid robot motion and a limited camera view can cause shifted targets to be missed, which reduces the efficiency of these scanning-based strategies.

To bridge this gap, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS) for robust open-vocabulary retrieval and dynamic object relocalization. As illustrated in Figure 1, OASIS avoids processing redundant context globally through an on-demand retrieval strategy. Our key insight is that indoor environments are inherently structured around stable, large-scale objects (e.g., beds, tables, sofas), which we define as semantic anchors. Inspired by human episodic memory, OASIS constructs an anchor-centric graph rather than a dense per-pixel map, retaining only salient semantic descriptions and high-quality representative frames. During retrieval, a Large Language Model (LLM) first reasons over the semantic anchors to filter irrelevant regions, followed by on-demand Vision-Language Model (VLM) verification of the retrieved representative frames. This strategy keeps memory lightweight while preserving the ability to distinguish fine-grained visual attributes. In dynamic settings, OASIS additionally maintains transient observations along the navigation trajectory in a lightweight buffer; if a target is missing at its initial anchor, the system queries this buffer and re-verifies candidate views for reliable relocalization.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We present OASIS, an online anchor-centric scene inference system that unifies online mapping, open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments.

We propose a human-inspired episodic memory curation mechanism that uses scale-aware scoring and spatio-semantic clustering to select representative frames, yielding a multimodal anchor-centric scene graph with integrated semantic, visual, and geometric representations.

Built upon this scene graph, OASIS supports hierarchical coarse-to-fine retrieval and view-driven navigation, and introduces a Transient Visual Buffer to reliably relocalize moved objects after scene changes.

We conduct extensive simulation and real-world experiments on retrieval and navigation under static and dynamic settings, demonstrating strong performance and reliable object relocation after scene changes.

1. We present OASIS, an online anchor-centric scene inference system that unifies online mapping, open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments.

2. We propose a human-inspired episodic memory curation mechanism that uses scale-aware scoring and spatio-semantic clustering to select representative frames, yielding a multimodal anchor-centric scene graph with integrated semantic, visual, and geometric representations.

3. Built upon this scene graph, OASIS supports hierarchical coarse-to-fine retrieval and view-driven navigation, and introduces a Transient Visual Buffer to reliably relocalize moved objects after scene changes.

4. We conduct extensive simulation and real-world experiments on retrieval and navigation under static and dynamic settings, demonstrating strong performance and reliable object relocation after scene changes.

title: Know When to Escalate: Critic-Guided Adaptive Execution for Cloud-Local Embodied Agents
authors: Wei Zhang,Lirong Xiang,Charles Fleming
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract:
Recent advances in foundation-model agents have enabled increasingly capable embodied systems for long-horizon planning and interaction. However, embodied agents require fast, closed-loop decisions as they continuously perceive and act on a changing environment. Deploying strong cloud agents leaves the platform idle for seconds between consecutive actions, while lightweight local models respond quickly but are more vulnerable to errors. Existing hierarchical architectures typically assign models fixed roles, whereas conventional model routers make stateless per-request decisions.
We present CARE, a critic-guided adaptive execution framework that dynamically determines when to escalate control from a local executor to a stronger cloud model. A lightweight critic model monitors execution reliability and triggers escalation when local execution becomes unreliable; once escalated, control persists until the agent recovers, avoiding step-wise switching. To support such control transfer, a shared handoff memory maintains execution context and task-level progress across executors, enabling the model to intervene without restarting from scratch.
Across diverse embodied benchmarks, CARE improves task success by 6.36.3–18.318.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline. CARE further approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.828.8–82.6%82.6\%.
introduction:
Executing long-horizon robotic tasks requires embodied agents to repeatedly interpret observations, select grounded actions, and update their decisions based on action outcomes. Recent advances in generative foundation models have strengthened these capabilities [1, 2, 3, 4], enabling such models to coordinate perception, decision making, and embodied skills as general-purpose reasoning modules [5, 6, 7, 8]. Because model inference lies directly within the perception–action loop, high inference latency can leave the agent acting on stale observations, potentially causing failure in time-sensitive interactions. To balance strong reasoning with responsive closed-loop interaction, recent hierarchical and slow–fast architectures pair powerful foundation models with lightweight local executors or specialized controllers [9, 10].

Despite these advances, long-horizon embodied execution remains challenging because each action affects what the agent observes and must do next. Consider an agent midway through a rearrangement task. An earlier action has displaced the target object, causing the next grasp to fail even though the resulting observation appears similar to the previous one. If the agent overlooks this feedback, it may repeat the same action, lose track of task progress, and compound earlier errors [9, 11]. Execution difficulty also changes along the trajectory. A lightweight executor may handle routine steps well but struggle after ambiguous observations, failed actions, or deviations from the expected state. The appropriate executor may therefore change as interaction unfolds.

This challenge is particularly pronounced in cloud–local embodied systems, where execution must continuously balance model capability against interaction latency. As shown in Figure 1, local models provide responsive interaction but may struggle in difficult states, whereas cloud models offer stronger reasoning at the cost of seconds per decision [2, 10, 1]. Existing hierarchical systems typically assign these models fixed planner–executor roles, implicitly assuming that the designated executor remains appropriate throughout the task. Replanning methods can revise plans or actions in response to feedback, but generally do so without reconsidering which model should execute the subsequent trajectory [7, 12, 13]. Per-query model routing likewise selects an executor independently for each request, without explicitly modeling how executor suitability evolves within an embodied trajectory [14].

We present CARE, a critic-guided adaptive execution framework for cloud–local embodied agents. Rather than routing individual actions independently, CARE uses a critic model to assess whether local execution should continue under the current interaction state and selectively escalates execution to the cloud when local execution becomes unreliable. Importantly, escalation is treated as a stateful control transfer rather than a one-step model selection: cloud intervention persists through the current recovery, avoiding premature hand-backs. Once the critic supports local execution again, control returns to the local executor to recover low-latency interaction. Meanwhile, a shared handoff memory preserves observations, completed progress, and failure context across model handoffs, allowing both executors to maintain a consistent execution state. By combining critic-guided control transfer with stateful handoff memory, CARE avoids both persistent cloud invocation and myopic per-action routing while adapting execution authority to the evolving difficulty of the task.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce a new formulation of cloud–local embodied collaboration as a stateful adaptive execution problem and propose a novel critic-guided execution framework that dynamically determines when execution should be escalated and when local control can be safely resumed.

We develop CARE, a novel stateful execution mechanism that combines persistent cloud intervention with shared execution memory, enabling reliable control transfer while preserving execution continuity across model handoffs.

We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of CARE across three long-horizon embodied benchmarks spanning diverse observation modalities and execution interfaces. CARE improves task success by 6.36.3–18.318.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.828.8–82.6%82.6\%.

title: Decision Making and Ride Comfort Evaluation Based on Lane-Change Prediction for Autonomous Vehicles
authors: Mohamed Manzour,Aditya Kumar,Rubén Izquierdo,Miguel Ángel Sotelo
abstract: Predicting surrounding vehicles’ lane-change intentions enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate potential hazards and respond proactively rather than relying solely on reactive maneuvers. This study investigates the benefits of integrating lane-change prediction, based on knowledge graph embeddings and Bayesian inference, into autonomous vehicle decision-making. Three driving strategies are evaluated in risky merging scenarios simulated in CARLA: reactive driving, prediction-based longitudinal action, and prediction-based lateral action. The proposed prediction model anticipates the surrounding vehicle’s lane change approximately 3-4 seconds before its occurrence, allowing the ego vehicle to adjust its behavior accordingly. In the representative simulation records, reactive driving results in a collision accompanied by aggressive deceleration. In contrast, prediction-based longitudinal action initiates early braking to establish a safe gap, while prediction-based lateral action performs a lane change when a safe adjacent lane is available. Both predictive strategies avoid collisions in the evaluated records. Compared with reactive driving, peak deceleration before impact is reduced by 31.5% with longitudinal action and 91.0% with lateral action. Additionally, an ISO 2631-1-based horizontal vibration estimate is used to provide a ride comfort assessment. Overall, the results highlight the potential of lane-change prediction to support safer and smoother driving through proactive decision-making, with additional insights into ride comfort provided by vibration-based estimates.
introduction:
Lane changes are among the most common driving maneuvers, yet unexpected lane changes can create hazardous situations, particularly when a vehicle merges into an occupied lane with limited space for braking or avoidance. Predicting such maneuvers before they begin gives an autonomous vehicle additional time to respond. However, the benefit of this anticipation depends on the driving decision taken, as different responses may have different implications for safety and ride comfort. Figure 1 illustrates a scenario in which a target vehicle approaches a slower preceding vehicle in the rightmost lane and intends to merge into the ego vehicle’s lane. Without anticipation, the ego vehicle may be unable to avoid a collision. With prediction, it can either brake to create a safe gap or change lanes when an adjacent lane is available.

While avoiding collisions is essential, the resulting vehicle motion also affects passenger comfort. Braking may introduce substantial longitudinal deceleration, whereas lateral avoidance produces acceleration in a different direction. Since discomfort depends on the magnitude, direction, and timing of vehicle motion [1, 4], these responses should be examined beyond their safety outcomes. This study investigates the effects of lane-change prediction on autonomous vehicle decision-making and ride comfort using an existing knowledge graph embedding and Bayesian inference framework [12, 13]. Three driving configurations are compared in CARLA: reactive driving, prediction-based longitudinal control, and prediction-based lateral control. Their behavior is analyzed through response timing, collision outcomes, acceleration, and jerk, while ride comfort is additionally assessed using an ISO 2631-1-based estimate of horizontal vibration.

title: PhysibleMDM: Enforcing Inference-Time Physical Feasibility Constraints on Motion Diffusion Models via Noise Optimization
authors: Maximilian Stölzle,David Müller,Agon Serifi,Ruben Grandia,Espen Knoop,Moritz Bächer
abstract:
Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) can generate diverse and visually appealing human motion; yet, the resulting trajectories frequently violate physical constraints, limiting their downstream use in simulation and control. We present PhysibleMDM, a framework that promotes physical feasibility of MDM output by optimizing at inference time the diffusion noise without retraining the generative model.
We introduce a set of surrogate feasibility constraints that can be evaluated without full trajectory simulation. These constraints combine kinematic checks (e.g., ground penetration, slip, and self-collision) with dynamic feasibility tests computed via an inverse-dynamics inner loop formulated as a cone program. We solve the resulting black-box noise optimization problem using the Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (Sep-CMA-ES), thereby avoiding reliance on computationally expensive and discontinuous gradients. An autoregressive scheme then chains optimized segments to synthesize long motion sequences. Across 100 motion styles on an SMPL humanoid, PhysibleMDM reduces mean ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and ground slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%, respectively, relative to unoptimized diffusion output. Across 11 sequences for a custom bipedal robot, it achieves median reductions of 89.5% in per-sequence mean acceleration-reconstruction error and 79.5% in the mean inverse-dynamics residual.
introduction:
Motion Diffusion Models (Tevet et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2023; Rempe et al., 2026) currently achieve state-of-the-art performance in synthesizing human-like motion for physics-based characters and robots. These generators are typically trained on large corpora of human motion capture data and can be conditioned on various signals, including text, style, goals, and semantic tasks (Dabral et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024a; Huang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). The generated motion commonly serves as a reference for Reinforcement Learning-based trackers (Peng et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2023; Serifi et al., 2024b; Liao et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026). Errors can arise at multiple stages of this pipeline. In particular, generated motions may exhibit physical artifacts that hinder their execution. Kinematic artifacts include joint-limit violations (Lee et al., 2025), self-collisions (Khazoom et al., 2022), ground penetration (Yuan et al., 2023), undesired ground slip (Pan et al., 2025), and foot placement in non-traversable regions (Nguyen et al., 2016). Dynamic artifacts include motions requiring joint torques beyond actuator limits (Herzog et al., 2014) or contact forces outside friction cones (Grandia et al., 2021), as well as trajectories inconsistent with the dynamics of unactuated coordinates, such as the floating base of a legged robot (Herzog et al., 2014; Grizzle et al., 2014). These artifacts degrade downstream tracking performance (Araújo et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026), as infeasible reference motions cannot be reliably tracked.

Several methods mitigate these artifacts before or during training, for example, by learning from motions tracked in physics simulation (Wu et al., 2025; Watanabe et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025), or fine-tuning the generator with physics-informed objectives (Serifi et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2026).
While effective in practice, these approaches can be resource-intensive, particularly when generative models and tracking policies are retrained across refinement iterations, and they do not inherently guarantee that all samples from the final diffusion model satisfy the desired physical constraints.

Inference-time optimization incorporates explicit objectives and constraints during generation without retraining the diffusion model. Common approaches steer intermediate denoising states through gradient guidance (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Karunratanakul et al., 2023) or projection onto feasible sets (Yuan et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2025; Watanabe et al., 2026). Noise optimization offers an alternative in which objectives and constraints are evaluated on fully denoised motions (Karunratanakul et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025). Gradient-based noise optimization requires costly backpropagation through both the diffusion sampler and the physical-feasibility evaluation. Contact-rich motion further introduces non-smooth objectives and constraints for which gradients may be poorly informative (Antonova et al., 2023; Paulus et al., 2026). Sampling-based optimization has shown promise for optimal control of contact-rich legged locomotion (Xue et al., 2025; Alvarez-Padilla et al., 2025; Schramm et al., 2026). Recent work also applies sampling-based optimization to diffusion noise for image generation and protein design (Kim et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2026), but does not address the kinematic and dynamic feasibility requirements of robotic motion. Efficient gradient-free optimization of initial and posterior diffusion noise for these requirements, while retaining characteristic motion style, remains unexplored.

To address this gap, we propose PhysibleMDM, a gradient-free method that jointly optimizes initial and posterior diffusion noise at inference time. Parallel forward passes through the frozen model generate a population of motions for evaluating task objectives, kinematic constraints, and constrained inverse-dynamics residuals. These evaluations guide Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (Ros and Hansen, 2008), whose diagonal covariance supports high-dimensional search, in iteratively refining the noise population. Noise standardization regularizes noise toward its training-time statistics to help limit deviations from the learned motion distribution. An autoregressive scheme chains optimized segments into long motion sequences.

In summary, the contributions of this paper are:

A physical-feasibility formulation for Motion Diffusion Models that combines kinematic constraints with constrained inverse-dynamics residuals, enabling inference-time refinement without a tracking controller or full trajectory simulation.

A scalable sampling-based method for high-dimensional noise optimization in Motion Diffusion Models (realized via Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy), evaluating non-smooth objectives and constraints on fully denoised motions without costly gradient computation.

A diffusion-noise optimization strategy, applicable to any pretrained MDM without architecture-specific changes, that combines joint initial and posterior noise optimization with noise standardization, balancing optimization flexibility against deviations from the model’s learned distribution and supporting motion-style retention in Motion Diffusion Models.

1. A physical-feasibility formulation for Motion Diffusion Models that combines kinematic constraints with constrained inverse-dynamics residuals, enabling inference-time refinement without a tracking controller or full trajectory simulation.

2. A scalable sampling-based method for high-dimensional noise optimization in Motion Diffusion Models (realized via Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy), evaluating non-smooth objectives and constraints on fully denoised motions without costly gradient computation.

3. A diffusion-noise optimization strategy, applicable to any pretrained MDM without architecture-specific changes, that combines joint initial and posterior noise optimization with noise standardization, balancing optimization flexibility against deviations from the model’s learned distribution and supporting motion-style retention in Motion Diffusion Models.

title: Externalise the Memory: A Pre-Registered Study of Where an Embodied Agent's Experience Should Live
authors: Cheng-Yin Tu
comment: . A 5-page version appears at the CL4FMAgents workshop, NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival). Code and pre-registration:this https URL
abstract:
Should an embodied agent’s accumulated experience be baked into its
policy weights, or kept external and retrieved at inference? We test
this directly. A memory-augmented teacher (a VLM that retrieves lessons,
with their episode images, from its own past attempts) produces trajectories on a
vision-conditioned single-arm reach task; from the same trajectories
we distil LoRA student policies and evaluate them under matched
protocols, including one that re-attaches the teacher’s frozen
retrieval buffer to a fixed set of student weights — a clean parametric-vs-contextual-memory contrast on identical weights. Because the
headline result is a null, we pre-registered the hypotheses, arms,
tests, and analysis rules before training and before any pp-value.
Distilling the memory-augmented behaviour into weights beat an
action-only control by only +1+1 pp (n.s.); the registered test proves
underpowered for its own minimum effect, so we withdraw — rather than
refute — the memory-in-weights claim. By contrast, attaching retrieval
to a fixed set of student weights added +34+34 pp (z=5.15z=5.15),
reaching the pooled memory-augmented teacher reference (49.3%); the
pre-registered protocol contrast agrees (+23+23 pp, z=3.36z=3.36); under a
pre-registered auto-reset sensitivity count the two are +36+36 and +29+29 pp.
An exploratory behavioural probe with pre-registered per-arm predictions is
consistent with a mechanism: behavioural distillation transfers the
marginal correction (a static prior every arm adopts) but not the
conditional, situation-specific correction that prompt-retrieved
memory supplies. The recipe that follows is to externalise the memory: in
follow-up controls registered before they ran, the same frozen buffer
lifts the base model with no adapter to 48% (sensitivity 48%) and each
of the other three adapters from 19–26% to 53–55% (sensitivity 17–21%
to 50–55%), so the retrieval effect does not
depend on the adapter, and the adapter adds nothing detectable once the
buffer is attached. On a second, harder task in the same family, the
retrieval advantage points the same direction but falls short of
significance (+6+6 pp, 95% CI [−4.5,+16.4][-4.5,+16.4]); exploratory diagnostics tie
the attenuation to memory coverage and a distance-gated conversion
threshold, suggesting the effect scales with the amount of retrievable
success experience.

title: Integrated Respiratory Sensing and Gated Control for Autonomous Needle Insertion Via CT Bore Robotic Arm
authors: Emma Huang,Moira Bohley,Krishna Jamakhandi,Rebecca Fellbaum,Sophia Tang,Sean Tutton,Albert Hsiao,Alexander Norbash,Changwei Chen,Derek Chen,Ananya Rao,Lizzie Peiros,Michael C. Yip
abstract: Currently, CT-guided lung biopsy is a highly manual procedure requiring patient breath-holding, iterative manual needle insertions, and repeated CT confirmation scans to accurately target a tumor. Automating this process within the CT bore—without relying on manual needle placement or patient breath-holding—has the potential to reduce procedure time, patient discomfort, and radiation exposure. In this work, we present an integrated sensing and control system capable of performing a gated needle insertion within the CT bore. The experiments demonstrate the system’s ability to track and predict patient breath cycles, perform autonomous respiratory-gated needle insertion, and detect breath cycle anomalies.

title: Tactile-Based Robotic Manipulation: From Mechanics-Driven to Data-Driven Perspectives
authors: Jingyi Xiang,Yixuan Wang,Wenzhen Yuan
comment: . Author accepted manuscript. Posted with permission from the Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems, Volume 10; copyright 2027 the author(s), this https URL. Published version:this https URL
abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct access to physical interactions at the contact interface, making it a critical modality for robust and dexterous manipulation. Over the past several decades, tactile-based manipulation research has evolved from mechanics-driven approaches, which explicitly interpret tactile signals through contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning, to data-driven approaches that learn tactile representations and manipulation policies directly from data. This paper reviews the development of tactile-based manipulation from these two complementary perspectives. We first introduce the fundamentals of tactile sensing, and then review, from a mechanics-driven perspective, how those signals form manipulation-relevant state representations and subsequently influence the robot action. We then examine the recent advances in data-driven tactile manipulation, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future opportunities toward scalable, generalizable, and robust tactile-enabled robotic systems.
introduction:
Manipulation is the process by which a robot physically interacts with and changes the state of objects in its environment. Because these interactions occur through contact, many manipulation-relevant quantities—including contact state, force distribution, slip, and local object geometry—can only be observed at the contact interface. Tactile sensing provides direct measurements of these interactions and therefore plays a critical role in enabling robust and dexterous manipulation.

Research on robotic tactile sensing and manipulation has existed for decades. A central question throughout this history has been how tactile signals can be transformed into actionable information for robot control. Early research largely approached this problem from a mechanics-driven perspective, seeking explicit connections between tactile measurements, description of physical interactions, and manipulation actions. For example, tactile feedback can be used to detect slip so as to secure grasp, guide insertion and assembly based on force feedback, or measure local geometry for contact alignment. Although different approaches have been proposed—including analytical models, handcrafted feature extraction, and supervised learning techniques—the common principle is the use of explicit knowledge about contact mechanics and task structure to interpret tactile signals and guide robot behavior. In this review, we collectively refer to these approaches as mechanics-driven tactile-based manipulation.

In recent years, the rapid progress of data-driven robot learning has profoundly reshaped tactile-based manipulation research. In contrast to mechanics-driven approaches, these methods typically do not require explicit modeling of intermediate physical quantities. Instead, they learn task-relevant implicit representations and action policies directly from data, often through imitation learning, reinforcement learning, or large-scale multimodal pretraining. This trend emerged alongside the remarkable success of vision-based robot learning, where end-to-end learning frameworks have demonstrated impressive performance across a wide range of manipulation tasks. Consequently, a major research direction in tactile-based manipulation has become the integration of tactile observations into learning architectures originally developed for vision. This direction is particularly promising because vision and touch provide highly complementary information: vision captures global scene context and long-range spatial relationships, while tactile sensing provides precise local measurements of contact and physical interaction. Recent advances in sensor development, scalable robot learning, and multimodal foundation models have further accelerated this trend, creating new opportunities for tactile-enabled manipulation while also introducing new challenges.

In this review, we examine tactile-based manipulation from both mechanics-driven and data-driven perspectives. We first discuss how tactile sensing captures the physics of contact and how tactile signals can be transformed into manipulation-relevant information through explicit reasoning. We then review recent advances in learning-based manipulation, including imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models that leverage tactile observations as part of large-scale multimodal learning frameworks. By bringing together these two perspectives, we aim to provide a unified understanding of how tactile information contributes to robotic manipulation, identify the connections between classical and modern approaches, and highlight the key challenges and opportunities that will shape the future of tactile-enabled robotics. Owing to the breadth of the field, we emphasize representative works that illustrate major ideas and trends rather than providing an exhaustive catalog of existing research.

title: MPBRS: Multi-Potential-Based Reward Shaping for Unified Reward Configuration in Humanoid Locomotion
authors: Van Chung Nguyen,Hung Manh La
abstract: Designing and tuning reward functions remains one of the main challenges in building effective reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines for humanoid locomotion. While shaping rewards can accelerate learning, naively formulated terms often conflict with the desired behavior, overfit to a specific robot, or become unstable under small weight changes. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) offers an alternative solution: shaping the reward via differences of a potential function to guide exploration without changing the optimal policy. In this paper, we study Multi-PBRS for humanoid locomotion and propose a unified reward configuration. We then evaluate the same reward structure and weights across nine humanoid robots, requiring only robot-specific metadata (joint/link mappings and default poses) rather than per-robot reward redesign. Our experiments show that, compared to standard shaping, MPBRS provides more consistent scaling behavior and reduced tuning sensitivity across robots, making it easier to tune without altering the optimal policy.
introduction:
Recently, reinforcement learning (RL) has become one of the most widely used approaches for humanoid locomotion. The use of RL for humanoid locomotion is due to its ability to learn coordinated, whole-body behaviors that are difficult to design by hand [1, 2]. However, despite the success of RL in humanoid locomotion, its application depends heavily on the reward function design [1, 2]. The design of the reward function greatly affects the behavior of the humanoid robot. For example, when the reward is specified in a naive way-such as a quadratic tracking error or a sparse task-success signal-the agent may learn strategies that maximize the reward while producing unintended behaviors that do not match the designer’s intent [3, 4]. Conversely, well-shaped rewards can substantially speed up learning, whereas poorly scaled or conflicting terms can cause brittle behaviors, reward hacking, unstable training, or policies that only work for a single morphology and fail under small changes in dynamics or sensing. As a result, developers often spend significant time tuning reward terms and weights to reach an acceptable balance between training stability and behavioral quality. This tuning process is further complicated by the sensitivity of humanoid RL to hyperparameters and reward scaling, which makes it difficult to isolate the effect of individual reward terms and tune them systematically. Furthermore, the design of the reward function is severe for humanoid locomotion since it involves high-dimensional control and contact-rich dynamics with foot-ground interactions, and morphology-dependent constraints. Consequently, many locomotion pipelines rely on extensive reward design and per-robot tuning: weights are repeatedly adjusted until training stabilizes and the resulting gait appears plausible. Unfortunately, this workflow is time-consuming, hard to reproduce, and often does not transfer even between similar humanoids. A reward that works well on one robot may require significant modification on another due to differences in morphology, actuation, or physical design.

In [1], Ng, Harada, and Russell proposed a class of shaping rewards defined by differences of a potential function that is policy-invariant in discounted MDPs. This method has appeared in many researchers because it can provide richer learning signals while leaving the baseline task objective unchanged, effectively separating task specification from convergence acceleration.

Later, several follow-up works [5, 6, 7] examined PBRS in RL and concluded that it leads to faster learning. However, this evidence is largely drawn from grid-worlds or other low-dimensional domains. Meanwhile, high-performing RL results in robotics-especially for legged locomotion-still depend on straightforward, manually tuned shaping rewards that provide no policy-invariance guarantees [8].

In this paper, we examine deep RL locomotion in 3D under a unified reward design and test how multi-PBRS compares to standard shaping when deployed unchanged on nine humanoid robots. Rather than delivering large improvements in convergence rate, MPBRS primarily improves training stability and portability, showing lower sensitivity to weight selection and reward magnitude. This reduces tuning overhead and supports more consistent reuse across diverse humanoid designs.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Chapter II covers the literature review, outlining the related work and providing an overview of the method. Chapter III presents the methodology of the potential-based reward shaping used in this paper. Chapter IV provides a system overview, including the case study of nine humanoid robots and the experimental setup used in this paper. Chapter V presents the results of the method. Finally, Chapter VI concludes the paper.

abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models.
A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation.
This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations.
In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step.
Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets.
We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better.

introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs; Pai et al. 2025; Liang et al. 2025; Kim et al. 2026b; Ye et al. 2026) have recently emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies. Built on pre-trained video diffusion models (VDMs; Wan et al. 2025; Ali et al. 2025), WAMs have shown strong generalization to unseen tasks (Ye et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026), adaptation to new robot embodiments (Ye et al., 2026), and skill transfer from human videos to robots (Dyna Robotics, 2026). Their core idea is to leverage the rich spatiotemporal priors learned from large-scale in-the-wild video datasets (Chen et al., 2024; Nan et al., 2024) by training a model to jointly predict future frames and corresponding actions. This allows the strong generalization capabilities of pre-trained video models to extend from future video prediction to robot control.

Recent works have shown that WAMs can achieve competitive performance with a separate action decoder that generates actions conditioned on intermediate hidden states of the VDM (Ma et al., 2026; Dyna Robotics, 2026; Qiu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). These hidden states are obtained from a single forward pass with Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\bm{\epsilon}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) as input.
This design substantially reduces inference latency by avoiding iterative denoising with large VDM backbones, making WAMs more practical for robot control. However, because the action decoder directly leverages these hidden states, policy performance depends on how well they capture future robot-object dynamics.

In this paper, we aim to improve the control performance of the recent line of WAMs that use a single VDM forward pass for action generation.
We start by performing an analysis of how well the VDM hidden states learn meaningful information to generate actions during WAM training.
We first find that VDM hidden states generated from noise already capture information about future robot motion. Specifically, a lightweight probe trained on frozen hidden states can predict future motion primitives, with classification accuracy increasing throughout WAM training (see Figure 1(a)).
Moreover, these hidden states become increasingly similar to those extracted from ground-truth future observations at the same VDM layer (see Figure 1(b)).
These findings suggest that the VDM progressively learns to generate future video representations from noise.
However, a clear gap in future-motion probing accuracy remains relative to representations extracted from clean future observations, suggesting that generating sufficiently informative future representations from noise remains challenging.

Inspired by this, we propose Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework for training WAMs to improve the future representations obtained from a single video denoising step for action generation; see the overview in Figure 2.
We train the VDM through self-distillation to align representations generated from noise with those extracted from ground-truth future observations, encouraging the model to capture richer future information for predicting actions.
Specifically, FRED uses a momentum teacher, implemented as an Exponential-Moving-Average (EMA) copy of the online VDM, to extract the target representations from noisy future observations at the same intermediate layer used for action conditioning.
We further condition the VDM on a short history of observations, providing temporal context that helps the intermediate hidden states better represent future robot motion.
As a result, FRED reduces the future-motion probing performance gap to representations extracted from clean future observations and further improves structural similarity to them (see Figure 1). Notably, this closer alignment with representations of future observations translates into better robot control performance (see Figure 4(c)).

To validate the generality and effectiveness of FRED, we conduct extensive experiments in diverse real-world robotic manipulation scenarios.
We first evaluate FRED on zero-shot environment generalization using a varied set of real-world manipulation tasks, including long-horizon manipulation, out-of-domain tasks, and object grounding.
Our results show that FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs in these settings, improving long-horizon performance from 61.7% to 81.7% and out-of-domain task success from 10.4% to 52.1% at the 14B scale.
We further evaluate FRED on human-to-robot skill transfer by co-training the video model on human videos without action labels, including tasks absent from robot training data.
We show that FRED significantly outperforms competing WAMs, improving task success from 19.4% to 50.0%, while achieving 97.2% instruction-following performance.
These results highlight that FRED improves future representation quality and achieves strong robot control in both zero-shot generalization and human-to-robot transfer.

We summarize the main contributions of this paper below:

We interpret the VDM in WAMs as a future representation generator that produces intermediate hidden states containing predictive information about future robot motion in a single forward pass.

We present FRED, a framework that improves future video representations generated from noise for action prediction through self-distillation using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets, and short-history conditioning for richer temporal context.

We show that FRED consistently outperforms baseline WAMs across diverse real-world manipulation settings: zero-shot environment generalization and human-to-robot skill transfer.

1. We interpret the VDM in WAMs as a future representation generator that produces intermediate hidden states containing predictive information about future robot motion in a single forward pass.

2. We present FRED, a framework that improves future video representations generated from noise for action prediction through self-distillation using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets, and short-history conditioning for richer temporal context.

3. We show that FRED consistently outperforms baseline WAMs across diverse real-world manipulation settings: zero-shot environment generalization and human-to-robot skill transfer.

title: TerraTransfer++: Demonstration-Free End-to-End Planner
authors: Zikang Xiong,Weixin Li,Zhouchonghao Wu,Akshay Rangesh,Saarth Bonde,Grantland Hall,Chen Tang,Yihan Hu,Wei Zhan
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks and real-world deployments.
Its standard training recipe, however, is expensive across all existing paradigms: imitation learning requires fleet-scale driving logs whose behavior distribution only thinly covers the safety-critical tail;
closed-loop reinforcement learning in a photorealistic simulator, while offering diverse behaviors, is bottlenecked by sample-efficiency, per-step cost of rendering, and a forward pass through a large vision backbone.
Self-play in vectorized simulators changes the economics: at millions of rollout steps per second, one can obtain a state distribution with natural diversity in collisions, near-misses, and recoveries that no driving log contains, and a highly reactive policy emerges from a basic driving-quality reward.
Our approach exploits this asymmetry by decoupling learning to drive and learning to plan from learning to see.
We pretrain a single policy by self-play, distill its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher that also plans, and train lightweight adapters on a frozen pretrained vision backbone to reproduce the latent space of either teacher through the action Kullback-Leibler divergence, a batch-relational low-rank structural loss, and, for the planner, a trajectory-matching loss.
Every target traces back to the self-play policy, so alignment never supervises against a logged trajectory: a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames suffices, with no need for the curated expert demonstrations that imitation pretraining is built on.
From this one self-play teacher we obtain two end-to-end students: a closed-loop policy that outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method on the photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark HUGSim, and a planner that reaches 59.459.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard, above every published method including DriveZero-Scale (57.157.1), and 95.595.5 PDMS on navtest, without human demonstrations.
introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving maps raw sensor inputs (e.g., camera
images) directly to control commands. Deep learning and large-scale driving
data have made this approach widely adopted and continuously improved across
benchmarks (Bojarski et al., 2016; Codevilla et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023; Chitta et al., 2023; Dauner et al., 2024a; Zhou et al., 2024).
However, this progress relies on expensive standard pipelines that follow
either of the two routes.

The open-loop strategy draws its behavioral supervision from fleet logs:
imitation copies logged human
driving (Codevilla et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023; Chitta et al., 2023), and open-loop reinforcement
learning (RL) optimizes against logged trajectories (Karkus et al., 2025).
These logs provide millions of multi-camera
hours (Caesar et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020; Caesar et al., 2021), yet
safety-critical events (collisions, near-misses, recoveries, etc.) remain
vanishingly rare in natural driving: at NHTSA crash rates, a collision
occurs only once every ∼16{\sim}16k driving hours (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 2025), so
logging a single rare event can easily cost over $1M in fleet operation
alone (Kelkar et al., 2025). Each sub-route inherits this scarcity in its
own way: imitation can only copy the actions the recorded drivers took, and
open-loop RL never sees how other vehicles would have responded to the
alternative actions it explores. Broadening interaction coverage with human
data therefore demands ever more collection and curation.

The closed-loop framework instead trains inside a photorealistic,
sensor-rendering
simulator (Dosovitskiy et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022; Chitta et al., 2023; Karkus et al., 2025),
where the policy experiences the consequences of its own actions. This
interaction, however, costs rendering and a heavy vision-backbone forward pass
at every step. Co-training multiple interacting agents multiplies these
per-step costs, so most image-based closed-loop work instead trains the ego
policy against scripted or log-replayed traffic, and the behavior
distribution stays close to the logged or hand-designed
content (Dosovitskiy et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022).
These costs confine this route to fine-tuning a pretrained imitation policy,
as in Figure 1, rather than pretraining driving competence
from scratch.

Recently, multi-agent self-play has risen as a promising alternative to offer
the missing interaction: one shared policy controls every agent, so each
policy improvement reshapes the traffic every other agent faces, and the
interactive behavior co-evolves with the policy. Vectorized simulation makes
this co-training highly efficient, executing millions of steps per second on
commodity hardware (Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2026; Seong et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026).
Training requires only a basic definition of driving quality as per-step
rewards: goal reaching, collision avoidance, comfort, and simple rule
compliance. These rewards specify general driving objectives rather than
separate rules for corner cases. The resulting interactions naturally produce
the collisions, recoveries, yielding, negotiation, and overtaking that logged
traffic seldom contains, all without expert trajectories or
behavior-specific rewards.

Despite its promise, however, self-play does not yield deployable end-to-end
driving policies per se, as they observe vectorized scene state rather than
raw sensors. Deploying these policies would require a two-stage perception
stack that recovers their HD-map-style inputs from images. Such a stack
demands high-quality perception, is sensitive to perception noise, and forfeits
the co-optimization of a fully differentiable end-to-end model. As a result,
it has mostly remained confined to traffic simulation rather than an
end-to-end
solution (Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2026; Seong et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026; Konstantinidis et al., 2026; Ahmadi et al., 2026).

In this work, we unite the strengths of self-play and end-to-end driving in a
paradigm that learns driving policies without expert demonstrations. Self-play
learns driving competence without human demonstrations but consumes vector
state; end-to-end recipes consume raw sensors but depend on human
demonstrations, whose coverage of rare interactions is the very gap identified
above. We bridge this gap by decoupling learning to drive and
learning to plan from learning to see, and we never use logged
demonstration trajectories as supervision. Figure 1 contrasts its three stages with the
conventional workflow.

In the first stage, we train a policy πθ\pi_{\theta} tabula rasa
through multi-agent self-play in TerraZero (Wu et al., 2026), our
vectorized driving simulator, in the spirit of
GigaFlow (Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025). One parameter set controls every agent
in every scene. The policy learns from the long-tail distribution of its own
behavior and never imitates a human trajectory. The resulting policy is a
strong planner, scoring 94.1994.19 on nuPlan val14 and 70.8770.87 on the
interactive long-tail InterPlan suite, above every imitation-based planner we
are aware of, and 0.6320.632 human-similarity on WOSAC 2023, on par with the
strongest learned sim agents.

In the second stage, the policy becomes the self-play teacher, and a
trajectory teacher learns to plan from its self-play rollouts. A closed-loop
policy emits one action per step, but planning interfaces and pseudo
closed-loop benchmarks score a multi-second trajectory. We therefore distill
the realized futures of these rollouts into the trajectory teacher through a
flow-matching head. Like the self-play teacher, it still reads vector state.

In the third stage, we freeze either teacher and align a vision student to
it: the self-play teacher yields the closed-loop student, and the trajectory
teacher yields the planning student. The student retains the teacher’s head unchanged and
learns encoders that produce its scene features for road elements and
surrounding agents from images instead of vector states; these encoders pair
a pretrained vision backbone (Siméoni et al., 2025) with learned adapters
supervised by paired (image, scene-state) frames of the same scene. The
teacher’s per-state action distribution trains the student to choose the same
actions. A feature-level structural loss preserves the teacher’s
pairwise similarities among scene features, following the empirical finding
that the teacher’s features are low-rank and redundant (§3.5).
For the planning student, a trajectory loss also matches the plan the trajectory
teacher selects among 1616 samples, so the student learns the selection and needs
none at test time.
The closed-loop and planning students are two interfaces of one self-play
teacher, and neither sees a human trajectory.

Our framework preserves the naturalistic driving competence learned through
self-play. On photorealistic closed-loop benchmarks, the closed-loop student
attains an aggregate HD-Score of 0.5480.548, exceeding every published
end-to-end baseline on every HUGSim dataset split
(Table 1). Likewise, on
NAVSIM, the planning student reaches 59.459.4 EPDMS on the NAVSIMv2
navhard split, above every published method including
DriveZero-Scale (57.157.1), and 95.595.5 PDMS on the NAVSIMv1 navtest
split, above every published sensor-based method
(Table 2). TerraTransfer++ extends our earlier
TerraTransfer report (Xiong et al., 2026) with trajectory distillation, the second stage.

The cost of learning to drive moves upstream into self-play. This one-time
compute is efficient and reusable.
The self-play policy is trained in 96 hours on 16 A100 GPUs, covering over 2.4B
kilometers of simulated driving without human demonstrations. It can then
supervise a range of vision frontends, alignment datasets, sensor stacks, and
downstream specializations.

During alignment, the vision encoder’s only teacher signals are the frozen
head’s per-state action distribution, the teacher’s scene-feature relations,
and, for the planning student, the trajectory teacher’s selected plan; all three
derive from the self-play teacher’s behavior and are computed on a paired dataset of
(image, scene-state) frames. No expert behavior is required anywhere. Any
retained perception labels are policy-agnostic and reusable across frontends.
They are obtainable offline through auto-labeling, which separates this
requirement from the demonstration-collection burden of behavior cloning.
In our case, the encoder is aligned over 1.831.83M paired nuPlan frames plus
300300K HUGSim domain-adaptation frames on 8 A100 GPUs in 10 hours. The
nuPlan paired frames are logged real camera images and the
domain-adaptation frames are rendered once offline, so training needs no
online rendering; rendering in the loop would be roughly 6,000×6{,}000\times
slower than vector rollout (175175k vs. 3030 fps across all cameras).

We make the following contributions:

A novel demonstration-free paradigm for learning end-to-end
driving policies. A policy πθ\pi_{\theta} first learns to drive through
multi-agent self-play in a vectorized simulator. Its per-state action
distributions then supervise encoders that produce the policy’s scene features
from images, with no logged-trajectory supervision at any stage.

Trajectory distillation from self-play. A flow-matching
trajectory teacher learns the realized futures of the self-play teacher’s
rollouts, and the same alignment recipe plus a loss on the teacher’s selected plan transfers it to a camera-only
planner (§2.3 and §2.4). The planner reaches 59.459.4 EPDMS
on NAVSIMv2 navhard, above every published method including
DriveZero-Scale (57.157.1), and 95.595.5 PDMS on NAVSIMv1 navtest,
above every published sensor-based method (Table 2).

A feature-level structural alignment mechanism. We align the
encoder directly with the teacher’s pooled scene features instead of
cascading reconstruction and detection. A batch-relational low-rank
structural loss matches the pairwise scene similarities induced by
the teacher.

Demonstration-free closed-loop driving beyond published
imitation-based end-to-end methods. On photorealistic closed-loop scenarios
in HUGSim, the camera-based closed-loop student, aligned to a teacher that
never observed a human demonstration, outperforms every published
imitation-based end-to-end method (Table 1).

1. A novel demonstration-free paradigm for learning end-to-end
driving policies. A policy πθ\pi_{\theta} first learns to drive through
multi-agent self-play in a vectorized simulator. Its per-state action
distributions then supervise encoders that produce the policy’s scene features
from images, with no logged-trajectory supervision at any stage.

2. Trajectory distillation from self-play. A flow-matching
trajectory teacher learns the realized futures of the self-play teacher’s
rollouts, and the same alignment recipe plus a loss on the teacher’s selected plan transfers it to a camera-only
planner (§2.3 and §2.4). The planner reaches 59.459.4 EPDMS
on NAVSIMv2 navhard, above every published method including
DriveZero-Scale (57.157.1), and 95.595.5 PDMS on NAVSIMv1 navtest,
above every published sensor-based method (Table 2).

3. A feature-level structural alignment mechanism. We align the

cascading reconstruction and detection. A batch-relational low-rank
structural loss matches the pairwise scene similarities induced by
the teacher.

4. Demonstration-free closed-loop driving beyond published

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into embodied robotic planning, combining natural-language goal decomposition with physical execution. However, standard evaluations typically focus on end-to-end task completion in nominal environments, obscuring where and why failures occur across the perception, planning, kinematic, and actuation stack. We present Alpha, a systematic fault-injection and robustness-evaluation framework for LLM-driven embodied manipulation in simulation. Alpha injects calibrated faults across four operational boundaries: perception (sensor lag), actuation (grip slip), kinematics (unreachable inverse-kinematics targets), and planning (planner-output corruption), alongside concurrent fault conditions. To cleanly separate environmental and physical fault vulnerabilities from planner-pipeline sensitivities, we introduce a matched evaluation methodology pairing an LLM agent (Llama-3 via Ollama) against a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner under identical seeds, task geometries, physics parameters, and safety-monitoring criteria across a balanced 150-episode matrix (75 episodes per planner). Across the full matrix, the Scripted Oracle achieves 64.0% (48/75) success while the LLM planner achieves 44.0% (33/75) (paired McNemar p=3.01×10−4p=3.01\times 10^{-4}). Crucially, when excluding planner-output corruption, performance across all physical and kinematic conditions is identical: 55.0% (33/60) for both planners with zero discordant pairs (McNemar p=1.00p=1.00). This demonstrates that physical actuator slip, kinematic reach boundaries, and perceptual staleness affect deterministic controllers and LLM planners equivalently. The aggregate performance difference is driven entirely by planner-output corruption (100% Oracle vs. 0% LLM), isolating the serialization and schema-validation sensitivity of the prompt-to-JSON interface rather than an intrinsic cognitive reasoning deficit. We also audit 169 historical pilot attempts to establish complete discard-bias transparency. Key limitations include a single simulated tabletop pick-and-place task, evaluation on a single local open-weight model, and n=5n=5 sample sizes per intensity cell.
introduction:
Embodied artificial intelligence systems increasingly combine probabilistic large language model (LLM) reasoning with physical robotic execution stacks [1, 2, 3]. In such systems, high-level task planners translate natural-language objectives and perceptual scene descriptions into structured action plans (e.g., approach, grasp, transfer, and release). While recent benchmarks have demonstrated impressive nominal task-completion rates across multi-step household and industrial manipulation tasks [4, 5], these evaluations overwhelmingly measure aggregate end-to-end success in nominal, unperturbed environments.

Consequently, when an embodied agent fails, existing evaluation protocols rarely localize the failure to its causal origin: did the failure stem from noisy or delayed sensor observations, physical actuator slip, kinematically infeasible joint commands, syntax errors at the serialization boundary, or flawed semantic reasoning? In real-world deployments, autonomous robots routinely encounter hardware degraded states, communication latencies, grasp disturbances, and mechanical limits [10, 11]. Understanding how embodied LLM architectures degrade under controlled, reproducible faults is essential before these agents can be safely deployed in safety-critical human environments.

Controlled fault injection provides a principled methodology for answering these questions. In distributed software engineering and cloud infrastructure, chaos engineering and active fault injection systematically subject running systems to synthetic faults to observe failure signatures and evaluate automated containment boundaries [16, 17]. However, translating this methodology to embodied robotic agents introduces fundamental challenges: physical simulation dynamics, closed-loop contact mechanics, non-deterministic language generation, and complex API interfaces must all be monitored synchronously without confounding the agent’s internal control logic.

Furthermore, evaluating an LLM planner in isolation leaves open a critical counterfactual question: is a given failure caused by an intrinsic limitation of the language model, or is it an unavoidable physical consequence of the injected disturbance that would equally thwart any competent controller? Without a strictly matched baseline, environmental physics failures (such as a slippery block falling out of a gripper) are easily conflated with planner cognitive failures.

To address these challenges, this paper presents Alpha, a reproducible fault-injection and robustness-evaluation harness for LLM-driven embodied manipulation in simulation. Alpha couples a modular middleware fault wrapper (ChaosRoboticsWrapper) with a high-rate validated safety monitor, structured telemetry logging, and an explicit counterfactual evaluation protocol. Alpha injects calibrated faults at four distinct boundaries of a manipulation pipeline: (1) sensor lag at the perception layer, (2) grip slip at the actuation layer, (3) unreachable inverse kinematics (IK) at the kinematic execution layer, and (4) planner-output corruption at the planning/serialization layer, in addition to multi-fault concurrent conditions.

To decouple environmental dynamics from planner vulnerabilities, we introduce a matched LLM-vs-Scripted-Oracle methodology. Under this protocol, an LLM agent powered by Llama-3 [20] and a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner are evaluated across an identical balanced matrix of 150 episodes (75 per planner), sharing identical random seeds, scene spawn coordinates, physical parameters, fault formulas, and safety-incident thresholds.

The primary empirical finding of this paper is that across all physical, kinematic, and perceptual perturbations (F1, F2, F3, and Concurrent F1+F2), the LLM agent and the Scripted Oracle perform identically: both achieve exactly 55.0% task success across 60 seed-matched episodes with zero discordant pairs. Physical actuator slip degrades both agents with identical monotonic decay, perceptual lag is accommodated within the grasp tolerance, and kinematic offsets prevent goal placement for both controllers. The overall difference between the two systems (64.0% Oracle vs. 44.0% LLM across the full 150-episode matrix) is driven entirely by F4 planner-output corruption, where text serialization breaks Pydantic schema validation. We show that this divergence isolates the serialization and schema-validation sensitivity of the prompt-to-JSON execution pipeline, rather than an intrinsic defect in LLM spatial or physical reasoning.

Contributions. This paper makes the following contributions:

Decoupled Fault-Injection Architecture: We present ChaosRoboticsWrapper, a modular middleware framework that injects calibrated perception, actuation, kinematic, and serialization faults into a simulated robotic manipulation pipeline without modifying the robot controller or prompt templates.

Synchronous Telemetry and Formal Safety Monitoring: We develop a 240 Hz safety-monitoring engine that enforces formal force thresholds, workspace spatial bounds, and a validated temporal deduplication window (15 simulation steps), distinguishing raw repeated contact scans from unique continuous safety incidents.

Matched Counterfactual Evaluation Methodology: We formulate a seed-matched comparative protocol pairing an open-weight LLM agent against a deterministic Scripted Oracle across 150 controlled episodes, isolating physical environmental limits from planner-specific interface sensitivities.

Empirical Robustness Characterization: We provide an empirical characterization of manipulation degradation under sensor staleness, grip constraint weakening, unreachable kinematic targets, and JSON syntax corruption, establishing that physical failure modes dominate independently of planner intelligence while interface schema parsing forms the primary point of software fragility.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work. Section III details the system architecture and safety monitoring framework. Section IV formalizes the fault taxonomy and intensity calibration. Section V describes the experimental setup and model provenance. Section VI presents the empirical results and statistical decomposition. Section VII audits historical pilot attempts for discard-bias transparency. Section VIII discusses core scientific takeaways, Section IX states threats to validity and limitations, and Section X concludes.

title: Sensorimotor Alignment: A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success
authors: Yunfei Xie,Howard H. Qian,Shiyi Lan,Kaiyu Hang,Chen Wei
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)

abstract:
Robotic foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, which motivates cheap offline proxies for model capability.
The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) [20] suggests that as representations improve, different modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion?
To examine this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment (S2\mathrm{S}^{2}), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model’s sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion.
We find that S2\mathrm{S}^{2} correlates positively with downstream robot task success across embodied model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. S2\mathrm{S}^{2} can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones even before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs).
Beyond this correlation, S2\mathrm{S}^{2} offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs).
With S2\mathrm{S}^{2}, we extend PRH to embodied models and make sensorimotor alignment empirically measurable, offering insight into why an embodied model succeeds beyond its closed-loop success rate.
introduction:
Robotic foundation models increasingly build on large pretrained vision-language models [4, 3], video models [48], and world action models [14, 27, 5]. Yet selecting and evaluating these models remains expensive: the most reliable test is still closed-loop rollout in simulation [29, 32] or the real world [1], where evaluation is slow, noisy, and benchmark-dependent. This expense motivates low-cost offline proxies for robotic capability.

A natural approach is to use existing perception-side proxies, such as visual question answering scores for VLMs [30, 55] or pixel-level video quality for world models [17, 50, 22]. However, these metrics measure passive perception or generation quality, not whether a representation is organized for action [57, 23, 45, 34]. Two scenes may look visually different but require similar robot motions; conversely, two visually similar scenes may demand different trajectories. For robot task success, a model must produce motions of different tasks even for scenes alike. This requires aligning the visual representation with the motor representation.

This perspective connects robotics to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) [20], which argues that as models of different modalities scale and solve diverse tasks, they are converging to a shared statistical model of reality in each of their own representation spaces.
For example, images and text are both projections of a common underlying reality.
As vision and language models scale,
they increasingly agree on the relative distances between data points.
We bring PRH to robotics and ask: can physical motion be viewed as another projection of the world, such that scaled embodied models better align vision and language representations with the structure of robot trajectories?

We test this prediction of PRH: the more capable an embodied model is, the more closely its sensory representations align with its motor representation. In other words, episodes nearby in sensory representation space should also be nearby in motor representation space.

We formalize this as Sensorimotor Alignment (S2\mathrm{S}^{2}), a training-free metric, illustrated in Figure 1. For each episode in a robot dataset, a model’s image and text features form its sensory representation, and the recorded end-effector trajectory forms its motor representation. We measure alignment by comparing each episode’s nearest neighbors in sensory and motor spaces. More overlap between the two neighbor sets means stronger sensorimotor alignment.

In Section 3, we show that S2\mathrm{S}^{2} correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families, in simulated and real-world settings. The correlation is strong for Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) in closed-loop manipulation, indicating that models with higher sensorimotor alignment tend to perform better. S2\mathrm{S}^{2} computed on raw Vision-Language Models (VLMs) also correlates with the success of the VLAs later fine-tuned from them, more strongly than their general visual question answering (VQA) scores do. For World Action Models (WAMs), S2\mathrm{S}^{2} is likewise a better indicator of success than video quality metrics such as FID [17], SSIM [50], and PSNR [18], and for real-robot policies, S2\mathrm{S}^{2} computed offline correlates with physical-robot success under consistent conditions. These results suggest sensorimotor alignment reflects embodied performance better than passive perception or pixel quality.

Prior work has observed several phenomena in VLAs and WAMs only through closed-loop results, without explaining them at the representation level. We use S2\mathrm{S}^{2}  to supply that explanation, as shown in Section 4. For example, fine-tuned VLAs often ignore the language instruction and act mainly on what they see; we find that their task success correlates with the S2\mathrm{S}^{2}  of their vision features, not their text features.

Our contributions are threefold:

Inspired by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, we propose a new view of embodiment: stronger embodied models should align their sensory representations more closely with their motor representation. To test this, we introduce S2\mathrm{S}^{2}, a training-free offline metric that measures alignment between sensory and motor representations.

Across model families, in simulation and on real robots, higher S2\mathrm{S}^{2} goes with higher task success, making S2\mathrm{S}^{2} a low-cost offline proxy for choosing models before closed-loop evaluation.

We further find that S2\mathrm{S}^{2} explains, at the representation level, phenomena that prior work observed only through closed-loop results, making it a diagnostic tool for understanding how design choices shape embodied models.

We make sensorimotor alignment measurable, offering a cheap, representation-level account of embodied model success that closed-loop success rates alone cannot reveal.
