title: Decentralized Bi-Level Optimization for Cooperative Orbital Transportation of a Rigid Payload
authors: Sidhdharth D. Sikka,Revathy Ravuri,Hei Yin Jowett Chan,Tim Echtermeyer,Shaoshuai Mou
subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: The rapid growth of the space economy, alongside increasing orbital congestion and debris, is driving demand for reliable on-orbit transportation of large and non-cooperative objects. Performing such transportation with a swarm of small spacecraft distributes risk and removes the single point of failure inherent to monolithic architectures, but requires solving a non-convex trajectory optimization coupling every agent’s cone-constrained thrust to the payload’s rotational dynamics. Existing approaches span decentralized control laws with asymptotic guarantees but limited constraint enforcement, and centralized and partially centralized planners that reintroduce a single point of failure. In this work, we present a decentralized bi-level framework driven by exact gradients: the problem is split into an inner convex thrust allocation and an outer search over payload torque trajectories. This decomposition yields fuel-efficient solutions quickly, without requiring full NLP convergence, and at short timescales its performance scales with the number of agents. Theoretical convergence guarantees are established, and the method is validated through extensive Monte Carlo simulation, including closed-loop recovery from in-flight faults. These properties make the framework well suited to spacecraft swarm applications.
introduction:
The rapid growth of the space economy has significantly increased demand for reliable and efficient on-orbit transportation solutions, to support both commercial and scientific applications. At the same time, increasing orbital congestion and the proliferation of large debris pose growing risks to sustainable space operations. Addressing these challenges requires transportation technologies capable of safely and efficiently altering the orbit of non-cooperative objects, whose tumbling motion and the limited thrust of servicing spacecraft already make even close-proximity operations demanding [1].

Monolithic mission architectures, with a single spacecraft performing the entire manoeuvre, are costly, risk prone, and lack redundancy. Multi-agent architectures offer a promising alternative, distributing the risk across multiple spacecraft, thereby also increasing robustness and operational flexibility through coordinated action.

While cooperative object transportation with multiple agents has been widely studied across terrestrial and aerial domains [2, 3, 4, 5], including decentralized learning-based [6] and model-predictive [7] controllers for multi-robot payload transport, its application in orbital settings is comparatively limited. Notable approaches include decentralized PD control [8], occlusion-based heuristics [9], back-stepping control for space manipulators [10], and cooperative multi-satellite detumbling of tumbling targets through designed torque control laws [11]. Formation-based methods have also been proposed, such as those by Meng et al. [12], re-framing cooperative transport as a formation tracking problem. However, these methods typically offer asymptotic guarantees with limited constraint enforcement and little attention to fuel efficiency or convergence time; factors that are critical to real-time orbital operations.

Partially centralized architectures have been explored for cooperative transportation tasks in orbit. In particular, mothership-style systems, featuring centralized planning and distributed actuation, have been proposed for missions such as asteroid exploration [13], telescope assembly [14], and orbital debris mitigation [15]. Most recently, cooperative transportation of passive free-flyers by pushing chaser spacecraft has been demonstrated under human-in-the-loop velocity commands, with stability and safety enforced by barrier conditions and thrust allocated by a centralized mixed-integer program [16]. While effective in many scenarios, these architectures concentrate planning or allocation in a single node and therefore remain vulnerable to single-point failures that can jeopardize overall mission success.

Fully decentralized architectures remove this vulnerability by distributing computation and decision-making across the agents, and are increasingly seen as essential as space operations scale up [17, 18]. A mature body of distributed control delivers decentralized transport with force distribution and fault response [12] and fault-tolerant formation flying under actuator loss [19, 20, 21]. However, these methods guarantee asymptotic tracking or synchronization, treats thrust-direction cones and terminal boundary conditions only approximately, and optimize no mission objective such as fuel. The nearest decentralized optimizer [22] uses duality to handle collision constraints between free-flying vehicles, not an objective coupled through a shared payload. Decentralized trajectory optimization with hard constraint satisfaction therefore remains open.

This paper addresses this problem of cooperative orbital transportation involving a rigid body and NN spacecraft agents that must collaboratively manoeuvre the object from an initial state to a desired final state while minimizing total fuel. Each agent is affixed to a fixed location on the payload’s surface and can exert thrust within a constrained angular range.

A constrained optimization framework is well-suited to this problem, as it naturally incorporates relative orbital dynamics, attitude dynamics, actuation constraints, and trajectory boundary conditions. Optimization-based planning has been applied to spacecraft swarms through sequential convex programming [23], reachable-set collision constraints [24], and hierarchical planning over dynamic communication topologies [25], but in centralized or hierarchical settings and for free-flying agents rather than agents rigidly coupled through a shared payload. However, the problem is inherently non-convex due to the coupling between agents’ control inputs and the rotational dynamics of the rigid body. Previous work [26] addressed this challenge using a centralized bi-level optimization approach where the overall problem was split into an inner convex problem that solved for optimal control input trajectory given a torque profile, while the outer non-convex optimisation problem used population-based heuristics to optimize the torque trajectory. This method is still susceptible to a single-point failure due to the centralised approach taken.

In this paper, we extend the previous approach to a decentralized setting, taking advantage of the multi-agent architecture and thereby removing the single point of failure. Rather than treating the outer torque search as a purely heuristic problem, we observe that the optimal value of the inner convex problem is differentiable in the torque trajectory, and that its exact gradient is available at relatively low computational cost once the inner solver has converged. The outer problem is then solved by projected gradient descent with random restarts, and decentralization acquires a precise role: each agent runs an independent restart stream from its own random seeds, so a swarm of NN agents draws NN times as many restarts per unit wall-clock and can therefore reach basins of attraction a single node would miss, and a single max-consensus round over a line-of-sight communication graph delivers the swarm-wide best trajectory to every agent. The same decentralized search is embedded in a closed-loop recovery mode that detects in-flight actuation and communication faults, detumbles the payload, identifies and removes failed agents, and replans with the survivors.

The key contributions of this paper are:

a first-order method for the outer problem of the bi-level formulation introduced in [26], using the exact envelope-theorem gradient of the inner optimal value;

a decentralized multi-start architecture whose solution quality improves with the number of agents; and

a closed-loop fault-recovery mode, made possible by the decentralization of the architecture.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section II describes the problem of interest, its bi-level reformulation, and the equivalence of the two. Section III presents the proposed method and establishes its convergence guarantee. Section IV evaluates the method through Monte Carlo testing against sampling-based and direct-NLP baselines across cone half-angles, compute budgets, and fleet sizes, including closed-loop fault-survivability statistics, and Section V reports the results. Section VI discusses implications and future work.

introduction:
In robotic control, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have rapidly advanced by leveraging semantic knowledge and generalization capabilities acquired through large-scale vision-language pretraining for robot action generation [28, 8, 49, 15, 20]. More recently, research has increasingly explored leveraging future dynamics and predictive and spatiotemporal priors acquired through video pretraining for action prediction and planning [16, 23, 45, 39, 19, 3]. In particular, diffusion/flow-based generative video models have emerged as key pretrained backbones for these approaches, as they can directly generate future visual dynamics [9, 35, 26, 27]. This growing reliance on pretrained video models makes it increasingly important to determine whether they have learned the physical dynamics required for robotic control.

To this end, various benchmarks and evaluation methods have been proposed to assess intuitive physics, physical plausibility, and motion consistency in input or generated videos [32, 11, 25, 7, 48, 2, 46]. In parallel, probing studies have investigated the physical information encoded within pretrained video models [18, 31, 12, 34]. This line of work has also extended beyond encoder-based representation models to the intermediate denoising representations of diffusion-based video generators, showing that physics-related information can be decoded from pretrained representations. However, these approaches primarily focus on predefined physical labels, model-level preferences, or physics-related signals encoded in intermediate representations.
Even when a physical inconsistency can be detected, they provide limited insight into which history-conditioned physical expectation conflicts with the observed behavior.

More fundamentally, physical consistency is not a static visual property of individual frames, but a temporal property that emerges from changes in object identity, state, motion, and interaction across time. Sparse or short observations may therefore miss brief violations or lack the context needed to determine what should have occurred. Likewise, a single plausibility score cannot reveal where the expected and observed dynamics begin to diverge. Evaluating physical consistency thus requires continuously relating local observations to the physical expectations established by their temporal history.

Rather than probing intermediate representations, a natural alternative is to directly ask a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to assess physical plausibility from video. However, Pixels to Principles [6] reports near-chance performance of recent MLLMs in challenging intuitive-physics settings on GRASP [17] and IntPhys 2 [11], despite physics-related cues being recoverable from their visual representations. Similarly, QuantiPhy [22] shows that, in quantitative kinematic inference from video, multimodal models often rely on pretrained world knowledge rather than faithfully integrating visual evidence with the provided physical prior. These findings suggest that current MLLMs are unreliable as direct judges of physical validity. Instead, we use the MLLM for reasoning over temporal context to formulate expected states, while physical consistency is assessed against the corresponding video evidence.

From this perspective, we propose PhysTrace, a training-free framework that traces physical consistency in videos through history-conditioned temporal video-language alignment. As illustrated in Fig. 2, PhysTrace uses the general contextual reasoning capability of an MLLM to formulate the state expected at the current time based on prior observations as temporal context. It then compares this expected state with the actual video observation in a shared multimodal embedding space, thereby tracing physical consistency over time.
By relating temporally separated events, this process enables temporal localization of physical violations while the jointly generated expected and observed states provide an interpretable description of which physical expectation diverges from the actual observation.

title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models
authors: Hossein Resani,Javen Qinfeng Shi
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque.
We introduce Inside-JEPA which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and show that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state.
On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065–.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050–.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking.
An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels.
Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs. .621).
For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.
introduction:
World models that predict in a learned latent space rather than in pixels can ignore what is unpredictable and keep what matters for acting [26, 4, 8], and they now support planning from images and video [5, 49, 7].
Their states, however, are opaque vectors.
A probe trained on relation labels can often read from them whether the cup is inside the bowl, but no part of the state is committed to that relation, so neither a goal nor what the model believes can be stated in those terms, although relations between objects are the natural vocabulary for both [46, 21, 47].
In our real-video evaluations, these relations are geometric predicates computed from 2D entity bounding boxes, so inside denotes an image-plane proxy for containment.

A direct remedy is to build the relations into the state: for every ordered pair of entities, a small vector of soft symbols, which we call relational channels, that the predictor consumes and forecasts like the rest of the latent.
Unlike neuro-symbolic pipelines that read predicates out of a representation with supervised heads [24, 46, 31], such channels sit inside the dynamics and are trained only through the world model’s own objectives, with no relation labels.
Nothing in a latent-prediction objective, however, says what they should mean.
A predictor is as well served by a static code, or by one that changes without tracking anything, as by a code for the relations: the symbol grounding problem [18], inside a world model.
To our knowledge, no prior work has tested whether relational channels in a world model learn meaningful relationships from real videos, or which training signals help them do so.

We study this question with Inside-JEPA ().
Our method adds one term to the JEPA objective, an inverse-dynamics loss in which a head must recover the action from the relational channels before and after it, so that the action labels an action-conditioned world model consumes anyway must explain how its relational channels change.
To find out what grounds the channels, we compare five models that differ only in whether and where the inverse gradient enters the state and in whether its targets are shuffled (Fig. 2), plus label-free and label-fraction controls.
Because post-hoc channel matching makes it easy to find meaning that is not there, each relation is matched to a single channel, and every model is also scored with its relation head replaced by a randomly initialised one, which sees the same box geometry (Fig. 3).

Across a controlled 2-D world, Something-Something V2 with Something-Else boxes [13, 32], RH20T robot episodes [12] and objects found by an off-the-shelf detector and tracker [28, 37], the pattern is the same (Fig. 4).
Latent prediction alone leaves the channels at or near the level of a random relation head, or below it.
Inverse dynamics grounds them: matched relational AUROC rises by .065–.103 in ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on robot episodes with end-effector actions and held-out tasks, and by .050–.061 with tracked objects on five relations; the gain is positive in all 18 settings of Fig. 4 and smallest with tracked objects on thirteen relations and with a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder (+.016 to +.042).
What grounds them is correct action labels that the channels themselves must explain: an inverse head on the entity latents decodes the action best of all models yet barely moves the channels, and shuffled labels, two label-free objectives and labels on 5% of the pairs do not ground them.
The grounded channels are useful: given an action, their forecasts of the relations that change score almost as well as the observed future, and a readout of the 16 channels selects actions towards relational goals better than a readout of the prediction-only model’s whole latent (top-5 .425 vs. .244, frequency prior .174).

Our contributions are:

Inside-JEPA, a JEPA world model with relational channels inside its latent state, and evidence that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground those channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone (INV-S) or as part of the full state (INV-Z) (Sec. 3).

A controlled account of what grounds the channels: five models that differ only in their inverse head, on two datasets with two kinds of action and with automatically found objects, scored by one-to-one matched AUROC and against a random relation head. Grounding needs an inverse head that reads the channels and correct action labels on thousands of pairs; latent prediction, shuffled labels and two label-free losses do not ground them (Secs. 5.1 and 5.2).

Uses and limits of the grounded channels: action-conditioned forecasting and one-step action selection towards relational goals on Something-Else, and a measured account of where grounding stops: left/right, a distributed code, a stronger encoder and a supervised ceiling (Secs. 5.3 and 5.4).

title: Navigating human-robot interaction challenges in private and residential aged care homes
authors: David Ahmedt-Aristizabal,Mohammad Ali Armin,Akila Pemasiri,Harshala Gammulle,Tharindu Fernando,David Silvera-Tawil,Simon Denman
subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Author-accepted manuscript of a book chapter published online in Elsevier's Reference Module in Materials Science and Materials Engineering (2026). Scheduled for inclusion in Comprehensive Robotics for Extreme and Challenging Environments (June 2027)
abstract:
This chapter explores how robotic systems and ambient intelligence can enhance care for older adults in residential aged care (RAC) homes and private homes. Although these settings differ, we frame both as extreme and challenging environments for human–robot interaction (HRI), characterised by cluttered and dynamic layouts, diverse resident needs, and limited on-site technical support. We review embodied and non-embodied systems that assist with daily living, safety monitoring, and social engagement, highlighting hybrid deployments where robots complement fixed and wearable sensors.
To ensure these technologies are usable and effective, design considerations consider the cognitive, physical, and social needs of older adults. Interaction design prioritises accessibility for older adults with low digital literacy, using robust but simple voice interfaces, small sets of non-verbal cues, accessible screen-based companions, and safe object handovers.
Privacy, trust, and acceptability are addressed via practical strategies such as on-device inference, data minimisation, visible consent controls, and transparent data handling aligned with emerging artificial intelligence (AI) and privacy regulation.
Evaluation emphasises real-world metrics including false alarms per day, time to recover from faults, staff workload, and long-term system reliability. We close by outlining open research challenges and future directions for scalable, regulation-ready deployments that support aging with dignity, safety, and independence.

title: Sensitive dependence of the motion of a legged robot on granular media
authors: Chen Li,Paul B. Umbanhowar,Haldun Komsuoglu,Daniel E. Koditschek,Daniel I. Goldman
subjects: Biological Physics (physics.bio-ph); Other Condensed Matter (cond-mat.other); Soft Condensed Matter (cond-mat.soft); Robotics (cs.RO); Quantitative Methods (q-bio.QM)
abstract: Legged locomotion on flowing ground (e.g. granular media) is unlike locomotion on hard ground because feet experience both solid- and fluid-like forces during surface penetration. Recent bio-inspired legged robots display speed relative to body size on hard ground comparable to high performing organisms like cockroaches but suffer significant performance loss on flowing materials like sand. In laboratory experiments we study the performance (speed) of a small (2.3 kg) six-legged robot, SandBot, as it runs on a bed of granular media (1 mm poppy seeds). For an alternating tripod gait on the granular bed, standard gait control parameters achieve speeds at best two orders of magnitude smaller than the 2 body lengths/s (≈60\approx 60 cm/s) for motion on hard ground. However, empirical adjustment of these control parameters away from the hard ground settings, restores good performance, yielding top speeds of 30 cm/s. Robot speed depends sensitively on the packing fraction ϕ\phi and the limb frequency ω\omega, and a dramatic transition from rotary walking to slow swimming occurs when ϕ\phi becomes small enough and/or ω\omega large enough. We propose a kinematic model of the rotary walking mode based on generic features of penetration and slip of a curved limb in granular media. The model captures the dependence of robot speed on limb frequency and the transition between walking and swimming modes but highlights the need for a deeper understanding of the physics of granular media.
